The doctrinal precision is in the recognition that 時 already carries — through its etymological structure of the sun's motion marked by ritual institution — the sense of articulated rather than abstract time. Dōgen's appropriation of 時 in 有時 leverages this register: time is always this time, this occasion, this concrete moment in which being is being and time is timing. The Uji fascicle works out the implications across multiple registers — the mountain is time, the standing-on-the-summit is time, the monk passing through the marketplace is time — each particular being is the timing of its being, and time is the being of its timing. The doctrinal claim is structurally distinct from any container-conception of time (time as the receptacle in which beings appear) and from any extrusion-conception of time (time as what flows past the static observer): 時 in Dōgen's articulation is the very mode of being's articulation.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, mapped onto the native Japanese word とき (toki, time) from the earliest stratum of Japanese literacy. Its ordinary use across Japanese is continuous and pervasive, covering both abstract duration and the particular moment. Its Dōgen-specific philosophical use in 有時 enters the Japanese vocabulary in the Kamakura period as one of the most technically dense compounds in the Shōbōgenzō, and the Uji fascicle's articulation of being-time has become — particularly through the modern reception of Dōgen's philosophy in twentieth-century Japanese and Western philosophy — one of the central reference points for cross-cultural philosophical dialogue about the nature of time.

gloss: To manifest, to appear, to become present — the polished surface of jade revealing what was internal; in Dōgen's 現成公案 the verb of full manifestation, the present already accomplished as the koan it is.

components.meaning: jade radical (4 strokes — variant of 玉 used as a left-side radical) — the semantic anchor: the polished stone whose worked surface reveals its inner pattern
to see (7 strokes) — phonetic and semantic: the act of seeing that the polished jade makes possible; the manifestation as that which is seen, not as an inner content imagined behind the surface

graphic_evolution.form_description: 玉 (jade) on the left beside 見 (to see) on the right — the composition names the manifestation that occurs when the polished jade makes its inner pattern available to sight
graphic_evolution.notes: The original concrete sense is the becoming-visible of jade's inner pattern through polishing — the patterning that was always there in the stone is brought to the surface where it can be seen. From this concrete sense the character extends to: to manifest, to appear, to become present, the present moment, the actual. The semantic logic carries throughout: 現 names not a making-something-from-nothing but a bringing-out-to-visibility of what was already there.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 11 strokes — 王 (jade radical, 4 strokes) on the left beside 見 (7 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 現 is widely productive: 現在 (genzai, the present), 現実 (genjitsu, reality, the actual), 現代 (gendai, the contemporary period), 現象 (genshō, phenomenon — the Meiji coinage for Phänomen), 表現 (hyōgen, expression), 出現 (shutsugen, appearance). The kun reading あらわれる (arawareru, to appear) names the appearing register in native Japanese. Dōgen's compound 現成 (genjō, manifestation-completion) deploys 現 in its precise sense of the already-accomplished present, and the celebrated fascicle title 現成公案 stages this register at its most technical.

doctrinal_notes: In Dōgen's 現成公案 (genjōkōan, the manifest fundamental point), 現 names the dimension of full present manifestation. The compound 現成 is doctrinally calibrated: 現 names the manifestation, 成 names the completion, and the compound names the present-already-completed condition in which reality stands forth as it is. The doctrinal stake is precise: the koan is not a problem to be solved nor a hidden truth to be uncovered, but the present moment of practice-realization itself, fully manifest and already complete in its standing-forth. The character's etymological resonance — the bringing-to-visibility of what was already in the jade — is doctrinally active in Dōgen's use: realization is not the production of a new condition but the manifestation of the always-already-the-case in the structure of practice. The compound also figures in the Meiji coinage 現象 (genshō, phenomenon) for Western philosophical translation, but the Dōgen-Zen and the Meiji-philosophical registers are doctrinally distinct and should not be conflated.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the early stratum of Buddhist scriptural transmission. Its Buddhist use is broad — 現世 (genze, the present world), 現報 (genpō, the immediate karmic result of an action) — and continuous from the Nara period. Its Dōgen-specific philosophical use in 現成公案 enters the Japanese vocabulary in the Kamakura period as one of the most technically dense compounds in the Shōbōgenzō. Its Meiji-period use in 現象 (Nishi Amane's coinage for Phänomen) opens a parallel philosophical register that runs alongside but doctrinally distinct from the Dōgen-Zen register; both registers are operative in modern Japanese philosophical writing, and the precise reading of 現 in any given context depends on the doctrinal frame of the discourse.

gloss: Not, non-, against — two wings spread oppositely from a central spine; in Dōgen's 非思量 the negative that opens a third register beyond thinking and not-thinking.

graphic_evolution.form_description: Two wings spread outward in opposite directions from a central spine — a pictograph of birds' wings extended in flight or of two things turned away from each other
graphic_evolution.notes: The original pictographic origin names opposition or facing-away — the two wings extending in opposite directions from the bird's body. From this concrete sense the character extends through classical Chinese usage to: not, the negation of identity (X is not Y), wrong, opposed, against. Doctrinally important: 非 is a negation distinct from 不 (the privative negative of arising/asserting) and 無 (the existential negative of absence). 非 specifically negates the predicate-relation: it is the negation of identity, of the X-is-Y structure.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 8 strokes — a vertical structure with paired horizontal extensions on either side of a central spine, preserving the original symmetry of the two opposing wings
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 非 is productive across compounds: 非常 (hijō, extraordinary, lit. 'not ordinary'), 非情 (hijō, unfeeling, lit. 'without feeling'), 是非 (zehi, right and wrong), 非難 (hinan, criticism). The character functions productively as a prefixed negative: 非公式 (hi-kōshiki, unofficial), 非合法 (hi-gōhō, illegal). The Dōgen-Zen technical use in 非思量 (hishiryō, non-thinking) deploys 非 in its precise sense as the third-register negative — neither the affirmation 思量 (shiryō, thinking) nor the privative 不思量 (fushiryō, not-thinking), but the opening of a register that includes and exceeds both.

doctrinal_notes: In Dōgen's 非思量 (hishiryō, non-thinking), 非 carries doctrinal weight that the choice of any other negative would not carry. The Yaoshan dialogue from which Dōgen takes the term distinguishes three registers: 思量 (shiryō, thinking) names the active discursive register; 不思量 (fushiryō, not-thinking) names the privative absence of thinking; 非思量 (hishiryō, non-thinking) names a third register that is neither thinking nor its mere absence but the awareness in which thinking arises and falls away without being either deployed or suppressed. Dōgen articulates this register in the Fukanzazengi as the proper mode of awareness in zazen: 'think non-thinking' (思量箇不思量底如何思量 — 非思量, how do you think non-thinking? — non-thinking). The doctrinal precision is in 非's function as the negation of identity rather than the negation of presence: hishiryō is not the absence of thinking but the absence of the X-is-thinking structure, the suspension of the predicative grammar that constitutes ordinary mental activity. The character also figures across other Buddhist negative-theological compounds — 非有非無 (neither being nor non-being), 非空非色 (neither emptiness nor form) — where the third-register negation operates with the same precision.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the earliest stratum of literate culture. Its function as a productive negative prefix is continuous across the history of Japanese writing. Its Buddhist-scholastic use in catuṣkoṭi-style negations (the four-cornered negation pattern of Madhyamaka logic) arrives with the Nara-period scriptural transmission and is operative across Mahāyāna technical vocabulary. Its Dōgen-specific use in 非思量 enters the Japanese vocabulary as a Sōtō technical term mediating Yaoshan's Tang-dynasty dialogue and remains the central reference point for the Sōtō articulation of awareness in zazen.

gloss: To think, to consider — the heart-mind doing its discursive work; in 非思量 the verb whose negation Dōgen uses to name the awareness that includes and exceeds discursive thinking.

components.meaning: in this character a graphic variant of 囟 (the fontanelle, the soft spot at the top of an infant's head; the seat of the brain in Chinese folk anatomy) (5 strokes) — semantic element: the brain as the upper seat of cognition

heart radical (4 strokes) — semantic element: the heart-mind as the lower seat of cognition; together with the upper element naming the unified cognitive activity that the Chinese tradition locates across both organs

graphic_evolution.form_description: 囟 (fontanelle, the head/brain) above 心 (heart) — the composition names the cognitive activity that takes place across head and heart
graphic_evolution.notes: The original composition is doctrinally interesting: Chinese folk anatomy locates cognition in both the brain (the upper element) and the heart-mind (the lower element), and the character 思 names the activity that takes place across both organs. From this concrete-anatomical sense the character extends to: to think, to consider, to long for, to remember. The upper element 囟 has been graphically simplified to 田 in the modern character, obscuring the original anatomical reading.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 9 strokes — 田 (graphic simplification of 囟, 5 strokes) above 心 (heart, 4 strokes)
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 思 is productive across cognitive vocabulary: 思う (omou, to think, to feel), 思想 (shisō, thought, ideology), 思考 (shikō, thinking, contemplation), 意思 (ishi, intention), 思索 (shisaku, speculation, philosophical reflection). The kun reading おもう (omou) covers both 'to think' and 'to feel,' preserving the original heart-and-brain unity that the etymological composition encodes. The Dōgen-Zen technical use in 思量 (shiryō, discursive thinking) and 非思量 (hishiryō, non-thinking) deploys 思 in its precise sense as the active-discursive register of cognition that zazen-awareness suspends.

doctrinal_notes: In Dōgen's 非思量 (hishiryō, non-thinking) and 思量 (shiryō, thinking), 思 names the active-discursive register of cognition — the engaged mental activity in which thoughts are deployed, judgments are made, and discursive reasoning unfolds. The doctrinal precision of the Sōtō articulation depends on distinguishing 思 (the active thinking) from the broader cognitive activity that includes the awareness in which thinking arises and falls away: zazen-awareness is not the absence of cognitive activity but the cognitive register that includes thinking without being deployed as thinking. The Yaoshan dialogue from which Dōgen takes 非思量 stages this distinction precisely — when asked what one thinks while sitting in steadfast composure, Yaoshan answers that one thinks the non-thinkable; when asked how one thinks the non-thinkable, he answers 非思量 — and the doctrinal point is that 思 names the register that 非思量 includes-and-exceeds rather than absents.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, mapped onto the native Japanese verb おもう (omou, to think, to feel) from the earliest stratum of Japanese literacy. Its ordinary use is continuous and broad, covering both cognitive thinking and affective feeling in the unified register that the native verb names. Its Buddhist-scholastic use in compounds for cognition and reflection arrives with the Nara-period transmission of Buddhist scholastic literature. Its Dōgen-specific use in 思量 and 非思量 enters the Japanese vocabulary in the Kamakura period as a Sōtō technical pair, articulated centrally in the Fukanzazengi and the Zazenshin fascicle of the Shōbōgenzō, and remains the central reference point for the Sōtō articulation of awareness in seated meditation.

gloss: To measure, to weigh, quantity — a vessel set on a scale; in 思量 paired with 思 to name the calculative-discursive mode of mental activity that zazen-awareness suspends.

components.meaning: in this character a graphic variant of an upper element depicting the lid or top of a vessel (4 strokes) — semantic element: the upper portion of the measuring instrument
village, league (7 strokes) — phonetic and partly semantic element providing the liáng sound; itself a measure of distance, contributing the sense of bounded measurement

graphic_evolution.form_description: A vessel set on a stand or scale — the original pictograph of a measuring instrument
graphic_evolution.notes: The original concrete sense is a measuring vessel — the standardized container by which grain or liquid is measured. From this concrete sense the character extends through classical Chinese to: to measure, to weigh, capacity, quantity, the calculative reckoning of amounts. The semantic logic preserves a precise relation between the act of measurement and what is measured: 量 names the activity of weighing-and-comparing, the calculative reduction of qualitative reality to quantitative comparison.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 12 strokes — an upper element preserved as 日 (graphically) above 里 (7 strokes)
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 量 is productive across quantitative vocabulary: 量 (ryō, amount, quantity), 計量 (keiryō, measurement), 大量 (tairyō, large quantity), 質量 (shitsuryō, mass), 量子 (ryōshi, quantum). The kun reading はかる (hakaru) names the act of measuring in native Japanese. The Dōgen-Zen technical compound 思量 (shiryō, thinking) deploys 量 in its precise sense of the calculative-comparative register, where 思 names the cognitive activity and 量 names its calculative-quantitative character — together naming the discursive-comparative mode of mental activity that zazen-awareness suspends.

doctrinal_notes: In 思量 (shiryō) and 非思量 (hishiryō), 量 carries the precise sense of calculation, comparison, and discursive reckoning. The choice of 量 rather than a broader cognitive character is doctrinally calibrated: 思量 names not all mental activity but specifically the calculative-comparative mode in which the mind weighs alternatives, reckons quantities, judges between possibilities. 非思量 is the suspension not of all awareness but specifically of this calculative register — the awareness that remains in zazen is fully present and fully cognitive but is not deployed in the calculative-comparative mode that 思量 names. The doctrinal stake is on this precision: hishiryō is not non-cognition but non-calculation, the awareness that includes thinking-as-it-arises without being deployed as calculative weighing.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the early stratum of literate culture. Its ordinary use across Japanese is broad and continuous, covering measurement, weighing, and quantitative reckoning. Its Buddhist-scholastic use in compounds for cognition and judgment arrives with the Nara-period transmission. Its Dōgen-specific use in 思量 and 非思量 enters the Japanese vocabulary in the Kamakura period as a Sōtō technical pair and remains stable across the tradition's articulation of awareness in seated meditation, with the Fukanzazengi's framing of 思量箇不思量底 (think the non-thinkable) as the locus classicus of the Sōtō handling of the term.

gloss: To cultivate, to practice, to refine — a person engaged in sustained, disciplined activity that polishes and perfects; in Buddhist usage the verb of cultivation that 修証 holds in inseparable identity with realization.

components.meaning: person radical (2 strokes) — semantic element: a person engaged in the cultivating activity
long, distant (7 strokes) — phonetic and partly semantic element providing the xiū sound; carries the sense of sustained extension that cultivation requires
delicate hairs, ornament (3 strokes) — semantic element: the polishing or refining strokes that complete the cultivating action

graphic_evolution.form_description: 亻 (person) on the left, 攸 (sustained extension) and 彡 (refining strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense combines the figure of a person in sustained activity (亻 + 攸) with the refining strokes of 彡: cultivation as the disciplined polishing of what one is across time. From this concrete sense the meanings 'to cultivate, to repair, to study, to practice' all develop.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 10 strokes — preserves the tripartite structure
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 修 carries the wide range of cultivation, study, and self-discipline: 修行 (shugyō, ascetic practice), 修学 (shūgaku, schooling), 修養 (shūyō, self-cultivation), 修理 (shūri, repair). In Buddhist usage 修 names the active verb of practice in compounds such as 修行, 修禅 (shuzen, Zen practice), and Dōgen's signature compound 修証一等 (shushō ittō, the oneness of practice and realization).

doctrinal_notes: In 修証一等 (shushō ittō), 修 names the verb of cultivation that the compound holds in inseparable identity with 証 (realization). The Sōtō articulation is that 修 is not an instrumental activity that produces 証 as its result but is itself the temporal-active expression of 証. Dōgen's calibration of 修 in this compound is precise: cultivation is not means to an end but the present-active form in which realization is realized. The character carries enormous doctrinal weight in the Sōtō tradition as the marker of the practice-side of the practice-realization unity, and Dōgen's articulation across the Bendōwa, the Genjōkōan, and the Gyōji fascicle treats 修 as the central technical term for the active dimension of the awakened mode of being.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its general meaning of cultivation and study. Its Buddhist register develops with the early scholastic transmission and is consolidated in the Heian period. Its load-bearing Sōtō use in 修証一等 belongs specifically to Dōgen's vocabulary, and the character has remained the principal marker of the practice-pole of practice-realization across the Sōtō tradition's articulation of the Way.

gloss: To witness, to verify, to realize — speech that proves what is the case; in Buddhist usage the experiential verification of awakening, distinct from the discursive proof of Western epistemology.

components.meaning: speech, word radical (7 strokes) — semantic element: the register of articulated testimony, the word that bears witness
correct, upright (5 strokes) — phonetic and semantic element providing the zhèng sound; the rectitude of what is verified, the uprightness of the testimony

graphic_evolution.form_description: 言 (speech) on the left, 正 (upright) on the right — articulated testimony of what is correct
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense joins the register of speech (言) with the rectitude of 正 to name the act of testifying to what is the case. From this concrete sense the meanings 'to witness, to verify, to prove, to attest' all develop. The traditional form 證 (with 登 on the right) was simplified to 証 in modern Japanese script reform; Chinese kept 證 in traditional contexts and uses 证 as the simplified form.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 12 strokes — modern Japanese form 証
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 証 covers the range of attestation: 証拠 (shōko, evidence), 証明 (shōmei, proof), 証言 (shōgen, testimony), 保証 (hoshō, guarantee). In Buddhist usage 証 names the experiential verification of awakening: 証悟 (shōgo, awakened verification), 証果 (shōka, fruit of realization), and Dōgen's 修証一等 (shushō ittō, the oneness of practice and realization).

doctrinal_notes: In Buddhist usage 証 carries a register distinct from Western epistemology's notion of proof. 証 is not the discursive demonstration that argues from premises to conclusion but the experiential verification by which the practitioner stands as witness to what awakening is. In the Chan/Zen tradition 証 names the moment in which the practitioner directly verifies the dharma in their own experience — not as inference from a teacher's claim but as first-person attestation. Dōgen's 修証一等 deploys 証 as the realization-pole of the practice-realization unity: 証 names not a result that practice produces but the awakened condition that practice is the active expression of. The character's etymological structure — articulated testimony of what is upright — preserves the witness-grammar that distinguishes Buddhist verification from Western proof.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the early Buddhist transmission in its scholastic register of verification and attestation. The Sōtō articulation of 証 in 修証一等 belongs specifically to Dōgen's Kamakura-period vocabulary, and the character has remained the principal marker of the realization-pole of practice-realization across the Sōtō tradition. The post-war script reform replaced the traditional 證 with the modern 証 across general usage; the older 證 form remains visible in pre-reform editions of the Shōbōgenzō and in Chinese-language transmissions.

gloss: Equal, of the same rank — bamboo strips of identical length used to mark sameness; in 修証一等 the qualifier of the structural identity of practice and realization.

components.meaning: bamboo radical (6 strokes) — semantic element: the bamboo strips that, when of identical length, mark sameness or equivalent rank
temple, court (6 strokes) — phonetic element providing the děng sound; partly semantic in the official-rank register, the formal grading of court positions

graphic_evolution.form_description: 竹 (bamboo) above 寺 (court) — bamboo strips of equal length used to mark official rank
graphic_evolution.notes: The original referent is bamboo strips cut to identical length to indicate the rank of officials at court. From this concrete sense the meanings 'equal, same rank, of the same kind, equivalent' all develop. By the classical period 等 functions as the standard marker of equivalence and as a pluralizer (e.g., 我等 'we, us').

graphic_evolution.form_description: 12 strokes — preserves the bamboo-over-court structure
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 等 functions both as the marker of equivalence (平等 byōdō, equality; 同等 dōtō, equivalence) and as a pluralizer (など, etc.). In Buddhist usage 等 names the equivalence at issue in compounds like 平等 (the equality of all beings before buddha-nature) and Dōgen's 修証一等 (the structural sameness of practice and realization).

doctrinal_notes: In 修証一等 (shushō ittō), 一等 names not numerical sameness but the structural identity of practice and realization. The character carries the precise sense of 'of the same rank, of one and the same kind' — not that practice and realization are two things that happen to be equal, but that they belong to the same structural rank, the same kind, the same condition. Dōgen's calibration of 等 in this compound is doctrinally important: the choice of 等 (rank-equivalence) rather than 同 (identity-as-sameness) preserves the structural articulation in which practice and realization are distinguishable as poles while being inseparable as condition.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its general registers of equivalence and pluralization. Its load-bearing Sōtō use in 修証一等 belongs to Dōgen's Kamakura-period vocabulary.

gloss: To obtain, to attain, to be able — a hand grasping treasure at the end of a journey; in Dōgen's 道得 the modal verb of capacity, naming the ability to articulate the Way rather than the acquisition of an object.

components.meaning: step, walking radical (3 strokes) — semantic element: motion along a path, the journey on which the obtaining takes place

in this character a graphic descendant of 貝 (cowrie shell, treasure) (5 strokes) — semantic element: the valued object that is grasped; in the modern form the original 貝 has been reduced to a square-and-line graphic indistinguishable from the unrelated 旦
hand, the inch (3 strokes) — semantic element: the hand that grasps the treasure; the action of acquisition

graphic_evolution.form_description: A hand (又) grasping a cowrie shell (貝)
graphic_evolution.notes: The earliest form is a hand reaching for and grasping a cowrie shell — the cowrie being the standard valuable in early Chinese economy. The original sense is 'to obtain, to acquire, to come into possession of.' From this concrete sense the meanings 'to gain, to attain, to be able to, to manage to' all develop.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 彳 (step) added on the left, hand-grasping-cowrie on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: The bronze and seal forms add the 彳 step radical, giving the character the additional sense of 'arriving at, reaching, attaining at the end of motion.' The successful acquisition becomes specifically the acquisition that completes a journey or process.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 11 strokes — 彳 on the left, 旦-over-寸 on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 得 covers a broad range of attainment and capacity: 得る (eru, to obtain), 取得 (shutoku, acquisition), 心得 (kokoroe, understanding), 得意 (tokui, one's strong suit). Crucially in classical Chinese and Japanese, 得 also functions as a modal-postverbal marker of capacity: V+得 means 'to be able to V, to manage to V, V successfully.' This grammatical use is the register Dōgen exploits in 道得.

doctrinal_notes: In Dōgen's 道得 (dōtoku), 得 functions as the modal-postverbal marker of capacity rather than as the verb of acquisition: 道得 is not 'to obtain the Way' but 'to be able to articulate, to manage to express, to successfully say' the Way. The classical Chinese grammatical pattern V+得 — preserved in Chan/Zen recorded-sayings and inherited by Dōgen — is the doctrinal hinge of the compound: 道 here functions verbally (to speak, to articulate) and 得 functions postverbally (able-to, successful-in). Dōgen's appropriation of the construction in the Dōtoku fascicle of the Shōbōgenzō makes 道得 the technical name for authentic articulation of the Way through words, actions, and silence. The character also carries doctrinal weight in the compound 心得 (kokoroe, heart-attainment, understanding) and in classical Buddhist contexts where 得 names the attainment of doctrinal stages, but Dōgen's specific use exploits the modal-postverbal register and is calibrated against any reading that would make 道得 an acquisition of the Way as object.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in both its substantive sense (to obtain) and its modal-postverbal sense (to be able to). The modal-postverbal use is preserved in classical Japanese kanbun reading (e.g., V得 read as V-uru) and is the register Dōgen exploits in 道得. The Sōtō articulation of 道得 in the Shōbōgenzō Dōtoku fascicle is one of the most doctrinally distinctive deployments of 得 in the Japanese Buddhist vocabulary.

gloss: Five — originally crossed lines marking the meeting of heaven and earth at the central position; in Buddhist usage the cardinal numeral of doctrinal taxonomies (five aggregates, five precepts, five ranks).

graphic_evolution.form_description: Two crossed strokes (X) sometimes drawn between two horizontal lines (二)
graphic_evolution.notes: The earliest form is a simple X — two crossed strokes — sometimes enclosed between an upper and lower horizontal line. The conventional etymological reading takes the upper and lower horizontals as heaven and earth and the crossed strokes as the meeting of the two at the central position; alternative readings see the X as a counting mark of unknown origin. From the original numeral the character extends into a wide range of taxonomic and ordinal uses.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 4 strokes — the X enclosed between upper and lower horizontals, simplified to the modern angular form
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 五 functions as the standard numeral for five and as the marker of fivefold taxonomies in countless compounds: 五月 (gogatsu, May), 五輪 (gorin, Olympic rings; the five rings), 五蘊 (goun, the five aggregates), 五戒 (gokai, the five precepts), 五位 (goi, the five ranks). The character is one of the most frequent in the writing system.

doctrinal_notes: In Buddhist usage 五 carries the load of doctrinal taxonomies — the most pervasive ordering principle of Buddhist scholastic analysis after the threefold (三) and fourfold (四) groupings. The five aggregates (五蘊, goun: form, sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness) decompose the experiential subject; the five precepts (五戒, gokai) structure lay ethical practice; the five ranks (五位, goi) of Dongshan articulate the dialectic of absolute and relative in Caodong/Sōtō. In 五位 specifically, the choice of five rather than three or seven is doctrinally calibrated: Dongshan's articulation of the absolute-relative dialectic requires precisely five distinct positions to articulate the full structural movement (relative-within-absolute, absolute-within-relative, coming-from-within-the-absolute, arrival-at-mutual-integration, attainment-in-both). The numeral does the work of structural articulation, not mere counting.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the earliest stratum of literate culture as the standard numeral for five. Its Buddhist-scholastic use in fivefold taxonomies arrives with the Nara-period transmission and is consolidated across all schools.

gloss: Rank, position, place, station — a person standing at their proper place; in Dongshan's 五位 the term for each of the five structural positions in the absolute-relative dialectic.

components.meaning: person radical (2 strokes) — semantic element: a person, the agent who occupies the position
to stand (5 strokes) — semantic and partly phonetic element: the act of standing in one's place; together with 亻 the figure of a person standing at their proper station

graphic_evolution.form_description: 亻 (person) on the left, 立 (to stand) on the right — a person standing in their place
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense is the position at which a person stands in court — the formal place assigned by rank and protocol. From this concrete sense the meanings 'rank, station, position, place, throne' all develop. By the classical period 位 functions as the standard term for ordered positions in any structured arrangement: the throne (王位 ōi), an official rank (官位 kan'i), a position in a sequence.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 7 strokes — preserves the person-and-stand structure
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 位 covers the range of ranked position: 位 (kurai, rank), 単位 (tan'i, unit), 順位 (jun'i, ranking), 王位 (ōi, throne), 五位 (goi, the five ranks). In Buddhist usage 位 names the doctrinal positions in scholastic taxonomies and the structural ranks in koan curricula.

doctrinal_notes: In Dongshan's 五位 (goi, the Five Ranks), 位 names not a sequential stage of progress but a structural position within the dialectical articulation of absolute (正, shō) and relative (偏, hen). Each 位 is a distinct configuration of the absolute-relative relationship, and the five together articulate the full dialectical movement. The character is doctrinally precise: 位 names a position in a structural arrangement rather than a step in a developmental sequence, and Dongshan's deployment is calibrated against any reading that would make the Five Ranks a hierarchical ladder. The character also functions in the koan curriculum as the marker of the structural positions in 五位顕訣 (Goi Kenketsu, the Manifest Articulation of the Five Ranks) and the related verses, where each 位 is presented through its characteristic image and verse.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its general meaning of rank and position. Its Buddhist-scholastic use in compounds for doctrinal positions develops with the early scholastic transmission. The Caodong/Sōtō articulation of 位 in the Five Ranks belongs to the Tang-dynasty stratum and is transmitted to Japan as part of Dōgen's Sōtō transmission.

gloss: Round, circle, complete — the closed curve that returns to itself; in Zen the figure of completeness, totality, and the cyclical structure of practice-realization, articulated calligraphically in the ensō tradition.

graphic_evolution.period: Seal script (篆書, traditional form 圓)
graphic_evolution.form_description: 囗 (enclosure) surrounding 員 (membership/circumference) — a closed bounded figure
graphic_evolution.notes: The traditional form 圓 is structurally 囗 (the bounded enclosure) surrounding 員 (originally a circular cauldron-mouth, later 'member, circumference'); the character names the closed bounded curve in its full geometric and symbolic register. From the original sense of the geometric circle the meanings 'round, complete, harmonious, perfect, full' all develop. The traditional form 圓 remained standard in classical Chinese writing across all genres.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 4 strokes — 冂 (open box) surrounding two short horizontal strokes; 圓 → 円
graphic_evolution.notes: The post-war Japanese script reform replaced the traditional 圓 with the radically simplified 円, reducing the 13-stroke traditional form to 4 strokes. The simplified form preserves the bounded-enclosure register of 冂 but loses the internal 員 of the traditional form. In modern Japanese 円 covers the range of the original character — 円 (en, yen, the unit of currency named for the round coin), 円形 (enkei, circular shape), 円満 (enman, harmony, completeness) — and the traditional form 圓 remains visible in pre-reform editions of Buddhist texts and in calligraphic and artistic uses. Modern Chinese uses 圆 as the simplified form, distinct from the Japanese simplification.

doctrinal_notes: In 円相 (ensō, the Zen circle), 円 names the closed curve that returns to itself — the geometric figure that, in the Zen calligraphic tradition, articulates the structure of practice-realization as a self-completing whole. The character carries the precise sense of 'round, complete, harmonious' — and the choice of 円 rather than 周 (circumference, cycle) or 環 (ring, loop) is doctrinally calibrated: 円 names the round-and-complete-as-such, the figure whose completeness is not a feature added to it but its structural condition. The 円 of 円相 is also doctrinally continuous with the broader Buddhist register of 円 as the marker of perfect-and-complete teaching: 円教 (engyō, the perfect teaching) in Tendai doctrinal classification, 円融 (enyū, perfect interpenetration) in Huayan-influenced contexts, 円満 (enman, complete fulfillment) across general Buddhist usage. The Zen ensō tradition deploys this register in calligraphic-meditative form, articulating the doctrinal claim through the brushstroke rather than the discursive proposition.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character (in its traditional form 圓), present in Japanese writing from the Nara period across the full range of its meanings. The Tendai use of 円 in 円教 belongs to the Heian-period scholastic transmission; the Zen calligraphic use in 円相 belongs to the Caodong/Sōtō and Linji/Rinzai traditions transmitted to Japan from the Kamakura period onward. The post-war script reform replaced the traditional 圓 with the modern 円 across general usage; the older 圓 form remains visible in pre-reform editions and in calligraphic ensō practice, where the brushstroke is sometimes performed using the traditional rather than the simplified form.

gloss: Mark, sign, appearance, mutual; minister — looking at a tree to discern its character; in Buddhist usage the lakṣaṇa-register of distinguishing marks and characteristics, and in 円相 the figure or mark that the circle is.

components.meaning: tree (4 strokes) — semantic element: the object on which the eye is focused, the form whose marks are being discerned
eye (5 strokes) — semantic element: the organ of perception that examines the form and discerns its characteristic marks

graphic_evolution.form_description: An eye (目) beside a tree (木) — the act of examining a form to read its character
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense is the act of looking at a tree to discern its character — the practical activity of forester or carpenter assessing the wood. From this concrete sense the meanings 'to inspect, to examine, to discern, to mark, sign, appearance, characteristic, mutual, together, minister' all develop. The semantic range extends through several distinct registers: (1) the act of perceiving and the marks perceived (appearance, sign, characteristic); (2) the mutual register of two parties looking at each other (mutual, together, reciprocal); (3) the official register of one who examines on behalf of the ruler (minister, prime minister).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 9 strokes — preserves the eye-and-tree structure
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 相 carries its full semantic range: 相手 (aite, partner, mutual), 相談 (sōdan, consultation), 相続 (sōzoku, inheritance), 首相 (shushō, prime minister), 形相 (gyōsō, form-and-appearance), 円相 (ensō, the Zen circle). The Buddhist register names the lakṣaṇa-marks of phenomenal appearance — the distinguishing characteristics by which phenomena are known — and is integral to the broader scholastic vocabulary.

doctrinal_notes: In Buddhist usage 相 names the lakṣaṇa-register of distinguishing marks and characteristics — the appearance-marks by which phenomena are known and the characteristic-features by which they are categorized. The Heart Sutra's celebrated 'no marks' (無相, musō) deploys 相 in the negative-register, articulating the suspension of the mark-grammar by which phenomena are ordinarily perceived. In 円相 (ensō), 相 functions in a distinct but related register: the circle is the 相 — the figure, the mark, the form — that the brushstroke articulates. The compound's structure is doctrinally precise: 円相 is not 'circle and mark' (additive) but 'the round-mark' (the mark whose form is the circle). The Zen calligraphic tradition deploys this structure to articulate the doctrinal claim that the brushstroke-circle is itself a 相 — a figure whose articulation is the practice-realization being expressed.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period across the full range of its meanings. The Buddhist scholastic use of 相 in compounds for the lakṣaṇa-register arrives with the Nara-period transmission. The Zen calligraphic use in 円相 belongs to the Kamakura-period transmission of the Caodong/Sōtō and Linji/Rinzai circle-figure traditions inherited from the Tang-dynasty Chan masters, particularly the Yangshan-Guishan lineage's 96 circle figures and the broader Caodong elaboration of the doctrine.

gloss: A ring, a circle that closes upon itself — a jade ring whose form returns to its starting point; in 行持道環 the figure of the Way as a self-sustaining circle that has no beginning, no end, and no leaking out.

components.meaning: jade radical (4 strokes) — semantic element: a piece of jade, the material from which a 環 was carved
huán (13 strokes) — phonetic element supplying the huán/kan reading; depicts an eye over a garment, classically associated with looking-around

graphic_evolution.form_description: 玉 (jade) beside 睘 (phonetic) — a jade ring named for its closed-curve form
graphic_evolution.notes: The classical referent of 環 is concrete: a jade ring of the kind worn as a pendant or used in ritual exchange. The ring's defining feature — the closed curve that returns to itself, the form whose end meets its beginning — generalizes into the abstract sense of cyclic return. Classical compounds preserve the geometric register: 循環 (xúnhuán, to circle around), 環状 (huánzhuàng, ring-shaped). From the geometric closed-curve sense the figurative register develops: 環 as the structural figure of any condition that returns to itself.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 17 strokes — preserves the 玉/睘 structure
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 環 carries the full range: 環境 (kankyō, environment), 循環 (junkan, circulation), 環状線 (kanjōsen, loop railway line), 一環 (ikkan, one ring of a chain). In Buddhist usage 環 appears most consequentially in Dōgen's compound 道環 (dōkan, the circle of the Way) within 行持道環 — the technical term for the self-sustaining circular structure of practice-realization.

doctrinal_notes: In 行持道環 (gyōji dōkan), 環 names the closed-curve figure under which Dōgen articulates the structure of practice-realization. The choice of 環 rather than 円 (round, complete), 周 (circumference, a full turn), or 輪 (wheel, cycle) is doctrinally calibrated. 円 names the round-and-complete-as-such — the figure of completeness without temporal register. 周 names the act of going around once — a single circuit. 輪 names the wheel, which in Buddhist usage carries the saṃsāric register of compulsive repetition (輪廻, rinne). 環, by contrast, names the ring as a structural figure: a closed curve that holds its own continuity, whose ends are joined into a self-sustaining whole. The 環 of 道環 names the Way's character as a structure that does not begin from outside itself or terminate in something other than itself — practice supports realization, realization supports practice, and the activity sustains itself across moments and generations as a single ring whose continuity is structural rather than effortful.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its general meaning of ring, jade ring, and cyclic return. Its load-bearing Sōtō register in 行持道環 is a Kamakura-period Dōgen articulation, deploying the classical Chinese register of 環 as closed-curve figure to name the structural condition of practice-realization. The character is also load-bearing in modern Japanese in 環境 (kankyō, environment) — the surrounding ring of conditions in which a being is situated — a coinage that became standard across East Asia in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

gloss: Together, joint, mutual — two hands lifting a shared object; the structural figure of joint action that Meiji translators recruited to render Latin respublica in 共和.

graphic_evolution.form_description: Two hands holding up a shared object — the figure of joint lifting
graphic_evolution.notes: The original image: two hands together raising or holding the same object. The joint-action register — two parties acting upon a single object — is the semantic core. From this concrete image the meanings 'together, mutual, joint, in common, shared' all develop. The classical compound 共和 (gònghé) refers in pre-Meiji Chinese specifically to the regency interregnum of 841–828 BCE, when the Zhou court was governed jointly by the Duke of Zhou Ding and the Duke of Shao after King Li's exile — the historical condition of joint rule that gives 共 its classical political register.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 6 strokes — two parallel verticals above a horizontal joint base
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 共 carries the full joint-action register: 共に (tomo ni, together), 共同 (kyōdō, cooperation), 共有 (kyōyū, joint ownership), 公共 (kōkyō, public), 共産 (kyōsan, communism), 共和 (kyōwa, republic). The post-Meiji political vocabulary makes 共 one of the most productive characters for translating Western concepts of public, common, and shared political life.

doctrinal_notes: In 共和 (kyōwa, republic), 共 carries the joint-action register: the polity is governed jointly by its citizens rather than by a single sovereign. The Meiji translation exploits the classical Chinese register of 共和 as the historical condition of joint regency (Zhou dynasty, 841–828 BCE) and extends it to name the structural political principle of non-monarchical government. In 公共 (kōkyō, public), 共 pairs with 公 (public, official) to name the shared domain of civil life. The character's productivity in modern East Asian political vocabulary — 共産主義 (communism), 共和国 (republic), 共同体 (community) — derives from its capacity to name the joint-shared register that Western political theory codes as 'public' or 'common.'
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its general meaning of together, joint, mutual. The native Japanese word とも (together, companion) is mapped onto 共 in the earliest stratum of Japanese writing. The character's load-bearing modern political register is Meiji-era: Mitsukuri Shōgo's 1845–46 use of 共和 to render 'republic' (Dutch republiek) in his Kon'yo Zushiki, popularized through Fukuzawa Yukichi's Seiyō Jijō, made 共 one of the central characters of Meiji political vocabulary, generating compounds for republic, communism, cooperation, and the public domain.

gloss: Hide, leather, change — an animal hide stretched out to be tanned; from the act of skinning and remaking comes the classical sense of changing, removing, transforming, and the Yijing's doctrine of 革命 (changing the mandate).

graphic_evolution.form_description: An animal hide stretched out for tanning — head at top, body in the middle, tail at the bottom
graphic_evolution.notes: The original image is concrete: a stripped animal hide laid out flat. The transformation involved in tanning — turning living skin into worked leather — generalizes into the abstract sense of changing, transforming, renewing. Classical Chinese preserves both registers: 皮革 (píngé, hide and leather), 革命 (gémìng, changing the mandate, revolution). The Yijing's 49th hexagram is named 革 and treats the doctrine of legitimate transformation: 'Tang and Wu changed the mandate, responding to Heaven and according with the people' (湯武革命、順乎天而應乎人). This is the classical locus of the political register that Meiji translators recruited to render 'revolution.'

graphic_evolution.form_description: 9 strokes — preserves the stretched-hide structure with horizontal lines articulating head, body, and tail
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 革 carries the full range: 皮革 (hikaku, leather), 革命 (kakumei, revolution), 改革 (kaikaku, reform), 革新 (kakushin, innovation). The transformation-register has become the dominant modern usage, with 'leather' largely confined to compounds explicitly naming the material.

doctrinal_notes: In 革命 (kakumei, revolution), 革 carries the classical Yijing register of legitimate transformation — the changing or removing of an established condition in response to higher imperative. The Yijing's 革 hexagram and its commentary on Tang and Wu (the founders of the Shang and Zhou dynasties respectively, who overthrew preceding rulers held to have lost legitimacy) provide the doctrinal frame: 革 names not arbitrary change but warranted transformation, the removal of an order that has lost its mandate. The Meiji translation of 'revolution' through 革命 thus imports a Confucian-Mencian register — revolution as the mandate of Heaven shifting to a new polity — into the modern political vocabulary, with consequences that have been continuously generative in East Asian revolutionary discourse from Sun Yat-sen through twentieth-century communist articulations.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in both registers — leather and transformation. The Yijing-derived political register of 革命 was available in classical Japanese learning across the medieval period but was activated in its modern political sense only in the Meiji era. The Meiji translation of 'revolution' through 革命 was reinforced by Sun Yat-sen's adoption of the term for the Chinese revolutionary movement in the early twentieth century — a moment in which Japanese-coined political vocabulary returned to Chinese usage as the operating language of an actual revolution.

gloss: Command, mandate, life — orders received from above, particularly the heavenly mandate (天命); the inherited classical register that 革命 transforms into the warrant of revolution.

components.meaning: mouth (3 strokes) — semantic element: the mouth from which the command issues
order, command (5 strokes) — semantic and phonetic element: a kneeling figure receiving orders from above

graphic_evolution.form_description: A kneeling figure beneath a roof, receiving orders — the canonical scene of command issued from above to subordinate
graphic_evolution.notes: The original image stages the political scene: a superior issues a command and a subordinate kneels to receive it. From this scene the meanings 'command, order, mandate' all develop directly, and the extended sense 'life, fate, destiny' develops from the idea of life as a mandate received from Heaven. The pairing of 天命 (tiānmìng, heavenly mandate) is one of the most consequential compounds in classical Chinese political theory: the ruler holds the mandate of Heaven, and the loss of that mandate warrants 革命 (gémìng, the changing of the mandate).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 8 strokes — 令 with 口 added below and to the side
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 命 carries the full range: 命令 (meirei, command), 命名 (meimei, naming), 生命 (seimei, life), 運命 (unmei, destiny), 寿命 (jumyō, lifespan), 革命 (kakumei, revolution). The two registers — command and life — both remain productive across modern Japanese usage.

doctrinal_notes: In 革命 (kakumei, revolution), 命 carries the classical political register of 天命 (the heavenly mandate) — the divinely-warranted authority by which a ruler legitimately rules. The compound's structural logic: 革 (change, remove) operates upon 命 (mandate), and 革命 names the changing of the mandate from one polity to another. The Yijing's commentary on the 革 hexagram — 'Tang and Wu changed the mandate, responding to Heaven and according with the people' — is the locus classicus, and the Meiji translation of 'revolution' through 革命 imports this entire classical-Confucian framework into modern political vocabulary. The other register of 命 — life, destiny, the lifespan — is also deeply embedded in Buddhist vocabulary: 寿命 (jumyō, lifespan), 命終 (myōjū, the end of life), 一命 (ichimei, a single life). The two registers — political mandate and biological life — share the structural logic of something granted from above and capable of being withdrawn.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in both registers. The native Japanese word いのち (life) is mapped onto 命 in the earliest stratum, and the political register of 命 in 天命 and related compounds is available across the classical and medieval periods through Confucian and Buddhist learning. The character's load-bearing modern political register in 革命 (revolution) is a Meiji activation of the classical Yijing register, popularized through translation of Western political theory and reinforced by the early twentieth-century adoption of 革命 as the operating term of the Chinese revolutionary movement.

gloss: Fundamental norm — the binding rule, the great statute, the constitutive ordinance; the character that names the law above ordinary law and that Meiji constitutionalists recruited to render Western 'constitution.'

components.meaning: roof radical (3 strokes) — semantic element: the architectural canopy under which the household and the polity are sheltered; here the constitutive frame within which subordinate orderings hold
net, eye (5 strokes) — semantic element derived from a horizontal eye-form; here the watching, surveying, judging gaze that the binding norm exercises over the polity it shelters
heart, mind (4 strokes) — semantic element: the moral-cognitive seat from which the binding norm issues; the inward register of the rule that constitutes the outward order

graphic_evolution.form_description: An eye element above a heart element, with a roof or canopy element above — the canonical scene of the watching, judging, ordering mind
graphic_evolution.notes: The character originally combined 害 (harm, severity) with 目 (eye) and 心 (heart), assembling the figure of the severe, watching, morally-binding norm. The classical sense of 憲 in Zhou-dynasty Chinese is 'fundamental rule, great statute, the binding ordinance' — distinguished from 法 (ordinary law, regulated procedure) by its register of constitutive normativity. In the Zuozhuan and Guoyu the compound 憲法 appears in the sense of 'great laws, fundamental statutes' of a polity, naming the constitutive ordinances rather than the day-to-day legislation.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 16 strokes — 宀 (roof, 3 strokes) at the top, 罒 (eye/net, 5 strokes) and intermediate elements in the middle, 心 (heart, 4 strokes) at the bottom
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 憲 is largely confined to the constitutional-political register: 憲法 (kenpō, constitution), 立憲 (rikken, constitutionalism), 違憲 (iken, unconstitutionality), 護憲 (goken, defense of the constitution). The pre-Meiji classical register of 憲 as 'fundamental rule' provided the doctrinal handle through which Meiji translators rendered the Western 'constitution' as the law above ordinary law.

doctrinal_notes: In 憲法 (kenpō, constitution), 憲 carries the classical register of 'binding fundamental ordinance' — the constitutive rule that orders the polity from above and that ordinary law must accord with. The Meiji translators' choice of 憲 over 法 as the head of the compound is doctrinally consequential: 法 (law, regulated procedure) names the operational level of legal order, but 憲 names the constitutive level above it. The compound 憲法 thus articulates the Western constitutional principle of higher law — a foundational instrument that constitutes and binds the political order itself — through the classical Chinese hierarchy in which 憲 stands above 法. The pairing exploits a doctrinal distinction the classical Chinese vocabulary already carried, and it allows Western constitutional theory to enter Japanese discourse without a paraphrastic explanation of why some laws are constitutive and others are merely operational. In compounds: 立憲 (constitutionalism, the doctrine of government bound by a constitution), 違憲 (unconstitutional, in violation of the binding ordinance), 護憲 (the defense of constitutional government as a political-movement register).
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, available in classical Japanese learning across the Nara and Heian periods through Confucian textual transmission, but deployed in classical Japanese contexts only in compounds carrying its general sense of 'rule, norm, model.' The character's load-bearing modern political register in 憲法 is a Meiji activation: late-Tokugawa scholars including Tsuda Mamichi and Mitsukuri Rinshō began using 憲法 to render Western 'constitution' in the 1860s and early 1870s, and the term was institutionalized through the promulgation of the Meiji Constitution (大日本帝国憲法) in 1889 under Itō Hirobumi's leadership. The Meiji-period 憲法 became the standard term across East Asian constitutional law — adopted into Chinese (xiànfǎ), Korean (헌법), and Vietnamese — and 憲 acquired its modern productivity (立憲, 違憲, 護憲) through the constitutional politics of the post-Meiji period.

gloss: State, country, nation — a bounded territory containing its sovereign treasure, classically the seat of a ruler with his jewel of authority; the modern simplified form of traditional 國.

components.meaning: enclosure radical (3 strokes) — semantic element: the bounded perimeter that demarcates the territorial extent of the polity from the surrounding non-polity

jade, jewel (5 strokes) — semantic element: the sovereign treasure within the bounded enclosure; the inner valuable that the perimeter protects and that signifies the rule-bearing center of the territorial polity

graphic_evolution.period: Oracle bone and bronze (甲骨文・金文)
graphic_evolution.form_description: An enclosure containing a weapon (戈) over a perimeter line — the original 或, figuring the polity as a bounded territory defended by armed force
graphic_evolution.notes: The original character was 或, picturing a bounded territory (囗 over 一) containing a halberd (戈) — the polity figured as armed defense of its territorial perimeter. The character was then extended by the addition of an outer enclosure to give 國 (traditional form), articulating the polity as enclosed-armed-territory within a further bounded frame. The post-war Japanese script reform (1946) replaced the inner 或 element with 玉 (jade, jewel) to give the modern simplified 国, semantically reframing the polity as territory containing its sovereign treasure rather than territory defended by arms — a doctrinally consequential simplification.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 8 strokes — outer enclosure 囗 (3 strokes) with inner 玉 (5 strokes); modern simplified form of traditional 國 (11 strokes)
graphic_evolution.notes: The traditional form 國 remains in classical and pre-war Japanese texts and continues to be used in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and other Traditional-Chinese-script contexts; the simplified People's Republic of China form 国 is identical to the post-war Japanese reform and is now universal across both contemporary Japanese and PRC Chinese usage. The semantic register of 国 across modern Japanese covers state, country, nation, and homeland: 国家 (kokka, state), 国民 (kokumin, citizen/national), 国際 (kokusai, international), 国会 (kokkai, national assembly), 外国 (gaikoku, foreign country), 帝国 (teikoku, empire).

doctrinal_notes: 国 is one of the most productive characters in modern East Asian political vocabulary. The post-Meiji wasei-kango compounds 国会 (national assembly), 国家 (state), 国民 (citizen), 国際 (international), 国籍 (nationality), 国境 (border), 国旗 (flag), 国歌 (anthem) all deploy 国 as the head element naming the territorial-political polity within which the second element operates. The classical Chinese register of 國 named primarily the bounded territorial domain of a ruler — the polity figured as armed-and-enclosed territory — and the Meiji repurposing extends this register to name the modern nation-state as the carrier of sovereignty, citizenship, and international standing. The post-war Japanese script reform's substitution of 玉 (jewel) for 或 (armed-territory) within the enclosure is doctrinally suggestive: the polity is reframed from armed-defense of territory to bearer of sovereign treasure, a shift that aligns with the 1947 Constitution's renunciation of war.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its traditional form 國. The native Japanese word くに (kuni, land, province, country) is mapped onto 國 in the earliest stratum, and the character's general territorial-political sense is available across all classical and medieval Japanese usage. The character's productivity in modern East Asian political vocabulary is largely Meiji-era: the wasei-kango compounds 国会, 国家, 国民, 国際 are all Meiji coinages that became standard across Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese political discourse. The post-war Japanese script reform of 1946 replaced traditional 國 with simplified 国, which is now universal in contemporary Japanese print and (independently arrived at by the People's Republic of China) standard in simplified Chinese print as well.

gloss: To select, to choose — to walk through alternatives and lift one out from among many; the picking-out that the modern political compound 選挙 (election) names as the citizen's act of choosing a representative.

components.meaning: movement, walking radical (3 strokes) — semantic element: the action of moving through, traversing, going-along; here the active register of the selector moving among the alternatives

the Yijing's Sun trigram (gentle wind, yielding); two 巳 over 共 (12 strokes) — phonetic element providing the xuǎn sound; carries a partial semantic register of yielding, deferring, presenting one above another

graphic_evolution.form_description: 辶 (movement) beside 巽 (yielding, presenting) — the figure of moving through alternatives and presenting one as the chosen
graphic_evolution.notes: The classical sense of 選 in Zhou and Han Chinese covers the full range from 'to select' (the active picking) through 'to be selected' (the chosen) to 'the selection itself' (the result of the choosing). The compound 選挙 is attested in classical Chinese in the context of the imperial examination system (科挙) and bureaucratic appointments (選官) — the formal selection of officials through merit-based procedures. This classical-bureaucratic register of 選挙 provided the doctrinal handle through which Meiji translators rendered the Western political concept of election.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 15 strokes — 巽 (12 strokes) above 辶 (3 strokes); the modern form preserves the classical structure
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 選 covers the full selection-register: 選択 (sentaku, choice), 選挙 (senkyo, election), 選手 (senshu, athlete/selected player), 当選 (tōsen, being elected), 落選 (rakusen, losing an election), 選別 (senbetsu, sorting). The political register of 選挙 became the dominant modern usage through Meiji constitutional politics, with the bureaucratic-examination register of the classical 選挙 largely displaced by 試験 (examination) in modern Japanese.

doctrinal_notes: In 選挙 (senkyo, election), 選 contributes the active register of selecting, choosing, picking out from among alternatives. The compound's classical Chinese register named the imperial-bureaucratic procedure of merit-based official appointment (選官 selecting officials, 選挙 selecting and recommending) — a procedure structurally distinct from the modern Western institutional concept of popular election. The Meiji repurposing extends 選挙 from this classical-bureaucratic register to name the modern democratic procedure of citizens selecting representatives, and the character 選 in this Meiji deployment carries the doctrinal weight of the active-citizen role: the citizen as the agent of selection rather than the bureaucratic-examiner as the agent. In compounds: 選挙権 (senkyoken, right to vote), 普通選挙 (futsū senkyo, universal suffrage), 選挙区 (senkyoku, electoral district), 当選 (tōsen, election to office), 立候補 (rikkōho, standing as a candidate).
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its general selection-register. The classical Chinese compound 選挙 in the imperial-examination and bureaucratic-appointment sense was available across Japanese classical learning through Confucian textual transmission, but Japan never adopted the Chinese imperial-examination system in the systematic form developed under the Tang and Song, so the bureaucratic register of 選挙 remained largely a textual reference rather than an institutional reality. The character's load-bearing modern political register in 選挙 (election) is a Meiji activation: the term acquired its modern political sense through the early Meiji translation of Western political vocabulary (Fukuzawa's Seiyō Jijō uses the variant orthography 撰挙 in this register) and was institutionalized through the 1889 election law and the first parliamentary elections of 1890. The Japanese coinage was subsequently adopted into Chinese (xuǎnjǔ) and Korean (선거) as the standard term for elections across the East Asian political vocabulary.

gloss: To raise up, to lift, to nominate — many hands lifting a single object; the structural figure of public elevation that the modern political compound 選挙 (election) deploys to name the raising-up of a representative by the votes of many.

components.meaning: the upper portion (simplified from 與): hands cooperating to lift a shared object (5 strokes) — semantic element: the joint-lifting register of multiple agents acting upon a single elevated object
hand (4 strokes, joined to upper element) — semantic element: the hand that does the lifting; the active register of the raising action

graphic_evolution.form_description: Four hands (the 與 element) above a single 手 (hand) — the canonical scene of multiple hands lifting a single object
graphic_evolution.notes: The traditional form 擧 (16 strokes) preserves the four-hand-with-supporting-hand structure that articulates the joint-lifting register: multiple agents acting together to raise a single object. The classical sense covers 'to raise, to lift up, to elevate' across multiple registers — physical (raising an object), nominal (raising someone to office, naming, nominating), and elevative (raising up to praise or commend). The classical compound 挙人 (jǔrén) named those raised up through the imperial examination system; 挙国 (jǔguó) names the entire nation rising up together; 挙手 (jǔshou) names raising the hand. The Meiji compound 選挙 deploys the nominating-elevating register: to elect is to raise up a candidate through the votes of many.

graphic_evolution.period: Regular script (楷書) — simplified form 挙
graphic_evolution.form_description: 10 strokes — simplified upper element 𭕄 over 手 (hand); the post-war Japanese script reform's simplification of traditional 擧
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 挙 carries the lifting-elevating register across multiple registers: 挙手 (kyoshu, raising the hand), 挙式 (kyoshiki, holding a ceremony), 一挙 (ikkyo, in one movement, all at once), 列挙 (rekkyo, enumerating), 選挙 (senkyo, election). The political register of 選挙 became the dominant modern usage through Meiji constitutional politics. The simplified form 挙 is universal in contemporary Japanese print; the traditional form 擧 remains in pre-war texts and in Traditional-Chinese-script contexts.

doctrinal_notes: In 選挙 (senkyo, election), 挙 contributes the elevating-nominating register: the elected representative is raised up by the votes of many, just as an object is lifted by the cooperative action of many hands. The compound's structural logic articulates the modern democratic procedure through the classical figure of joint elevation: 選 names the active picking-out of the candidate, 挙 names the raising-up of the chosen. The classical-Chinese register of 挙 in the imperial-examination context (挙人, those raised up by examination) provided the doctrinal handle through which Meiji translators rendered the modern Western institutional concept of election as the raising-up of representatives by popular vote. The character is also productive across other Meiji-era institutional vocabulary: 列挙 (enumerating), 挙国一致 (kyokoku-itchi, national unity, all the country acting together), and the broader register of joint-collective action that modern Japanese political discourse codes through 挙.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its traditional form 擧. The native Japanese verb あ.げる (ageru, to raise, to lift up) is mapped onto the character in the earliest stratum, and the lifting-elevating register is available across all classical and medieval Japanese usage. The character's load-bearing modern political register in 選挙 (election) is a Meiji activation through translation of Western political vocabulary, institutionalized through the 1889 election law and the first parliamentary elections of 1890. The post-war Japanese script reform of 1946 replaced traditional 擧 with simplified 挙, which is now universal in contemporary Japanese print.

gloss: To govern, government, political affairs — the rectification of the polity through structured authority; correctness administered with a guiding hand. The classical character that organizes Confucian political vocabulary and the modern character that heads compounds of state and party.

components.meaning: correct, upright, true (5 strokes) — semantic and phonetic element providing the zhèng sound; the rectitude that government enforces, the standard against which the polity is regulated
to strike, to rap, the rod radical (4 strokes) — semantic element: the hand-with-stick that administers correction; the active register of authority guiding or compelling rectitude

graphic_evolution.form_description: 正 (correct) beside 攵 (hand with stick) — the figure of correction administered by authority
graphic_evolution.notes: The character's structural logic is the Confucian definition of government articulated in the Analects: 'To govern (政) is to correct (正)' — 政者正也, with the homophonic-phonetic identity of zhèng-zhèng (政-正) carrying a doctrinal claim about the essence of government. The classical sense of 政 covers the full range from 'to govern' (the active administering) through 'government' (the institution that governs) to 'political affairs' (the domain of governance) and 'policy' (the specific measures of governance). The compound 政治 (zhèngzhì, governance) and the compound 政事 (zhèngshì, political affairs) are foundational Confucian-political vocabulary. The native Japanese kun reading まつりごと (matsurigoto, literally 'matters of worship/celebration') reflects the archaic Japanese conception of governance as ritual administration — a reading-pair that preserves a doctrinally distinct register from the Confucian 政=正 articulation.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 9 strokes — 正 (5 strokes) on the left beside 攵 (4 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 政 is one of the most productive characters in political vocabulary: 政治 (seiji, politics), 政府 (seifu, government), 政策 (seisaku, policy), 政党 (seitō, political party), 行政 (gyōsei, administration), 内政 (naisei, domestic affairs), 外政 (gaisei, foreign policy), 政権 (seiken, political power/regime). The character heads the entire vocabulary of modern political institution-formation across East Asia, with the Meiji-era and post-Meiji compounds carrying 政 across Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese political discourse.

doctrinal_notes: In 政党 (seitō, political party), 政 carries the modern register of political affairs — the domain of governance and policy in which parties compete. The Meiji compound 政党 articulates the modern Western institutional concept of the political party as an organized association of citizens contesting elections and seeking governmental authority, and 政 in this deployment names the domain (the political) within which 党 (the organized faction) operates. The classical Confucian register of 政=正 (government as correction, governance as rectification) continues to inflect the modern usage in subtle ways: in East Asian political discourse the question whether parties pursue genuine policy (政策) or merely partisan advantage has often been articulated through the persistent classical register in which 政 names the rectifying-administrative function rather than the partisan-competitive function. The character's productivity across the Meiji-and-after political vocabulary — 政治, 政府, 政党, 政策, 行政, 政権 — makes 政 one of the structural anchors of modern East Asian political language.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period through Confucian textual transmission. The native Japanese word まつりごと (matsurigoto, archaic 'governance' as ritual administration) is mapped onto 政 in the earliest stratum, and the Confucian-political register of 政 is available across all classical and medieval Japanese usage. The character's productivity in modern political vocabulary is largely Meiji-era: the wasei-kango compounds 政治 (politics, in its modern systematic-disciplinary sense), 政府 (government, in its modern institutional sense), 政党 (political party), 政策 (policy), 行政 (administration), 政権 (political power/regime) are all Meiji coinages or Meiji re-coinages of classical compounds, and they became standard across Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese political discourse through the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

gloss: Faction, association, party — a group bound by common interest or affinity; classically carrying the negative valence of factional intrigue, repurposed at Meiji to name the legitimate institutional form of the modern political party.

components.meaning: to esteem, to honor; the upper element (8 strokes) — phonetic and partly semantic element providing the dǎng sound; carries the register of shared elevation, the common esteem that binds the group together
legs, person walking (2 strokes) — semantic element: the persons whose legs walk together; here the embodied figure of the joint-acting members of the party

graphic_evolution.period: Bronze and seal (金文・篆書) — traditional form 黨
graphic_evolution.form_description: 尚 above 黒 (black) — the figure of those who share the same blackness, those bound by common (often hidden, suspect) affinity
graphic_evolution.notes: The traditional form 黨 (20 strokes) combined 尚 (esteem, common elevation) with 黒 (black, dark) and carried in classical Chinese a strongly negative valence: a 黨 was a faction, a clique, a conspiracy of those who acted together in pursuit of partisan interest against the public good. Confucian political vocabulary regularly contrasts 党 with 公 (public, just): 党争 (dǎngzhēng, factional strife) is figured as the corruption of public deliberation, and the Confucian gentleman 君子 is said to be 不党 (not factional). The Analects articulates the classical tension: 君子は和して同ぜず、小人は同じて和せず ('the gentleman harmonizes without conforming, the petty man conforms without harmonizing'). The post-war Japanese script reform's substitution of 㠯 (or 兄/儿) for 黒 in the simplified 党 (10 strokes) graphically detaches the character from the original 'blackness' element, semantically aligning the modern form with the more neutral register of organized association.

graphic_evolution.period: Regular script (楷書) — simplified form 党
graphic_evolution.form_description: 10 strokes — 尚 element above 儿 (legs) — modern simplified form of traditional 黨
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 党 carries the legitimate-association register: 政党 (seitō, political party), 自由党 (Jiyū-tō, Liberal Party), 民主党 (Minshu-tō, Democratic Party), 共産党 (Kyōsantō, Communist Party), 党首 (tōshu, party leader), 党員 (tōin, party member), 入党 (nyūtō, joining a party), 脱党 (dattō, leaving a party). The post-Meiji repurposing of 党 from its negative classical register to its positive institutional register remains one of the most striking examples of the wasei-kango re-coinage strategy.

doctrinal_notes: In 政党 (seitō, political party), 党 carries the modern Western institutional register of the legitimate political party — an organized association of citizens contesting elections and seeking governmental authority. The Meiji repurposing of 党 from its negative classical register (faction, clique, conspiracy) to its positive modern register (legitimate political association) is doctrinally consequential and has been continuously contested in East Asian political discourse. The classical register has not been entirely displaced: in twentieth- and twenty-first-century East Asian political rhetoric, accusations of partisan factionalism (党派性, 党争) regularly invoke the classical register against contemporary political parties, and the question whether parties serve the public good or merely partisan interest remains framed in vocabulary that the classical 党 carries. The character's productivity across the modern political-party vocabulary — 政党, 与党 (yotō, ruling party), 野党 (yatō, opposition party), 政党政治 (seitō seiji, party politics), 一党制 (ittōsei, one-party system), 多党制 (tatōsei, multi-party system) — makes 党 the structural anchor of modern East Asian party-political language.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its traditional form 黨 and carrying the classical negative valence of faction or clique. The character was available across classical and medieval Japanese usage primarily in the Confucian-political register of 党争 (factional strife) and related negatively-valenced compounds, and the native Japanese word なかま (nakama, companion-group) maps onto 党 with a more neutral register of mutual-association. The character's load-bearing modern political register in 政党 (political party) is a Meiji activation: the wasei-kango compound 政党 was coined to render the Western institutional concept of the political party, and the founding of the Liberal Party (自由党, Jiyū-tō) by Itagaki Taisuke in 1881 and the Constitutional Progressive Party (立憲改進党) by Ōkuma Shigenobu in 1882 — the first modern East Asian political parties — institutionalized the modern positive register of 党. The post-war Japanese script reform of 1946 replaced traditional 黨 with simplified 党, which is now universal in contemporary Japanese print.

gloss: Balance, weight, and thence authority and right — the counterweight on a steelyard whose calibration measures and adjudicates; in Meiji vocabulary the load-bearing character that carries both 'right' (as juridical claim) and 'power' (as authority), the dual register of the Western Recht / droit / right.

components.meaning: tree, wood (4 strokes) — semantic element: the wooden beam of the steelyard or balance-scale on which the original sense of 権 as a weighing instrument depends

heron, observation-bird (right element, 18 strokes in classical form, contributing the quán phonetic) — phonetic element supplying the reading; also carrying the secondary register of attentive observation appropriate to the calibration of weight

graphic_evolution.form_description: 木 (tree, wooden beam) on the left with the phonetic-semantic 雚 element on the right — the figure of a steelyard or balance
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense of 権 is the counterweight on a balance-scale (権衡, quánhéng), the calibrated weight that establishes the measure against which other things are weighed. From this concrete sense the character extends through 'that which adjudicates / that which decides' to the abstract registers of authority and prerogative: the one who holds the counterweight is the one who measures and decides, and 権 acquires the political register of authoritative power. In classical Chinese 権 is paired with 経 (the constant, the standard) in the dialectical 経権 (jīngquán), in which 経 names the unchanging principle and 権 names the discretionary authority to weigh circumstances and adjust action — a load-bearing distinction in Confucian and Legalist political theory.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 15 strokes — 木 (4 strokes) on the left, 雚 (11 strokes in modern simplification) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 権 is one of the most productive characters in legal and political vocabulary. The Meiji repurposing recruited 権 to render the Western Recht / droit / right and the Western power / pouvoir / Macht across a long series of compound coinages: 権利 (kenri, right), 主権 (shuken, sovereignty), 人権 (jinken, human rights), 政権 (seiken, political power, regime), 特権 (tokken, privilege), 三権 (sanken, the three branches of government), 大権 (taiken, prerogative), 権限 (kengen, authority/competence), 権威 (ken'i, authority/prestige).
