Classical extensions track this anchor across multiple registers: throwing a thing (投石 tōseki, casting stones), casting a vote (投票 tōhyō, casting a ballot), surrendering or submitting (投降 tōkō, throwing down arms; 投げ出す nageдasu, casting down), entering or going into (投宿 tōshuku, lodging by 'casting oneself' into a place; 身を投じる, casting oneself into something), administering or applying (投薬 tōyaku, administering medicine), and committing resources toward a venture (投資 tōshi, investment — the casting-forth of capital).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 7 strokes — 扌 (3 strokes) on the left, 殳 (4 strokes) on the right; the seal-script structure preserved
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 投 is productive across multiple registers. Verbal-active: 投げる (nageru, to throw, to cast). Compound-physical: 投手 (tōshu, baseball pitcher), 投球 (tōkyū, pitch, throwing of a ball), 投石 (tōseki, stone-throwing). Compound-political: 投票 (tōhyō, voting, balloting — casting one's vote), 投書 (tōsho, letter to the editor — casting one's words into public space). Compound-medical: 投薬 (tōyaku, administration of medicine), 投与 (tōyo, dosage, administration). Compound-modern-economic: 投資 (tōshi, investment), 投資家 (tōshika, investor), 投機 (tōki, speculation), 投資信託 (tōshi shintaku, investment trust), 設備投資 (setsubi tōshi, capital investment in equipment), 海外投資 (kaigai tōshi, foreign investment). The Meiji-Taishō deployment of 投 in the financial compound 投資 calibrates the classical casting-and-committing register for the Western political-economic category of investment: the directed casting-forth of capital toward a productive venture, in expectation of a future return.

doctrinal_notes: In 投資 (tōshi, investment), 投 carries the register of casting-forth and directed commitment paired with 資 (resources, supplied means, capital). The compound articulates the Western economic category of investment — the deployment of capital toward a productive venture in expectation of a future return — through a Sino-Japanese binomial in which 投 names the casting-forth action and 資 names the substance cast. The compound's structural transparency is doctrinally precise: investment in the modern economic sense is precisely this directed casting of capital, distinct from mere expenditure (which lacks the future-oriented return), from saving (which lacks the active deployment), and from speculation (投機 tōki, which the Sino-Japanese vocabulary distinguishes by the 機 'machinery / opportunity' element naming the speculative-mechanical register). The compound 投資 thus stands at the head of a precisely-articulated cluster of modern Japanese financial-economic compounds — 投資, 投機, 投資家, 投資信託, 設備投資, 海外投資 — that calibrate the Western financial-economic vocabulary across an extended structural-functional taxonomy.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its classical casting-and-committing registers as the rendering for throwing, casting, submitting, and committing. The modern financial compound 投資 was developed in the Meiji period as the standardized rendering of the Western category of 'investment' / 'Investition,' stabilized through the late-Meiji and Taishō financial-institutional discourse — the Bank of Japan (founded 1882), the Tokyo Stock Exchange (founded 1878), the broader development of the modern Japanese capital-market and corporate-finance system. The compound was adopted into Chinese (tóuzī, 投资 in simplified script) and Korean (투자 tuja) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of investment in its economic-financial sense and is productive across the modern East Asian financial vocabulary: 投資家 (investor), 投資信託 (investment trust), 設備投資 (capital investment), 直接投資 (direct investment), 海外投資 (foreign investment).

gloss: Sharp gain — the blade meeting the standing grain at harvest, and from there profit, advantage, benefit; in Meiji legal vocabulary the bearer of 'interest, claim, entitlement,' paired with 権 to render Western 'right' as a juridical claim subjects possess against authority.

components.meaning: standing grain (5 strokes) — the stalk of the cereal plant; semantic element grounding the character in the agricultural register of harvest and yield
knife radical (vertical form of 刀, 2 strokes) — the cutting edge of the harvesting blade; together with 禾 the figure is the sickle meeting the grain

graphic_evolution.form_description: 禾 (grain) beside 刀 (knife) — a sickle cutting standing grain
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense is the act of harvest itself: the sharp blade meeting the ripe stalk. From this concrete agricultural scene the character extends through 'sharpness' (利刀, sharp blade), 'efficacy / effective working' (利く, kiku, to take effect), 'advantage' (利益, profit) and finally to the abstract registers of benefit, interest, and gain. In classical Chinese 利 is paired and contrasted with 義 (rightness): the Mengzi opens with the famous repudiation of King Hui of Liang's question about 利 (How can my state be benefited?) in favor of 義 — a load-bearing dichotomy across Confucian moral-political vocabulary.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 7 strokes — 禾 (5 strokes) on the left, 刂 (2 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 利 is highly productive in financial, commercial, and legal compounds. Financial-commercial: 利益 (rieki, profit, benefit), 利子 / 利息 (rishi / risoku, interest), 金利 (kinri, interest rate), 高利 (kōri, high interest, usury), 元利 (ganri, principal and interest), 営利 (eiri, commercial gain), 暴利 (bōri, exorbitant profit). Legal-political: 権利 (kenri, right), 権利義務 (kenri gimu, rights and duties), 私利 (shiri, private interest), 公利 (kōri, public interest), 利害 (rigai, interests-and-injuries / stake), 利害関係 (rigai kankei, vested interest). The Meiji recruitment of 利 to render Western 'right' (in the juridical-claim register) is one of the structural moves of modern East Asian legal vocabulary: paired with 権 (the Sino-Japanese register of authority and calibrated power), 利 supplies the recipient-side register of advantage / claim / entitlement that 権 alone could not carry, producing the compound 権利 in which the two characters together articulate 'a power-and-benefit one is entitled to assert.'

doctrinal_notes: In 権利 (kenri, right), 利 carries the recipient-side register of claim and entitlement — what the rights-bearer is positively due — paired with 権 in its calibrated-power register to articulate 'a benefit one is authorized to claim.' The Mengzi-derived classical opposition between 利 and 義 (the Confucian dichotomy of self-interested gain versus moral rightness) was a structural impediment to the Meiji recruitment of 利 for the juridical-rights vocabulary: in the classical register, 利 carries a faint moral suspicion as the merely-self-interested category, while 義 carries the morally-elevated register. Early Meiji translators experimented with alternative compounds — Nishi Amane and others tried 権理 (kenri, with 理 'principle' instead of 利) precisely to avoid the merely-self-interested register, and the variant orthography 権理 / 権利 circulated through the 1870s before 権利 stabilized as the standard form by the 1880s constitutional drafting period. The choice of 利 over 理 was doctrinally consequential: it located the rights-vocabulary within the calculus of advantage and claim rather than within the deontological register of principle, calibrating the modern East Asian rights-vocabulary closer to the English 'right' (as benefit one may claim) than to the Kantian Recht (as principle of practical reason).
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its classical agricultural and commercial registers as the rendering of 'sharpness, advantage, profit, interest.' Classical and medieval Japanese usage covers the agricultural register (利く, to take effect; 利刀, sharp blade), the commercial-financial register (利息, interest; 元利, principal-and-interest), and the broader register of benefit and gain (利益, advantage). The Buddhist deployment of 利 as 'benefit, blessing' (利他, benefiting others; 自利利他, self-benefit and other-benefit) also enters Japanese with the Buddhist transmission and remains a load-bearing register in Mahāyāna soteriological vocabulary. The Meiji recruitment of 利 to render Western 'right' in the juridical sense was developed across the 1860s–1880s through the work of Mitsukuri Rinshō, Tsuda Mamichi, and the broader translation apparatus of the early-Meiji legal-political vocabulary, with the compound 権利 stabilizing as the universal modern East Asian rendering of right by the 1880s constitutional drafting period.

gloss: Work that must be done — the binding force of duty pressed upon one by office, station, or relation; in Meiji legal vocabulary the bearer of 'obligation' as a juridical bond, paired with 義 to render Western 'duty' as the structural correlate of right.

components.meaning: spear, halberd (5 strokes) — phonetic element supplying the wù sound; in the older etymological reading also semantic in the register of forceful application
to follow, to walk slowly (3 strokes) — semantic element of action carried out under direction
strength, force (2 strokes) — semantic element marking the exertion of effort that must be applied

graphic_evolution.form_description: 矛 (spear) above 力 (strength) with action element 夂 — applying force as one is directed
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense is the forceful application of effort under direction — work that one is required to perform, the discharge of task or office. From this concrete sense the character extends to 'duty, office, charge, business' across classical Chinese administrative-political vocabulary. In classical usage 務 is bound up with the Confucian register of office and station: 君子務本 ('the gentleman attends to the root,' Analects 1.2) places 務 in the deontological register of what one must structurally apply oneself to.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 11 strokes — 矛 above-left, 夂 above-right, 力 below
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 務 is productive across administrative, professional, and legal compounds. Administrative: 公務 (kōmu, public office), 公務員 (kōmuin, civil servant), 任務 (ninmu, mission, charge), 職務 (shokumu, official duty), 業務 (gyōmu, business operations). Office-political: 外務 (gaimu, foreign affairs), 内務 (naimu, internal affairs), 法務 (hōmu, legal affairs), 財務 (zaimu, financial affairs), 総務 (sōmu, general affairs). Legal-juridical: 義務 (gimu, obligation, duty), 義務教育 (gimu kyōiku, compulsory education), 義務違反 (gimu ihan, breach of duty), 債務 (saimu, debt obligation), 義務者 (gimusha, the duty-bound party). The Meiji recruitment of 務 in the legal compound 義務 calibrates the classical register of office-bound-duty for the Western juridical category of obligation as a structural correlate of right.

doctrinal_notes: In 義務 (gimu, obligation/duty), 務 carries the register of binding-task — the work one is structurally required to perform — paired with 義 (rightness, what is properly due) to articulate the Western juridical category of obligation as the structural correlate of 権利 (right). The compound is calibrated against 権利 / 義務 as the paired axis of modern legal subjecthood: the rights one may claim and the duties one is bound to discharge. The Confucian register of 務 as office-bound-duty (the Analects's 務本, the Mencian register of 務 as the structural application of effort to what is properly one's task) supplies the underlying classical resonance, while the Meiji deployment in 義務 calibrates the term for the modern juridical register of obligation as a legally-enforceable bond.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its classical administrative and bureaucratic registers as the rendering of 'office, duty, charge.' Classical and medieval Japanese usage covers the full range of Sino-Japanese administrative compounds (公務 public office, 政務 governmental affairs, 職務 official duty, 任務 charge or mission) and the broader register of structural-deontological binding (務める, tsutomeru, to perform one's duty / to serve in office). The Meiji recruitment of 務 in 義務 (as the structural correlate of 権利 in the modern legal-juridical vocabulary) was stabilized across the 1860s–1880s through the early Meiji legal-translation apparatus — Mitsukuri Rinshō's translations of the French Civil and Penal Codes, the early Meiji constitutional drafting process, and the broader institutional articulation of modern Japanese legal vocabulary. The compound 義務 was adopted into Chinese (yìwù), Korean (의무), and Vietnamese (nghĩa vụ) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of legal-juridical obligation.

gloss: Pitch-pipe and ordinance — the calibrated tube that fixes the standard tone, and from there the rule that fixes the standard order; carries musical, monastic, and legal registers across its classical history, with the Meiji deployment in 法律 calibrating it for Western statutory law.

components.meaning: step, walking radical (3 strokes) — semantic element related to ordered walking, the regular gait that follows a path
writing brush, the act of inscribing (6 strokes) — semantic-phonetic element: the writing-down that fixes the rule

graphic_evolution.form_description: 彳 (step) on the left beside 聿 (writing brush) on the right — ordered conduct fixed in writing
graphic_evolution.notes: The classical etymology connects 律 to the calibrated bamboo pitch-pipes (律呂, lǜlǚ) used in Chinese musical-theoretical practice to fix the standard tones of the twelve-tone scale (十二律, the twelve lǜ). From this primary musical-calibrational register the character extends through 'rule, standard, ordinance' to the legal-administrative register: a 律 is the calibrated standard against which conduct is measured, the fixed rule that orders human action as the pitch-pipe orders musical tone. The classical Chinese legal codes from the Qin and Han onward used 律 as the operating term for the body of statutory criminal law (秦律, 漢律, 唐律), and the term remained the standard Sino-Japanese legal-statutory category across the imperial Chinese tradition.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 9 strokes — 彳 (3 strokes) on the left, 聿 (6 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 律 carries three principal registers. Musical: 律呂 (ritsuryo, the twelve calibrated pitches), 旋律 (senritsu, melody), 音律 (onritsu, pitch). Monastic-Buddhist: 律宗 (risshū, the Vinaya school of Buddhist monastic discipline), 戒律 (kairitsu, monastic precepts), 律師 (risshi, vinaya master). Legal-statutory: 法律 (hōritsu, statutory law), 律令 (ritsuryō, statutory and administrative codes — the Tang-style codes adopted in Nara-Heian Japan, e.g., the 大宝律令 Taihō Code of 701), 一律 (ichiritsu, uniform application of the rule), 自律 (jiritsu, autonomy, self-rule), 規律 (kiritsu, discipline, regulation). The Meiji deployment of 律 in 法律 calibrates the classical statutory-code register for the modern Western category of statute / legislation — the operational legal rule produced by a legislative body within the constitutional order.

doctrinal_notes: In 法律 (hōritsu, statutory law), 律 carries the calibrated-rule register — the fixed standard issued by authoritative legislation — paired with 法 in its operational-regulatory register to articulate the modern Western category of statutory law. The compound is doctrinally distinguished from 憲法 (constitutional law, the foundational instrument) within the modern East Asian legal vocabulary: 憲法 names the constitutive higher-law standing above ordinary legislation, while 法律 names the ordinary statute enacted by the legislature within the constitutional framework. The Buddhist register of 律 as 'monastic discipline, vinaya' (the regulatory code of the saṅgha) provides the underlying classical resonance for the calibrational-regulatory dimension of the term: a 律 is what fixes and orders the conduct of those bound by it, whether the bound community is a monastic saṅgha or a modern political subject-population. The classical East Asian legal codes (秦律, 漢律, 唐律, 律令) supply the deeper structural-statutory register through which 律 entered modern Meiji legal vocabulary as the operating element for the Western category of statute.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its classical statutory and musical registers. The Nara-period adoption of the Tang-style 律令 (ritsuryō) legal-administrative system — the 大宝律令 (Taihō Code, 701) and 養老律令 (Yōrō Code, 718) — established 律 as the operating term for the statutory-criminal-law portion of the imperial-administrative code, with 令 (ryō) as the operating term for the administrative-regulatory portion. The Buddhist register of 律 as monastic vinaya (戒律, the precepts) entered Japanese with the Buddhist transmission and remained a load-bearing register in Japanese Buddhist vocabulary, especially in the 律宗 (Risshū, the Vinaya school) brought to Japan by Ganjin (鑑真) in 754. The Meiji recruitment of 律 in 法律 was stabilized through the early Meiji legal-translation apparatus, with the compound becoming the universal modern East Asian rendering of statutory law across Chinese (fǎlǜ), Korean (법률), and Vietnamese (pháp luật).

gloss: To cut and shape — the tailor's blade laying out the cloth, and from there to decide, to adjudicate; in Meiji legal vocabulary the bearer of 'judicial discrimination,' paired with 判 to render Western 'trial' as the formal cutting-apart of truth from claim.

components.meaning: garment, cloth (6 strokes) — semantic element: the cloth being cut, the material on which the tailoring action is performed
the cutting-blade element (6 strokes) — semantic-phonetic: the cutting motion, supplying both meaning and the cái sound

graphic_evolution.form_description: 衣 (cloth) wrapped around 𢦏 (cutting blade) — the tailor's cut
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense is the tailor's act of cutting cloth to shape — the determinate severing that produces a fitted garment. From this concrete sense the character extends through 'to cut, to shape, to decide upon' to the abstract registers of judgment and adjudication: a judicial decision is structurally a cutting — a determinate severing of one party's claim from another's, the fitting of facts to law as the tailor fits cloth to body. Classical Chinese usage carries the dual register of tailoring (裁縫, sewing-and-tailoring) and adjudication (裁断, judicial decision).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 12 strokes — 衣 wrapped around 𢦏
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 裁 carries three principal registers. Tailoring-shaping: 裁縫 (saihō, sewing and tailoring), 裁断 (saidan, cutting cloth; also judicial cutting/decision), 体裁 (teisai, outward form, appearance). Discretionary: 裁量 (sairyō, discretion, discretionary judgment), 制裁 (seisai, sanction, punitive measure), 仲裁 (chūsai, arbitration, mediation). Judicial: 裁判 (saiban, trial, adjudication), 裁判所 (saibansho, court of law), 裁判官 (saibankan, judge), 民事裁判 (minji saiban, civil trial), 刑事裁判 (keiji saiban, criminal trial). The Meiji deployment in 裁判 calibrates the classical adjudicatory-cutting register for the modern Western category of judicial trial, with the compound becoming the operating term across the modern Japanese judicial system.

doctrinal_notes: In 裁判 (saiban, trial), 裁 carries the register of authoritative judicial cutting — the determinate severing by which the court decides between competing claims — paired with 判 (to determine, to mark, to discriminate) to articulate the Western category of judicial adjudication. The compound names the formal procedure by which competing legal claims are presented to a court and resolved through authoritative determination, calibrating the classical East Asian adjudicatory vocabulary for the modern Western judicial system. The classical register of 裁 as tailoring supplies the underlying doctrinal resonance: a judicial decision is structurally a cutting and fitting — the cutting of facts to law, the fitting of remedy to claim — and the Sino-Japanese metaphor preserves the determinate-shaping register that the Western 'trial' (from try, to test) does not foreground.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its classical tailoring and discretionary registers. Classical and medieval Japanese usage covers the tailoring sense (裁縫) and the broader register of authoritative cutting-and-deciding (裁定, authoritative decision; 裁断, decisive judgment). The judicial-adjudicatory register was present in classical legal usage but acquired its modern systematic articulation through the Meiji judicial reforms of the 1870s–1890s — the establishment of the modern Japanese court system through the Justice Ministry (司法省, established 1871), the codification of criminal procedure through the 治罪法 (1880) and the modern 刑事訴訟法 (1890), and the broader institutional articulation of an independent judiciary modeled on French and German judicial-administrative practice. The compound 裁判 was stabilized as the operating term for the modern Western judicial trial through this Meiji judicial-reform process and adopted into Chinese (cáipàn), Korean (재판), and Vietnamese (tài phán) as the universal modern East Asian rendering.

gloss: To split and decide — the blade halving what was joined, and from there to discriminate, to pronounce judgment; in Meiji legal vocabulary the bearer of 'authoritative determination,' paired with 裁 to articulate the formal pronouncement that resolves a legal claim.

components.meaning: half (5 strokes) — semantic-phonetic element: the action of halving, supplying both the sense of dividing-into-two and the pàn sound
knife radical (vertical form of 刀, 2 strokes) — the cutting blade by which the halving is effected

graphic_evolution.form_description: 半 (half) on the left beside 刂 (knife) on the right — the blade dividing what was whole
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense is the determinate cutting that produces two parts from one — the splitting that resolves a whole into discriminated halves. From this concrete sense the character extends through 'to discriminate, to distinguish' to the abstract registers of judgment and authoritative determination: a 判 is a determinate pronouncement that resolves a question by separating the parts that must be distinguished. Classical Chinese usage covers 判決 (judicial decision), 判官 (judge or magistrate), 判別 (to discriminate).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 7 strokes — 半 (5 strokes) on the left, 刂 (2 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 判 is productive across discriminative, evaluative, and judicial compounds. Discriminative-evaluative: 判別 (hanbetsu, discrimination, distinction), 判断 (handan, judgment, decision), 批判 (hihan, criticism, critical judgment), 判定 (hantei, evaluation, ruling). Judicial-formal: 裁判 (saiban, trial), 判決 (hanketsu, judicial verdict), 判事 (hanji, judge), 判例 (hanrei, judicial precedent). Evidentiary: 印判 (inban, seal, stamp), 判子 (hanko, personal seal). The Meiji deployment of 判 in 裁判 and 判決 calibrates the classical register of discriminative-determination for the modern Western category of judicial pronouncement, with the compound 裁判 stabilizing as the operating term for trial across modern East Asian judicial vocabulary.

doctrinal_notes: In 裁判 (saiban, trial), 判 supplies the pronouncement-side register of judicial determination — the authoritative decision that resolves a legal claim — paired with 裁 in its adjudicatory-cutting register. The compound is structurally articulated as 'the cutting and the deciding' — 裁 (the determinative severance) + 判 (the formal pronouncement) — preserving the dual structure of a judicial trial as both the procedural cutting-apart of competing claims and the authoritative determination by which the court resolves the claim. The classical East Asian judicial register of 判 (the magistrate's pronouncement, the formal verdict) supplies the underlying structural register through which the term entered modern Meiji legal vocabulary, with the broader cluster of compounds — 判決, 判事, 判例, 判官 — articulating the operational vocabulary of the modern judicial system.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its classical discriminative and judicial registers. Classical and medieval Japanese usage covers the discriminative sense (判じる, hanjiru, to discriminate or interpret) and the broader register of authoritative pronouncement (判官, hangan, classical magistrate; 判決, hanketsu, decree). The character is also load-bearing in classical Japanese seal-and-stamp vocabulary (花押, kaō, the ceremonial signature; 印判, formal seal), with the modern Japanese hanko (判子) inheriting this evidentiary register. The Meiji deployment in the modern judicial vocabulary — 裁判, 判決, 判事, 判例 — was stabilized through the 1870s–1890s judicial-reform process and adopted into Chinese (pàn), Korean (판), and Vietnamese (phán) as the standard modern East Asian rendering of the judicial-determinative register.

gloss: Person — the primitive figure of a standing human, one of the most elementary pictographs in the script; in modern political-legal vocabulary the structural unit of the rights-bearing subject, calibrated against 国民 (citizen-of-a-nation) and 臣民 (imperial subject) toward the universal-anthropological register that the natural-law tradition requires.

graphic_evolution.form_description: A side view of a standing person — head suggested above, two legs descending below, the torso slightly inclined forward
graphic_evolution.notes: One of the most immediately legible oracle bone pictographs. The figure stands in profile rather than facing the viewer, with the body's vertical axis carried by the legs and the slight forward inclination suggesting a person engaged in motion or work. The character is foundational not only as a stand-alone graph but as a structural element across the script: variants of the human figure appear as the radicals 亻 (left-side person), 儿 (legs of a person), and 入 (entering), anchoring the entire vocabulary of human-related characters.

graphic_evolution.form_description: The figure stylizes — the legs become two diverging strokes, the torso a single curving line above
graphic_evolution.notes: The bronze form abstracts the pictograph while preserving its essential bipedal-vertical structure. By the Bronze period the character is already functioning as the primary semantic element across the broader script, with compound characters using the human-figure component developing across the bronze inscriptions in registers from kinship-and-name vocabulary to ritual-religious terminology.

graphic_evolution.form_description: Two strokes — a downward-leftward stroke and a downward-rightward stroke meeting at the top
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 人 retains the bipedal structure of the original pictograph in radically simplified form. The character is enormously productive across compound vocabulary: 人間 (ningen, human being), 個人 (kojin, individual), 人民 (jinmin, the people), 人類 (jinrui, humankind), 人生 (jinsei, human life), 人格 (jinkaku, personhood), 人権 (jinken, human rights), 人口 (jinkō, population). The doubled-character form 人々 (hitobito, people) deploys 人 reduplicatively through the iteration mark 々, articulating the indigenous register of plurality.

doctrinal_notes: In 人権 (jinken, human rights), 人 carries the universal-anthropological register: the rights articulated are not those of a citizen, subject, or member of a particular polity, but of the human being as such — the structural unit of the natural-law tradition that articulates rights as inhering in human nature prior to and independent of political institution. The character's structural role in this register is doctrinally consequential: 国民 (kokumin, citizen-of-a-nation) and 臣民 (shinmin, imperial subject) calibrate the rights-vocabulary toward national-political membership, while 人 calibrates it toward universal humanity. The Meiji-period vocabulary of 天賦人権 (tenpu jinken, heaven-endowed human rights), prominent in the 1870s–1880s Freedom and People's Rights Movement (自由民権運動), deploys 人 specifically to articulate the natural-law register in which rights are pre-political moral entitlements grounded in the structure of human nature itself rather than imperial-grant prerogatives bestowed by political authority.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character — present in Japanese writing from the earliest stratum of script adoption in the 5th–6th centuries, mapping onto the native Japanese ひと (hito, person) in indigenous vocabulary. Classical and medieval Japanese usage covers the full range of Sino-Japanese registers across philosophical, legal, religious, and literary contexts, with the character functioning across both the Sino-Japanese on-readings (じん, にん) and the native kun-reading (ひと) in productive complementary distribution. The character's load-bearing modern political-legal register is largely Meiji-era: the wasei-kango compounds 個人 (kojin, individual), 人権 (jinken, human rights), 人民 (jinmin, the people), 人格 (jinkaku, personhood), and the broader vocabulary of liberal-political-philosophical subjecthood are Meiji coinages or Meiji re-coinages of classical compounds, and they became standard across Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese political-legal discourse through the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

gloss: To incise, to bind by mutual incision — the original sense is the carving of matching tally-sticks that, when broken in two and rejoined, prove a contract between parties; in modern legal vocabulary the structural element of binding agreement, anchoring the compound 契約.

components.meaning: incised marks (3 strokes) — the upper element representing the cuts inscribed on a tally-stick that constitute the evidentiary record of agreement
knife (2 strokes) — semantic element: the cutting instrument by which the incisions are made; here in the broader register of formal-instrumental act

great (3 strokes) — the lower element, in this position serving as a structural ground rather than a strict semantic contributor; the character's classification under the 大 radical reflects this graphic positioning

graphic_evolution.form_description: 丯 (incised marks) above 刀 (knife) above 大 (the figure of a person) — the act of inscribing tally-marks under the witness of a third party
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense of 契 is the inscription of paired tally-marks on a wooden or bamboo stick, which was then split between contracting parties as evidentiary proof of mutual agreement: when the two halves were rejoined and the cuts aligned, the contract was authenticated. This concrete sense of physical-evidentiary mutual binding generates the broader semantic field of the character: 契 names the structurally-binding agreement between parties whose mutual commitment is established through formal procedure. Classical Chinese deploys 契 across a range of compounds — 契文 (carved inscription, used of oracle-bone writing), 契約 (mutual agreement), 黙契 (silent compact), 契合 (mutual fit, accord) — that all preserve the underlying structural register of mutual binding through formal articulation.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 9 strokes — the upper element 丯 simplified, 刀 (2 strokes) on the upper right, 大 (3 strokes) at the bottom
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 契 carries the binding-agreement register across legal and personal compounds. Legal: 契約 (keiyaku, contract), 契約書 (keiyakusho, contract document), 雇用契約 (koyō keiyaku, employment contract), 売買契約 (baibai keiyaku, sales contract), 婚姻契約 (kon'in keiyaku, marriage contract), 違約 (iyaku, breach of agreement). Personal-relational: 契り (chigiri, bond, pledge — used of marital and intimate vows), 黙契 (mokkei, tacit agreement). The character's load-bearing modern legal register is anchored in the compound 契約, the operating term of modern continental civil-law contract doctrine across East Asia.

doctrinal_notes: In 契約 (keiyaku, contract), 契 supplies the structural-binding register: the mutual incision-and-pledge by which parties commit themselves to a determinate undertaking, with the evidentiary structure of the classical tally-stick standing as the etymological ground of the modern doctrinal articulation. The Meiji recruitment of 契 to render the Western category of contract was not a coinage but a calibration: the classical compound 契約 already named mutual agreement in pre-modern Sino-Japanese vocabulary, and the Meiji legal-translation apparatus recalibrated the term toward the systematic continental-civil-law category of contract as a juridically-enforceable bond between abstract legal subjects. The classical-relational register of 契 (intimate pledge, tacit accord) continues to inflect the modern legal-juridical register subtly: a 契約 carries faint resonance of relational commitment that the bare Anglo-American 'contract' as bargained-for exchange does not fully convey, and this resonance shapes the doctrinal style of modern Japanese contract law.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its classical register of mutual binding through formal articulation. Classical Japanese usage preserves both the legal-contractual register (契約) and the personal-relational register (契り, the marital or intimate pledge), with the latter prominent in Heian-period vernacular literature — the famous opening of the Tale of Genji's 'Yūgao' chapter pivots on a chigiri (契り) that binds the protagonist to an unforeseen intimacy, and the term carries the Buddhist register of karmic predetermination of relational bonds across many medieval literary deployments. The character's load-bearing modern legal register is Meiji-era: the wasei-kango compound 契約 was recalibrated through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus, particularly through Mitsukuri Rinshō's translations of the French Civil Code in the 1870s, as the operating term for the modern continental civil-law category of contract. The compound has been adopted into Chinese (qìyuē, 契约 in simplified script), Korean (계약 gyeyak), and Vietnamese (khế ước) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of contract in its juridical-enforceable sense.

gloss: To bind with a cord, to tighten into a knot — the silk-thread radical with a phonetic; by extension to make a promise, to commit to a terse formulation, to constrain into a determinate form. In contractual vocabulary the binding-element that ties parties to a determinate undertaking; in mathematical and rhetorical vocabulary the abridging-element that compresses to essentials.

components.meaning: silk thread radical (6 strokes) — semantic element: the cord or thread by which binding is effected; here the structural register of the binding-and-tying that the character names
ladle, spoon (3 strokes) — phonetic-semantic element supplying the yuē sound; also carrying the secondary register of measured-portion appropriate to the calibrated tightness of binding

graphic_evolution.form_description: 糸 (silk thread) on the left with the phonetic 勺 element on the right — the figure of a thread tightened into a measured binding
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense of 約 is the binding of an object with a cord pulled tight to a determinate measure — the physical-mechanical act of securing through tightening. From this concrete sense the character extends across a wide semantic range: to bind by mutual agreement (約束, the tied-and-bound), to abridge or compress into essentials (要約, the boiling-down), to approximate or estimate (約数, the calibrated portion), to economize (節約, the disciplined tightening). The structural register of all these extensions is the same: the act of compressing or constraining into a determinate form.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 9 strokes — 糸 (6 strokes) on the left, 勺 (3 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 約 is highly productive across legal, mathematical, rhetorical, and economic vocabulary. Legal-contractual: 契約 (keiyaku, contract), 約束 (yakusoku, promise), 条約 (jōyaku, treaty), 婚約 (kon'yaku, engagement), 解約 (kaiyaku, cancellation of agreement), 違約 (iyaku, breach). Rhetorical-abbreviative: 要約 (yōyaku, summary), 概約 (gaiyaku, outline), 節約 (setsuyaku, economy/thrift). Mathematical-approximative: 約 (yaku, approximately), 約数 (yakusū, divisor). The character's load-bearing register across these domains is the structural sense of binding-and-compressing into determinate form.

doctrinal_notes: In 契約 (keiyaku, contract), 約 supplies the binding-and-determining register: the parties are tied to a determinate undertaking through the agreed terms, with the structural sense of cord-tightened-to-measure standing as the etymological ground of the contractual bond. The compound's pairing of 契 (mutual incision, evidentiary articulation) with 約 (binding-tightening, determinate constraint) articulates the dual structure of contract as both formal mutual articulation and structural binding-into-obligation, preserving in the Sino-Japanese compound a doctrinal precision that the bare English 'contract' (from contrahere, to draw together) does not foreground. The character's broader productivity across treaty (条約), promise (約束), and abridgment (要約) calibrates 約 as the operating element of binding-formal-articulation across the modern East Asian vocabulary of agreement and compression.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period across both the legal-contractual register and the broader register of binding-and-compression. Classical Japanese usage covers the full range — 約束 (yakusoku, promise) is attested across classical and medieval texts as the operating term for personal pledge, 条約 (jōyaku, formal treaty) is deployed in classical diplomatic vocabulary, and the rhetorical register of 要約 is productive across classical Sino-Japanese commentary. The character's load-bearing modern legal register is Meiji-era: 契約 was recalibrated through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus as the operating term for contract, and 条約 was institutionalized through the Meiji diplomatic apparatus as the operating term for international treaty (the Ansei Treaties of 1858, the Treaty of Friendship and Commerce with the United States, and the unequal-treaty negotiations of the 1860s–1890s deploy 条約 as the standard term). The compound 契約 has been adopted into Chinese (qìyuē), Korean (계약), and Vietnamese (khế ước) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of contract.

gloss: To transgress, to commit a violation — the dog/beast radical with a phonetic-semantic element articulating the act of crossing a forbidden boundary; in modern legal vocabulary the structural element of the criminal act, anchoring the compound 犯罪.

components.meaning: beast radical (3 strokes), the side form of 犬 (dog) — semantic element: the wild or unrestrained register against which civilized order defines itself; here naming the unrestrained transgressive act
kneeling figure (2 strokes) — phonetic-semantic element supplying the fàn sound and contributing the register of bent or transgressive posture against an upright authority

graphic_evolution.form_description: 犭 (beast radical) on the left with the phonetic 㔾 element on the right — the figure of a beast-like transgressor crossing the bounded order
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense of 犯 is the transgression of a boundary — the crossing-over by which one violates an established order, originally articulated through the imagery of a wild beast crossing the boundary of civilized space. Classical Chinese usage extends 犯 across a wide range of registers: the transgression of legal prohibitions (犯法, fànfǎ), the violation of taboo (犯禁, fànjìn), the offending of one's superiors (犯上, fànshàng), the affront to ritual propriety (犯礼, fànlǐ). The structural register across all these uses is the same: the act of crossing a normatively-bounded line that ought not to be crossed.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 5 strokes — 犭 (3 strokes) on the left, 㔾 (2 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 犯 carries the violation-and-transgression register across legal and broader normative compounds. Legal: 犯罪 (hanzai, crime), 犯人 (hannin, perpetrator), 犯行 (hankō, criminal act), 共犯 (kyōhan, accomplice), 主犯 (shuhan, principal offender), 再犯 (saihan, repeat offense), 防犯 (bōhan, crime prevention). Broader normative: 侵犯 (shinpan, infringement), 犯す (okasu, to violate). The character's load-bearing modern legal register is anchored in the compound 犯罪, the operating term of modern continental criminal-law doctrine across East Asia.

doctrinal_notes: In 犯罪 (hanzai, crime), 犯 supplies the active-transgressive register: the act of crossing the legal-normative line, the doing-side of the criminal occurrence as distinguished from 罪 (the structural-juridical category of the punishable wrong). The dual articulation 犯 + 罪 carries the structure of the criminal occurrence as both act and category — the agent's transgression and the legal system's classification of the transgression as falling within the category of punishable wrong. The Meiji recruitment of 犯 to render the Western criminal-law concept of the offending act calibrates the classical register of normative boundary-crossing toward the systematic continental-civil-law category of the criminal act, with the broader vocabulary of agentive criminal terms — 犯人 (perpetrator), 共犯 (accomplice), 主犯 (principal offender) — articulating the operational structure of modern criminal procedure.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period across the full range of classical Sino-Japanese registers — legal transgression (犯法), ritual violation (犯禁), and broader normative crossing-of-bounds. The native Japanese verb おか.す (okasu, to violate, to commit, to brave) is mapped onto 犯 in the earliest stratum of indigenous vocabulary and preserves the active-transgressive register in classical and modern Japanese usage. The character's load-bearing modern legal register is Meiji-era: the wasei-kango compound 犯罪 was stabilized through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus, particularly through Mitsukuri Rinshō's translations of the French Penal Code (刑法) in the 1870s, as the operating term for crime within the modern continental criminal-law tradition. The compound has been adopted into Chinese (fànzuì, 犯罪), Korean (범죄 beomjoe), and Vietnamese (phạm tội) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of crime.

gloss: A net catching wrongdoing — the original character placed a net (罒) over wrong (非), naming the entanglement of the wrongdoer in the structures of legal-ethical accountability; in modern legal vocabulary the structural-juridical category of the punishable wrong.

components.meaning: net radical (5 strokes) — semantic element: the net by which wrongdoing is caught and the wrongdoer is held to account; here the structural register of legal-juridical apprehension
wrong, not, opposing (8 strokes) — phonetic-semantic element supplying the lower portion of the character; the register of negation and opposition that constitutes the wrongdoing the net catches

graphic_evolution.form_description: 罒 (net) above 非 (wrong, opposition) — the figure of a net catching that which opposes the proper order
graphic_evolution.notes: The character 罪 was reformed in the Qin period as a substitute for the earlier graph 辠 (a self-inflicting nose-cutting figure that originally named the punishment of facial mutilation for serious wrongdoing). The Qin substitution produced 罪 as the standard graph, articulating the structural register of legal-juridical accountability through the imagery of the net catching the wrongdoer. The character's classical Chinese usage covers the full range from concrete legal-criminal categories (罪人 the criminal, 罪状 the indictment, 死罪 the capital offense) through broader moral-ethical wrongdoing (罪過 the moral fault) to religious-sin registers (Buddhist 罪業 zaigō, the negative karmic burden of evil action; Christian-translation 罪 as the rendering of sin).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 13 strokes — 罒 (5 strokes) above 非 (8 strokes)
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 罪 carries the legal-juridical register across criminal-law compounds. Legal: 犯罪 (hanzai, crime), 罪人 (zainin, criminal), 罪状 (zaijō, charges), 罪悪 (zaiaku, evil-and-wrong), 有罪 (yūzai, guilty), 無罪 (muzai, innocent), 罪刑法定主義 (zaikei hōteishugi, the principle of nulla poena sine lege). Religious-moral: 罪業 (zaigō, Buddhist karmic burden), 原罪 (genzai, original sin — Christian-translation rendering). The native Japanese kun-reading つみ (tsumi) carries the broad register of wrongdoing across legal, moral, and religious contexts in indigenous vocabulary.

doctrinal_notes: In 犯罪 (hanzai, crime), 罪 supplies the structural-juridical register: the category of punishable wrong within which the criminal act falls, the system-side classification as distinguished from 犯 (the agent-side act of transgression). The Meiji recruitment of 罪 to render the Western legal-criminal category of the offense calibrates the classical register of legal-ethical-religious accountability toward the systematic continental-civil-law category of the criminal offense, with the broader vocabulary of criminal-classification terms — 重罪 (jūzai, felony), 軽罪 (keizai, misdemeanor), 死罪 (shizai, capital offense) — articulating the operational typology of modern criminal law. The character's broader productivity across moral and religious registers — 罪業 (Buddhist karmic burden), 原罪 (Christian original sin), 罪悪感 (zaiakukan, sense of guilt) — preserves the multi-register polysemy that the modern legal vocabulary harnesses for the specifically juridical category while leaving the broader moral-ethical resonance available to inflect legal usage.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period across the full range of classical Sino-Japanese registers — legal-juridical (罪状, 死罪), Buddhist-karmic (罪業 zaigō, the negative karmic burden of unskillful action), and broader moral-ethical (罪過). The native Japanese つみ (tsumi) is mapped onto 罪 in the earliest stratum of indigenous vocabulary, with the Shinto register of 罪 as ritual pollution requiring purification (祓 harae) preserved in the Engishiki ritual codes and broader pre-modern religious vocabulary. The Buddhist register of 罪 as karmic-negative action is foundational across Japanese Buddhist vocabulary from the Nara period through the medieval and Tokugawa periods, with the standard Pure Land doctrinal vocabulary deploying 罪 in the broader register of human moral-karmic burden that the nenbutsu addresses. The character's load-bearing modern legal register is Meiji-era: the wasei-kango compound 犯罪 was stabilized through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus as the operating term for crime, with the broader cluster of criminal-law compounds — 罪状, 罪刑, 有罪, 無罪 — articulating the modern Japanese criminal-law vocabulary. The compound 犯罪 has been adopted into Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese as the universal modern East Asian rendering of crime in its juridical-criminal sense.

gloss: To wear, to be covered by, to receive — the clothing radical with a phonetic; in modern legal vocabulary the passive-receiving prefix that marks the subject who is acted upon, anchoring 被告 (defendant), 被害者 (victim), 被保険者 (the insured).

components.meaning: clothing radical (5 strokes), the side form of 衣 (garment) — semantic element: the garment that covers; here in its broader figurative register of being-covered or being-acted-upon
skin, hide (5 strokes) — phonetic-semantic element supplying the bèi sound; also contributing the secondary register of covering-surface that aligns with the garment-covering register of the radical

graphic_evolution.form_description: 衤 (garment) on the left with the phonetic-semantic 皮 element on the right — the figure of a garment covering the body
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense of 被 is to wear or to cover with — the concrete-sartorial register of putting on a garment. From this concrete sense the character extends through the figurative register of 'being covered by' to the grammatical register of the passive marker: in classical Chinese 被 is the principal grammatical particle that converts an active sentence into a passive one (X 被 Y, 'X is acted upon by Y'). The grammatical-passive deployment generated through the late-classical period a productive prefix-formation pattern in which 被 + verb articulates the passive-receiving role: 被告 (the one informed-against, defendant), 被害 (the one harmed, victim), 被疑 (the one suspected, suspect), 被保険 (the one insured).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 10 strokes — 衤 (5 strokes) on the left, 皮 (5 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 被 carries the passive-receiving register across legal, insurance, and broader administrative vocabulary. Legal: 被告 (hikoku, defendant), 被告人 (hikokunin, the accused — distinguished in modern Japanese procedural law from 被告 used in civil contexts), 被害者 (higaisha, victim), 被疑者 (higisha, suspect), 被告席 (hikokuseki, the dock). Insurance and administrative: 被保険者 (hihokensha, the insured), 被扶養者 (hifuyōsha, dependent), 被選挙権 (hisenkyoken, right to be elected — the passive-recipient counterpart to 選挙権 the right to vote). The native Japanese kun-readings こうむ.る (kōmuru, to suffer/incur), おお.う (ōu, to cover), かぶ.る (kaburu, to wear/put on) preserve the structural register of being-acted-upon in indigenous vocabulary.

doctrinal_notes: In 被告 (hikoku, defendant), 被 supplies the passive-receiving register: the subject who is informed-against rather than the subject who informs (which is 原告 genkoku, the plaintiff). The dual articulation 被 + 告 carries the structural relation of the procedural opposition: 告 names the act of formally lodging a charge or claim, and 被 names the receiving-side position of the party against whom the charge is lodged. The Meiji recruitment of 被 as the systematic passive-prefix across legal-procedural compounds — 被告, 被害者, 被疑者, 被選挙権, 被保険者 — calibrates the classical-Chinese passive-grammatical register for the modern continental-civil-law procedural vocabulary, with the prefix-formation pattern productive across the broader modern East Asian legal-administrative landscape. The character's structural role as the passive-receiving marker is one of the load-bearing features of modern Sino-Japanese legal vocabulary.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period in its concrete-sartorial register (garment, covering) and the broader figurative register of being-covered or being-acted-upon. The native Japanese kun-readings こうむ.る (kōmuru, to suffer or incur — used of receiving an unwanted action), おお.う (ōu, to cover), かぶ.る (kaburu, to wear or put on the head) preserve the structural register of receiving-and-being-covered in indigenous vocabulary. The character's classical-Chinese grammatical register as the passive-marker particle was understood by classically-trained Japanese readers but did not enter productive everyday Japanese grammar (Japanese has its own native passive construction with the auxiliary -reru/-rareru). The character's load-bearing modern legal register is Meiji-era: the wasei-kango passive-prefix pattern 被 + verb was systematized through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus as the operating mechanism for rendering the passive-recipient roles of modern continental procedural law — 被告 (defendant), 被害者 (victim), 被疑者 (suspect) — and has been adopted into Chinese (bèi-prefix, 被告 bèigào), Korean (피- prefix, 피고 pigo), and Vietnamese (bị- prefix, bị cáo) as the universal modern East Asian passive-recipient legal-procedural prefix.

gloss: To declare, to inform, to lodge formal complaint — a mouth (口) below an upper element articulating speech that brings something to authoritative attention; in legal vocabulary the formal-charge register through which prosecution and complaint are constituted.

components.meaning: ox (4 strokes) — upper element; the classical etymological reading takes the ox as a sacrificial offering whose presentation is announced to the spirits, with the announcement-element supplying the speech-act register of formal declaration
mouth (3 strokes) — semantic element: the organ of speech through which the declaration is uttered; the formal-speech register that constitutes the authoritative announcement

graphic_evolution.period: Oracle bone and bronze (甲骨文・金文)
graphic_evolution.form_description: 牛 (ox) above 口 (mouth) — the figure of a sacrificial announcement made over the offered ox
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense of 告 is the formal announcement made in ritual context — the speech-act by which a sacrifice is presented to the spirits or by which a matter is brought to authoritative attention. From this concrete-ritual sense the character extends across the broader register of formal-declarative speech: to declare (告白, gàobái), to announce (告知, gàozhī), to inform-against (告発, gàofā), to lodge complaint (告訴, gàosù), to publish or proclaim (公告, gōnggào). The structural register across all these extensions is the same: speech that brings a matter to authoritative attention through formal articulation.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 7 strokes — 牛 (4 strokes) above 口 (3 strokes)
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 告 is highly productive across legal, advertising, and broader declarative vocabulary. Legal: 告訴 (kokuso, criminal complaint), 告発 (kokuhatsu, denunciation), 被告 (hikoku, defendant), 原告 (genkoku, plaintiff), 申告 (shinkoku, formal declaration — used of tax filings, customs declarations, etc.), 通告 (tsūkoku, formal notification), 警告 (keikoku, warning). Advertising-public: 広告 (kōkoku, advertisement), 公告 (kōkoku, public notice), 予告 (yokoku, advance notice). Personal-declarative: 告白 (kokuhaku, confession). The native Japanese verb つ.げる (tsugeru, to inform, to tell) maps onto the character's basic informative-declarative register in indigenous vocabulary.

doctrinal_notes: In 被告 (hikoku, defendant), 告 supplies the formal-charge register: the act of authoritative complaint or accusation through which the legal proceeding is initiated, with 被 supplying the passive-receiving prefix that marks the party against whom the complaint is lodged. The dual articulation in the procedural pair 原告 (the one who informs / plaintiff) and 被告 (the one informed-against / defendant) preserves the structural relation between the active-charging side and the passive-receiving side of the litigation, with 告 functioning as the structural-articulating element on both sides of the relation. The Meiji recruitment of 告 as the operating term across the procedural-vocabulary cluster — 告訴 (criminal complaint), 告発 (denunciation), 被告 (defendant), 原告 (plaintiff) — calibrates the classical-Sino-Japanese register of formal declaration toward the systematic continental-civil-law procedural vocabulary of charge and complaint.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period across the full range of classical Sino-Japanese registers — ritual-religious announcement (告祭文, ritual prayer), legal-juridical complaint (告訴), and broader declarative speech (告知). The native Japanese verb つ.げる (tsugeru, to inform, to announce) is mapped onto 告 in the earliest stratum of indigenous vocabulary and preserves the basic informative-declarative register across classical and modern Japanese usage. The character's load-bearing modern legal register is Meiji-era: the wasei-kango procedural-vocabulary cluster — 告訴 (criminal complaint), 告発 (denunciation), 被告 (defendant), 原告 (plaintiff), 申告 (formal declaration) — was stabilized through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus, particularly through Mitsukuri Rinshō's translations of the French procedural codes in the 1870s, and has been adopted into Chinese (gào in 被告 bèigào, 原告 yuángào, 告诉 gàosù), Korean, and Vietnamese as the universal modern East Asian procedural-declarative vocabulary.

gloss: Origin, source, plain, the original — a spring (泉) flowing out from beneath a cliff (厂); the originating-source register that grounds compounds of cause, principle, and the active-charging procedural side of litigation.

components.meaning: cliff, factory radical (2 strokes) — semantic frame: the overhanging cliff beneath which the spring rises; the place from which the source emerges

spring, fountain (9 strokes — historically 白 over 水, white-water; in the modern composed form rendered as the elements beneath 厂) — the originating-source element, the water emerging from the rock and beginning its flow downhill

graphic_evolution.form_description: 厂 (cliff) above an element representing 泉 (spring) — a spring emerging from beneath a cliff
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense of 原 is the spring or source — the water emerging from rock at the foot of a cliff and beginning its flow. From this concrete-hydrological sense the character extends through the figurative register of origin, beginning, and source: 原因 (yuányīn, cause), 原則 (yuánzé, principle), 原理 (yuánlǐ, fundamental principle), 起原/起源 (qǐyuán, origin). A parallel-extended register names the open plain across which a stream flows: 平原 (píngyuán, plain), 草原 (cǎoyuán, grassland), 高原 (gāoyuán, plateau) — preserving the topographic-source register of the spring's outflow into the surrounding landscape.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 10 strokes — 厂 (2 strokes) above the modified 泉 element (8 strokes in this composition)
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 原 carries the originating-source register across legal, scientific, and topographic vocabulary. Legal-procedural: 原告 (genkoku, plaintiff — the originating-charging party in litigation), 原審 (genshin, the original trial / lower court), 原本 (genpon, the original document), 原状 (genjō, the original state). Scientific-causal: 原因 (gen'in, cause), 原則 (gensoku, principle), 原理 (genri, fundamental principle), 原子 (genshi, atom — the originating particle), 原素/元素 (genso, element). Topographic: 平原 (heigen, plain), 草原 (sōgen, grassland), 高原 (kōgen, plateau). The native Japanese kun-readings はら (hara, plain / field — preserved in many Japanese place-names and surnames) and もと (moto, origin / source — preserved in the verb もと.づく, motozuku, to be based on) preserve the originating-topographic register in indigenous vocabulary.

doctrinal_notes: In 原告 (genkoku, plaintiff), 原 supplies the originating-active register: the party from whom the legal proceeding originates through the active lodging of the formal complaint, with 告 supplying the formal-charge register. The dual articulation in the procedural pair 原告 (the one who informs / plaintiff) and 被告 (the one informed-against / defendant) preserves the structural relation between the active-originating side and the passive-receiving side of the litigation, with 告 functioning as the structural-articulating element on both sides of the relation and the prefix-pair 原 / 被 marking the active-passive opposition. The Meiji recruitment of 原 as the originating-active prefix in 原告 calibrates the classical-Sino-Japanese register of source-and-origin toward the systematic continental-civil-law procedural vocabulary of plaintiff-defendant opposition. The character's broader productivity across causal-principial vocabulary — 原因, 原則, 原理 — preserves the structural register of fundamental-originating principle that grounds the modern Japanese scientific and philosophical vocabulary.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period across the full range of classical Sino-Japanese registers — topographic (平原, 高原, the open plain), causal-principial (原因, 原本, the originating cause and source-document), and broader source-vocabulary (起原, 本原). The native Japanese kun-readings はら (hara, plain / field) and もと (moto, origin / source) are mapped onto 原 in the earliest stratum of indigenous vocabulary, with the topographic-はら register preserved across Japanese place-names (秋葉原 Akihabara, 関ヶ原 Sekigahara, 小田原 Odawara) and surnames (原田, 藤原, 萩原), and the source-もと register preserved across verbal-and-nominal vocabulary (もと.づく motozuku, to be based on; もと, the foundation or source). The character's load-bearing modern legal register is Meiji-era: the procedural compound 原告 was stabilized through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus, particularly through Mitsukuri Rinshō's translations of the French procedural codes in the 1870s, and has been adopted into Chinese (yuángào), Korean (원고 wŏn'go), and Vietnamese (nguyên cáo) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of the procedural plaintiff.

gloss: Punishment, criminal sanction — the knife (刂) wielded in juridical execution; the original Sino-Japanese register of state-administered penal sanction that the modern Penal Code (刑法) inherits and recalibrates toward the rule-of-law-grounded criminal-law tradition.

components.meaning: balance, level, frame (4 strokes — historically 幵, two interlocking measures suggesting the calibrated frame of judgment) — semantic and partly phonetic element supplying the xíng sound and the structural register of measured-and-framed application

knife radical (2 strokes), the side form of 刀 — semantic element: the cutting instrument that executes the punishment; the juridical-instrumental register that carries the full force of state-administered penal sanction

graphic_evolution.period: Oracle bone and bronze (甲骨文・金文)
graphic_evolution.form_description: An element on the left (variously interpreted) beside 刂 (knife) on the right — the figure of a punishment executed by the knife
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense of 刑 is state-administered punishment, particularly corporal and capital punishment — the juridical-violent register through which the early Chinese imperial state articulated its penal authority. The classical Chinese imperial-legal tradition deployed 刑 across the foundational vocabulary of imperial penal administration: the Five Punishments (五刑, wǔxíng — branding, cutting off the nose, cutting off the feet, castration, death) as the canonical typology of corporal sanctions, the Tang Code (唐律, c. 624) as the foundational systematic articulation that subsequent East Asian penal codes inherited (Japanese Yōrō Code 養老律令 718, Korean Goryeoryul, Vietnamese Hồng Đức Code), and the broader cluster 刑罰 (xíngfá, criminal sanction), 刑名 (xíngmíng, the typology of punishments), 刑律 (xínglǜ, penal statute) supplying the operating institutional vocabulary.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 6 strokes — 开 (4 strokes) on the left, 刂 (2 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 刑 carries the criminal-penal register across the systematic vocabulary of modern continental criminal law. Statutory-systematic: 刑法 (keihō, criminal law / penal code), 刑事 (keiji, criminal matter — distinguished from 民事 minji, civil matter), 刑罰 (keibatsu, criminal sanction), 刑期 (keiki, prison sentence duration), 刑務所 (keimusho, prison / penitentiary). Doctrinal-procedural: 量刑 (ryōkei, sentencing), 求刑 (kyūkei, sentencing recommendation by the prosecution), 死刑 (shikei, capital punishment), 無期刑 (mukikei, life imprisonment), 有期刑 (yūkikei, fixed-term imprisonment), 罪刑法定主義 (zaikei hōteishugi, the principle of nulla poena sine lege). The character has no productive native Japanese kun-reading: it operates in the systematic Sino-Japanese register of state-administered penal sanction, with the broader vocabulary of native Japanese punishment-words (罰 batsu, 仕置 shioki) operating in adjacent but distinct registers.

doctrinal_notes: In 刑法 (keihō, criminal law), 刑 supplies the penal-sanction register: the state-administered punishment that responds to the legally-defined wrong, with 法 supplying the systematic-statutory register that constitutes the ordered framework within which the punishment is determined. The dual articulation 刑 + 法 articulates the doctrinal structure of modern continental criminal law: the criminal sanction (刑) is administered only within and through the systematic statutory framework (法) — the foundational principle of nulla poena sine lege (罪刑法定主義) that grounds the modern continental criminal-law tradition descending from Beccaria's On Crimes and Punishments (1764) and Feuerbach's Lehrbuch (1801). The Meiji recruitment of 刑 as the operating term across the criminal-penal vocabulary cluster — 刑法, 刑事, 刑罰, 死刑 — calibrates the classical-Sino-Japanese imperial-penal register toward the systematic continental-civil-law penal-doctrinal apparatus, with the doctrinal vocabulary 罪刑法定主義, 量刑, 求刑 articulating the modern rule-of-law-grounded penal-administrative framework. The character's institutional-historical depth across the East Asian imperial-legal tradition (Tang Code, Yōrō Code, Goryeoryul) supplies a doctrinal-vocabulary continuity that the modern wasei-kango compound 刑法 inherits while substantially recalibrating its doctrinal foundation toward the modern Western criminal-law tradition.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period through the Yōrō Code (養老律令, 718) — the foundational systematic articulation of imperial-Japanese penal-and-administrative law modeled on the Tang Code (唐律, 624) — which deployed 刑 across the operating vocabulary of classical Japanese imperial-penal administration. The character carried across the Heian, medieval, and Tokugawa periods the institutional register of state-administered punishment, with the classical Sino-Japanese vocabulary 刑罰, 五刑, 死刑 supplying the operating vocabulary of pre-modern Japanese penal authority. The Tokugawa period developed substantial penal-administrative apparatus through the bakufu's 公事方御定書 (Kujikata Osadamegaki, 1742) and the broader han-administrative legal apparatus, with the operating vocabulary continuing to deploy 刑 in its classical Sino-Japanese register. The character's load-bearing modern criminal-law register is Meiji-era: the wasei-kango compound 刑法 was stabilized through the early-Meiji legal-translation apparatus, particularly through Mitsukuri Rinshō's translations of the French Code Pénal across 1870–1874, and the broader Meiji criminal-law codification process — the Boissonade Penal Code (旧刑法, drafted by Gustave Boissonade, promulgated 1880, in force 1882–1908) and the German-influenced current Penal Code (現行刑法, 1907, drafted under the influence of the Reichsstrafgesetzbuch of 1871) — supplied the institutional-doctrinal apparatus through which 刑 was recalibrated for the modern continental criminal-law tradition. The compound 刑法 has been adopted into Chinese (xíngfǎ), Korean (형법 hyŏngpŏp), and Vietnamese (hình pháp) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of criminal law.

gloss: To warn, to alert, to be vigilant — speech (言) of admonition that places the hearer on guard; in modern institutional vocabulary the prefix that anchors the entire vocabulary of state policing and public-order administration.

components.meaning: to revere, to be respectfully attentive (12 strokes — 苟 over 攵, the figure of attentive reverence rendered through ritual gesture) — semantic and phonetic element supplying the jǐng sound and the structural register of vigilant-respectful attention
speech, word (7 strokes) — semantic element: the speech-act through which the warning or admonition is delivered; the verbal-instrumental register that carries the warning to the hearer

graphic_evolution.form_description: 敬 (reverent attention) above 言 (speech) — speech delivered with the structural register of vigilant-respectful attention
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense of 警 is the warning or admonition — speech that calls the hearer to vigilant attention. From this concrete-speech-act sense the character extends through the broader register of vigilance, alertness, and protective watchfulness: 警戒 (jǐngjiè, vigilance / guard), 警告 (jǐnggào, warning), 警報 (jǐngbào, alarm / alert), 警備 (jǐngbèi, guard / security). The classical Chinese deployment of 警 carried the broader register of admonitory-vigilant attention across military, administrative, and moral vocabulary, with the figure of the watchful sentry supplying the structural metaphor for the broader semantic field.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 19 strokes — 敬 (12 strokes) above 言 (7 strokes)
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 警 carries the institutional-policing register across the systematic vocabulary of modern state policing and public-order administration. Institutional: 警察 (keisatsu, police), 警察官 (keisatsukan, police officer), 警察署 (keisatsusho, police station), 警視庁 (Keishichō, Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department), 警察庁 (Keisatsuchō, National Police Agency). Operational: 警備 (keibi, security / guard duty), 警戒 (keikai, alert / vigilance), 警報 (keihō, alarm / warning), 警告 (keikoku, warning), 警鐘 (keishō, alarm bell / warning), 警笛 (keiteki, warning horn), 県警 (kenkei, prefectural police). Rank-and-title: 警部 (keibu, police inspector), 警視 (keishi, superintendent), 警視総監 (keishi-sōkan, superintendent-general). The character is one of the principal institutional-prefix elements of modern Japanese administrative vocabulary, with the wasei-kango compounding pattern 警 + X generating the systematic vocabulary of modern policing across the modern East Asian languages.

doctrinal_notes: In 警察 (keisatsu, police), 警 supplies the vigilance-and-warning register: the institutional function of vigilant watchfulness over public order, with 察 supplying the investigation-and-discernment register. The dual articulation 警 + 察 calibrates the modern Western institutional category of the police force toward the structural pairing of vigilant prevention (警) and investigative discernment (察) — the two structural functions of the modern state police institution. The Meiji recruitment of 警 as the operating prefix across the institutional-policing vocabulary cluster — 警察, 警察署, 警備, 警報, 警視庁 — calibrates the classical-Sino-Japanese register of admonitory-vigilant attention toward the systematic modern administrative vocabulary of state policing, with the broader Meiji institutional-administrative apparatus (the 1874 establishment of the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Bureau under Kawaji Toshiyoshi, the 1875 reorganization of the national police system) supplying the institutional context within which the compound was stabilized.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period across the classical Sino-Japanese registers of admonition, vigilance, and watchful attention. The native Japanese verb いまし.める (imashimeru, to admonish / to warn) is mapped onto 警 as one possible kun-reading, although the character operates predominantly in the systematic Sino-Japanese register across both classical and modern Japanese usage. The character's load-bearing modern institutional register is Meiji-era: the wasei-kango compound 警察 was stabilized through the early-Meiji institutional-administrative apparatus, particularly through Kawaji Toshiyoshi's (川路利良, 1834–1879) 1872–1873 European mission to study the French (and to a lesser extent the Prussian) police systems, his subsequent reports establishing the foundational vocabulary, and the 1874 establishment of the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Bureau (警視庁) under his leadership as the institutional vehicle through which the operating vocabulary of modern state policing was stabilized. The compound 警察 has been adopted into Chinese (jǐngchá), Korean (경찰 kyŏngch'al), and Vietnamese (cảnh sát) as the universal modern East Asian rendering of police.

gloss: To examine, to observe, to discern — the roof (宀) under which sacrificial offerings are inspected (祭); the investigative-discerning register that anchors the modern vocabulary of police inquiry, judicial examination, and the prosecutorial function.

components.meaning: roof radical (3 strokes) — semantic element: the sheltering frame within which the examination is conducted; the institutional-spatial register that locates the act of inspection within an authoritative space

sacrifice, ritual offering (11 strokes — 月 (meat) and 又 (hand) over 示 (altar), the figure of meat being placed by hand on the altar) — semantic and phonetic element supplying the chá sound and the structural register of careful-attentive inspection of the offering presented for ritual examination

graphic_evolution.form_description: 宀 (roof) above 祭 (sacrifice) — sacrificial offerings examined under the roof of the ritual space
graphic_evolution.notes: The original etymology connects 察 to the careful-attentive inspection of sacrificial offerings within the ritual space — the priest's discerning examination of the offering to verify its acceptability for the sacrifice. From this concrete-ritual sense the character extends through the broader register of careful examination, attentive observation, and discerning judgment: 観察 (guānchá, observation), 視察 (shìchá, inspection), 考察 (kǎochá, examination / consideration), 察知 (cházhī, to discern / to perceive). The classical Chinese deployment of 察 carried the broader register of careful-attentive examination across administrative, judicial, and moral vocabulary, with the figure of the discerning observer supplying the structural metaphor for the broader semantic field.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 14 strokes — 宀 (3 strokes) above 祭 (11 strokes)
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 察 carries the investigative-discerning register across the systematic vocabulary of modern policing, prosecution, and administrative inspection. Police: 警察 (keisatsu, police), 警察官 (keisatsukan, police officer), 警察署 (keisatsusho, police station). Prosecution: 検察 (kensatsu, prosecution / public prosecutor's office), 検察官 (kensatsukan, public prosecutor), 検察庁 (Kensatsuchō, Public Prosecutors Office), 地方検察庁 (chihō kensatsuchō, district public prosecutors office). Inspection: 視察 (shisatsu, official inspection / observation tour), 監察 (kansatsu, supervision / oversight), 観察 (kansatsu, observation), 考察 (kōsatsu, careful examination / consideration), 査察 (sasatsu, inspection / audit), 診察 (shinsatsu, medical examination). The character has no productive native Japanese kun-reading: it operates in the systematic Sino-Japanese register of investigative-administrative discernment, with the verb 察する (sassuru, to surmise / to discern / to sympathetically infer) preserving the discerning-observation register in modern Japanese usage.

doctrinal_notes: In 警察 (keisatsu, police), 察 supplies the investigation-and-discernment register: the institutional function of investigative inquiry into public-order violations and the discerning observation of social conditions, with 警 supplying the vigilance-and-warning register. The dual articulation 警 + 察 articulates the structural pairing of preventive-vigilant function (警) and investigative-discerning function (察) that constitutes the modern state police institution. In the parallel compound 検察 (kensatsu, prosecution), 察 supplies the same investigation-and-discernment register, paired with 検 (to examine / to verify / the prosecutorial-investigative function) to articulate the prosecutorial function as the systematic verification and investigation of criminal complaints. The Meiji recruitment of 察 as the operating prefix-and-suffix element across the institutional-investigative vocabulary cluster — 警察, 検察, 視察, 監察, 査察 — calibrates the classical-Sino-Japanese register of careful-attentive examination toward the systematic modern administrative vocabulary of state-investigative function, with the broader Meiji institutional-administrative apparatus supplying the institutional context within which the compounds were stabilized.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese writing from the Nara period across the classical Sino-Japanese registers of careful-attentive examination, ritual inspection, and discerning observation. The character operated predominantly in the systematic Sino-Japanese register across both classical and modern Japanese usage, with the verb 察する (sassuru) developing as the principal Japanese verbal form preserving the discerning-observation register in indigenous-vocabulary usage (preserved in expressions such as お察しします, o-sasshi shimasu, the polite-empathetic 'I sympathetically discern'). The character's load-bearing modern institutional register is Meiji-era: the wasei-kango compounds 警察 (keisatsu) and 検察 (kensatsu) were stabilized through the early-Meiji institutional-administrative apparatus, particularly through Kawaji Toshiyoshi's establishment of the modern Japanese police system (1874) and Mitsukuri Rinshō's translations of the French procedural codes (1870–1874) that institutionalized the prosecutorial function. The compounds have been adopted into Chinese (警察 jǐngchá, 检察 jiǎnchá), Korean (경찰 kyŏngch'al, 검찰 kŏmch'al), and Vietnamese (cảnh sát, kiểm sát) as the universal modern East Asian institutional vocabulary of policing and prosecution.

gloss: Sustained looking that becomes a perspective — the gaze trained on a thing until what shows itself becomes a stance; recruited by Meiji philosophy as the suffix for the cognitive viewpoint.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 雚 (heron — phonetic) beside 見 (to see) — fixed, attentive looking
graphic_evolution.notes: 雚 (guān, heron) carries the phonetic; 見 supplies the semantic frame of seeing. The combined image evokes the heron's stillness over the water — the patient, sustained gaze that is more than a glance.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 雚 (15 strokes) over 見 (3 strokes) — 18 strokes total in the modern Japanese form (観); traditional form 觀 retains the fuller 雚 element
graphic_evolution.notes: Carries the contemplative register in Buddhist usage (止観 shikan, calm-and-insight; 観音 Kannon, the bodhisattva who sees the world's suffering; 観想 visualization-meditation). Reused by Meiji philosophical translators as the suffix for cognitive perspective: 主観 (subjective view), 客観 (objective view), 観念 (idea), 世界観 (worldview), 価値観 (sense of values).

doctrinal_notes: Two registers operate in modern Japanese. In Buddhist vocabulary, 観 names contemplative insight (vipaśyanā) — the meditative seeing-into the nature of phenomena (止観, 観想, 観音). In Meiji philosophical vocabulary, 観 is the suffix that locates a cognitive perspective: 主観 / 客観 stabilize the German Subjekt / Objekt distinction by treating the cognitive relation as a relation of viewing, with 主 and 客 marking which side the view proceeds from. The doctrinal continuity between the two registers is the reading of cognition as cultivated, sustained looking rather than discrete acts of judgment.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present from the early Buddhist transmission as the operating term of contemplative practice — the Tendai 止観 system codified by Zhiyi, the visualization meditations of Pure Land and Esoteric practice, the Avalokiteśvara cult under the name 観音. The Meiji repurposing extends 観 from this contemplative register to a cognitive-perspectival register through the coinages 主観 and 客観 (Tetsugaku Jii, 1881), transferring the classical sense of trained observation onto the Kantian subject-object structure. The character has remained productive in this dual register across modern Japanese intellectual vocabulary: 観念 (idea, notion), 観点 (point of view), 観察 (observation), 楽観 (optimism), 悲観 (pessimism), 世界観 (worldview).

gloss: The one who arrives from elsewhere — the guest under another's roof; recruited by Meiji philosophy to mark the side opposite the host in the cognitive relation.
