graphic_evolution.form_description: 宀 (roof) over 各 (to arrive — phonetic and partly semantic)
graphic_evolution.notes: 宀 (a roof, a dwelling) supplies the semantic frame of habitation; 各 (kè/gè, originally 'to arrive') supplies both the phonetic and a semantic resonance: one who arrives at a dwelling. The combined image: the visitor under your roof, the guest who is not the host.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 宀 (3 strokes) over 各 (6 strokes) — 9 strokes total
graphic_evolution.notes: Carries the host-and-guest dialectic 主客 (shukyaku) across classical Sino-Japanese usage: in poetry, in courtly ritual, in Linji's host-and-guest dialectics (四主客, 'four host-and-guests' of the Linji-lu). Recruited by Meiji philosophy as the second character of 客観 (objective view), where it preserves the host-and-guest pairing — the side from which the view is not taken, the externality.

doctrinal_notes: The host-and-guest pair 主客 has a long career across East Asian intellectual vocabulary. In Tang-period Linji Chan, the four host-and-guest dialectics (四主客) name structural positions in the encounter between master and student. In Meiji philosophical translation, the same 主 / 客 pairing is reused for Subjekt / Objekt: 主観 (the master's view, the side from which knowing proceeds) and 客観 (the guest's view, the side that stands over against the knower). The repurposing is structurally elegant — the dialectical pairing was already built into the classical compound — but it carries Linji's relational register into a Kantian transcendental frame for which it was not designed.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, used across classical Sino-Japanese vocabulary for guest, visitor, traveler, and (in commercial registers) customer (顧客 kokyaku, 観客 kankyaku, 客船 kyakusen). The doctrinally consequential reuse is Meiji: 客観 (kyakkan, objective) and 客体 (kyakutai, the object as substantival counterpart to 主体 shutai) recruit 客 as the marker of the externality-side of the cognitive relation, with the host-and-guest dialectic of classical usage supplying the structural template for the Kantian subject-object distinction.

gloss: The leveling stroke that sweeps the top of a heaped measure — abstraction as the act of taking the general view across particulars; recruited as the leading character of the Meiji term for concept.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 木 (wood) beside 旣 (already / having finished — phonetic and partly semantic)
graphic_evolution.notes: 木 supplies the material-semantic element: the leveling stick used in classical East Asian grain-measuring was a piece of carved wood. 旣 (jì, already / finished) supplies the phonetic and the sense of the completing action — the sweep that finishes the measure by leveling off the heap. Original concrete sense: the wooden stick that scrapes the top of a measure flat, distinguishing what is in the measure from what overflows.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 木 (4 strokes) beside 既 (10 strokes) — 14 strokes total in the modern Japanese form
graphic_evolution.notes: From the concrete sense of leveling-stroke the character extends across an arc of related senses: 'in general,' 'roughly,' 'outline,' 'gist' (大概 taigai, generally; 概要 gaiyō, outline; 概略 gairyaku, summary; おおむね ōmune, roughly). The Meiji recruitment of 概 as the leading character of 概念 (gainen, concept) draws on this generalizing register: the concept as the abstract sweep that takes the general view across particulars.

doctrinal_notes: The character's productive Meiji compound is 概念 (gainen, concept / Begriff), where 概 supplies the register of generality and abstraction and 念 supplies the register of mental act. The compound was standardized in the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and supplies the operating East Asian term for the German Begriff and English 'concept' across Kantian, Hegelian, and broader philosophical vocabulary. Related compounds — 概観 (gaikan, general view), 概論 (gairon, introductory survey), 概説 (gaisetsu, outline) — share the generalizing register.
japanese_transmission: Present in classical Sino-Japanese vocabulary in its concrete sense (the leveling stroke) and extended generalizing senses, but operating as a relatively low-frequency character through the pre-Meiji period. Its load-bearing modern register is the Meiji philosophical coinage 概念, which made the character one of the workhorses of academic Japanese: any introductory treatment of any subject is a 概論 (gairon), any general overview is a 概要 (gaiyō), any concept is a 概念. Adopted into modern Chinese (gài) and Korean (개) usage in parallel.

gloss: Present mind on its object — the act of holding something in attention, recollecting it, mentally directing toward it; the operating character across Buddhist mindfulness and modern philosophical 'idea' alike.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 今 (now — phonetic and partly semantic) over 心 (heart-mind)
graphic_evolution.notes: 今 (jīn, now / present) supplies the phonetic and the temporal-semantic register of the present moment. 心 supplies the cognitive-affective frame of the heart-mind. The combined image: the heart-mind in present focus, the moment of attentive holding.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 今 (4 strokes) over 心 (4 strokes) — 8 strokes total
graphic_evolution.notes: Operates across a wide semantic range in classical and modern usage: thought, attention, recollection, recitation, intention, mindfulness. Buddhist usage anchors the contemplative register: 念仏 (nenbutsu, the recollection / recitation of the buddha-name), 正念 (shōnen, right mindfulness — the seventh of the Eightfold Path's items, smṛti), 一念 (ichinen, a single thought-moment). Meiji philosophical usage anchors the cognitive register: 観念 (kannen, idea / Vorstellung), 概念 (gainen, concept / Begriff), 理念 (rinen, ideal / Idee in the Hegelian-Platonic register), 信念 (shinnen, belief / conviction).

doctrinal_notes: The character is structurally load-bearing across both Buddhist contemplative vocabulary and Meiji philosophical vocabulary. In Buddhist usage, 念 is the operating term of mindfulness (smṛti / sati): the seventh limb of the Eightfold Path is 正念 (right mindfulness), and 念仏 (nenbutsu) names the central practice of Pure Land Buddhism. In Meiji philosophical usage, 念 is the suffix that names a mental act or content: 観念 carries Vorstellung (representation / idea), 概念 carries Begriff (concept), 理念 carries Idee (ideal). The Meiji repurposing extends the Buddhist contemplative register of 念 as present-mental-holding to the modern philosophical register of mental content, retaining the structural sense of cognition as a directed mental act.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, deeply embedded in Japanese Buddhist vocabulary from the Nara period through the present (the term 念 carries the central Pure Land practice 念仏 from Hōnen and Shinran's thirteenth-century articulation through to contemporary Jōdo and Jōdo-Shin liturgy). The Meiji philosophical repurposing — 観念, 概念, 理念, 信念 — recruits the character into modern intellectual vocabulary while the Buddhist register continues in parallel. The character is also productive across modern emotional-and-volitional vocabulary: 残念 (zannen, regret), 専念 (sennen, devotion), 無念 (munen, chagrin / regret — the secularized counterpart to its Buddhist sense of 'no-thought').

gloss: To draw out, pull forth, extract — the hand drawing a single strand clear of the bundle; in 抽象 the verb of abstraction itself, the drawing-out of the common form from the mass of particulars.

components.meaning: hand radical (3 strokes — the left-side variant of 手) — the semantic anchor: abstraction is figured as a manual act of drawing-out, not a passive seeing
from, by way of, cause (5 strokes) — phonetic element supplying the chōu sound; partly semantic in carrying the sense of that-out-of-which something issues, the source from which the strand is drawn

graphic_evolution.form_description: 手 (hand) beside 由 (the phonetic-semantic element naming that-from-which) — the composition names the hand drawing something clear of what contained it
graphic_evolution.notes: The concrete original sense is the hand pulling a single strand — a stalk, a thread, a sprout — free of the bundle or ground that held it. From this the character extends through classical Chinese usage to: to extract, to select out, to draw (a lot), to put forth (a shoot). The semantic logic is preserved precisely: 抽 names not the cutting or breaking of what is drawn but its clean withdrawal intact, the strand separated from the mass while both remain whole.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 8 strokes — 扌 (hand radical, 3 strokes) on the left beside 由 (5 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 抽 is productive in the vocabulary of extraction and selection: 抽出 (chūshutsu, extraction), 抽選 (chūsen, drawing of lots), 抽斗 / 引き出し (hikidashi, a drawer — that which is pulled out). The Meiji philosophical compound 抽象 (chūshō, abstraction) deploys 抽 in its precise sense of drawing-the-common-strand clear of the particulars: abstraction figured not as the erasure of the concrete but as the manual withdrawal of the shared form from the bundle of instances in which it was embedded.

japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese literate culture from the early stratum and stable in its concrete sense of drawing-out across the classical and modern periods. Its philosophically load-bearing use enters with the Meiji translation of Western logic and epistemology, where 抽象 (chūshō) is recruited to render the Latin abstractio (abs-trahere, 'to draw away from') — the Japanese compound and the Latin source converging on the identical underlying metaphor of a drawing-away, so that 抽 carries the etymological figure of the Western term with unusual fidelity. The compound was stabilized through the Meiji philosophical-translation apparatus and the Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881), regularly paired against its contrary 具象 / 具体 (the concrete).

gloss: Elephant; and thence image, form, the appearing — the creature the ancient north knew only from its bones and so reconstructed in imagination; the character by which Chinese thought came to name representation itself.

components.meaning: whole-body pictograph (12 strokes) — a single unanalyzable graph depicting the elephant: trunk, head, body, legs; the character is classified for ordering under the 豕 (swine) radical but is not compositionally derived from it

graphic_evolution.form_description: A clear pictograph of an elephant in profile — the long trunk uppermost, the heavy body and legs below
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense is the animal itself. The semantic extension to 'image, form, representation' is given a celebrated rationale in the Han Feizi (解老): living elephants were rarely seen in the ancient Chinese north, so people, finding the bones of a dead elephant, would reconstruct (想) the living animal from the skeleton — and therefore whatever is imagined from a representation came to be called 象. Whether or not the etymology is historically exact, it fixed the character's philosophical destiny: 象 became the name for that which is known by its image rather than by direct presence.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 12 strokes — the pictograph regularized; classified under the 豕 (swine) radical for lexicographic ordering
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 象 carries two registers. The concrete: 象 (zō, elephant), 象牙 (zōge, ivory). The abstract-philosophical: 現象 (genshō, phenomenon — the appearing), 抽象 (chūshō, abstraction — the form drawn out), 対象 (taishō, object — that which stands over against), 象徴 (shōchō, symbol), 印象 (inshō, impression). Across this second register 象 functions as the standard Sino-Japanese morpheme for the appearing-as-image, and it is this register the Meiji philosophical translators recruited to render the Western vocabulary of phenomenon and abstraction.

japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese from the earliest literate stratum in both its concrete (elephant) and extended (image, form) senses. Its philosophically load-bearing use is concentrated in the Meiji period, when the appearing-as-image register of 象 was recruited across the cluster 現象 (phenomenon), 抽象 (abstraction), 対象 (object), and 象徴 (symbol) to render the Western epistemological vocabulary of how reality presents itself to a knowing subject; the compounds were stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881) and remain the operating East Asian vocabulary of phenomenon and representation.

gloss: The proper ordering of human relations — the person set within the graded bonds of the Confucian five relationships; the character by which East Asian thought names ethical order as relation rather than as rule.

components.meaning: person radical (2 strokes — the left-side variant of 人) — the semantic anchor: what is ordered here is persons, the human standing-with-others
orderly arrangement, to set in sequence (8 strokes — 亼 gather over 冊 bound bamboo slips) — phonetic and semantic element: the marshalling of things into proper order, here applied to persons

graphic_evolution.form_description: 亻 (person) beside 侖 (orderly sequence) — the composition names persons set into their proper graded order
graphic_evolution.notes: The component 侖 (lún) names the act of arranging into sequence — bamboo slips gathered (亼) and bound into an ordered register (冊). Joined to the person radical, 倫 names the ordering proper to persons: the structured, graded relations within which a human being stands. From this the classical sense extends to: a relationship, one's kind or sort, moral order. The same 侖 ordered-sequence sense generates 論 (ordered speech, argument); 倫 and 論 are respectively the ordering of persons and the ordering of discourse.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 10 strokes — 亻 (person radical, 2 strokes) on the left beside 侖 (8 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: The classical-Confucian load of 倫 is the doctrine of the 五倫 (gorin, the Five Relationships): ruler–minister, father–son, husband–wife, elder–younger sibling, friend–friend — the five graded bonds within which, for the Confucian tradition, the whole of moral life is enacted. In modern Japanese the character is dominated by the Meiji compound 倫理 (rinri, ethics) and its derivatives 倫理学 (rinrigaku, the discipline of ethics), 倫理的 (rinriteki, ethical); the older native sense survives in 人倫 (jinrin, human relations / the moral order of relationships) and 不倫 (furin, the breach of a proper relation, now specifically adultery).

doctrinal_notes: 倫 carries into the Meiji rendering of Western Ethik a doctrinal commitment that the Greek-derived 'ethics' (ēthos, settled character / custom) does not foreground: that the moral domain is constituted relationally, as the proper ordering of the graded bonds between persons, rather than as the cultivation of individual character or the application of universal rule. The Confucian 五倫 inheritance means that 倫理 names ethics first as the rectification of relationship — the right ordering of ruler and minister, parent and child, the bonds within which a self is always already situated — and only derivatively as a theory of obligation or value abstracted from those bonds. This relational inheritance has shaped the East Asian reception of Western moral philosophy: Kantian deontology and utilitarian consequentialism both arrive in a vocabulary whose root character locates the ethical in the structure of human relations, generating a productive friction with moral theories built on the autonomous individual.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese from the earliest Confucian-textual stratum and load-bearing across the Edo-period reception of Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism, where the 五倫 doctrine structured the moral-pedagogical curriculum of the samurai and merchant academies. Its modern philosophical use is the Meiji compound 倫理 (rinri), coined to render Western Ethik / ethics: the translators recruited the Confucian relational-order character precisely because it already named the domain of right human relation, and the compound was stabilized in the disciplinary form 倫理学 through Nishi Amane's coinages and the Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881).

gloss: Ordered speech — discourse marshalled into sequence and consequence; argument, treatise, theory, and, in the Meiji recoinage 論理, the Western logos rendered as the order of reasoning itself.

components.meaning: speech radical (7 strokes) — the semantic anchor: what is being ordered here is language, the said
orderly arrangement, to set in sequence (8 strokes — 亼 gather over 冊 bound bamboo slips) — phonetic and semantic element: speech gathered and bound into proper sequence, hence reasoned discourse

graphic_evolution.form_description: 言 (speech) beside 侖 (orderly sequence) — the composition names speech set into ordered, consequent arrangement
graphic_evolution.notes: 侖 (lún) is the same ordered-sequence component that gives 倫 the ordering of persons; in 論 it gives the ordering of speech. The concrete classical sense is collated, sequenced discourse: the Lúnyǔ (論語, the Analects) is the 'ordered / collated sayings' of Confucius. From this the character extends to: to discuss, to argue, to assess, a treatise, a doctrine. The semantic core is consistent — 論 is not mere speech (言) but speech brought into order and consequence.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 15 strokes — 言 (speech radical, 7 strokes) on the left beside 侖 (8 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Japanese 論 is among the most productive characters of intellectual vocabulary: 議論 (giron, debate), 理論 (riron, theory), 論文 (ronbun, treatise / academic paper), 論証 (ronshō, demonstration), 結論 (ketsuron, conclusion), 論争 (ronsō, controversy), 評論 (hyōron, critique). The Meiji philosophical compound 論理 (ronri, logic) pairs 論 (ordered discourse) with 理 (principle, rational order) to name the principle of right reasoning — the science of the order that valid discourse must observe.

japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present from the earliest stratum of Japanese literacy through its load-bearing classical use in 論語 (the Analects) and the Buddhist treatise-genre 論 (ron, śāstra — the doctrinal treatises of the canon, as against sūtra and vinaya). Its modern philosophical use is the Meiji compound 論理 (ronri), coined to render Western 'logic'; the compound entered Chinese as well but was there partly displaced by Yan Fu's phonetic rendering 邏輯 (luóji), so that 論理 marks one of the relatively rare points where the Japanese semantic calque and a competing Chinese transliteration both survived. The disciplinary form 論理学 (ronrigaku) was stabilized through Nishi Amane's coinages and the Tetsugaku Jii (哲学字彙, 1881).

gloss: The heart sounding itself out — 音 (sound) over 心 (heart): mind as directed intent, the leaning of awareness toward a meaning it means.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 音 (sound) set above 心 (heart) — what the heart utters or holds in voice
graphic_evolution.notes: The composition reads as the heart-mind making a sound: intention as the inner saying that precedes the spoken word. From this come the two great senses — "meaning" (what is meant) and "intent / will" (the meaning-toward-something).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 立 + 日 (the reduced 音) over 心 — 13 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Stable from the clerical reform onward. Functions across the Meiji mental-philosophical vocabulary as the directed-mind element: 意識 (consciousness), 意志 (will), 意味 (meaning), 注意 (attention).

doctrinal_notes: In Yogācāra scholasticism 意 renders manas — the seventh, deliberative-and-self-grounding consciousness — held distinct from 心 (citta) and 識 (vijñāna) in the canonical triad 心意識. This prior technical saturation as the *directed, appropriative* aspect of mind is exactly what made 意 available, in Meiji, as the volitional-intentional half of compounds for Western mental concepts.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character, present from the earliest stratum of Sino-Japanese literacy and used in its ordinary senses ("meaning," "intention") throughout the classical language. Its specialized depth is Buddhist: Nara- and Heian-period Hossō (Yogācāra) study fixed 意 as a technical term for manas within the 心意識 triad. The Meiji philosophical-translation movement then drew on that depth, recruiting 意 as the intentional/volitional component of 意識, 意志, and the broader vocabulary of mind, will, and attention now standard across Japanese, Chinese, and Korean.

gloss: Knowing as marking-off — 言 (word) beside 戠 (banner, distinguishing mark): cognition that discriminates one thing from another; the Buddhist vijñāna.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 言 (speech / word) with phonetic-semantic 戠 (a marked banner, an emblem that distinguishes)
graphic_evolution.notes: The 戠 element carries the sense of a distinguishing mark or sign; with 言 the character names knowing-by-discrimination — to recognize is to tell apart and to name. The reading ショク preserves the sense "to record, to mark down" (as in 標識).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 言 radical at left, 音 + 戈 at right — 19 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Stable in the received script. As a single character it means "to know / discriminate / recognize"; as a Buddhist technical term it is the dominant rendering of vijñāna and the head of the eight-consciousness taxonomy (八識).

doctrinal_notes: The load-bearing Yogācāra term: 識 = vijñāna, "consciousness" as discriminating cognition, enumerated as the eight consciousnesses (八識) culminating in the 阿頼耶識 (ālaya-vijñāna, store-consciousness). Because 識 had for a millennium *been* the East Asian Buddhist word for consciousness, the Meiji coiners did not invent a sign for "consciousness" so much as bind this saturated term to the directed-mind 意, letting 意識 inherit a depth no neologism could have supplied.
japanese_transmission: Entered Japanese with the earliest Buddhist textual transmission and was technically deepened by the Nara Hossō and Kusha scholastic traditions, where 識 was the operating term for vijñāna and the architecture of the eight consciousnesses. It remained a doctrinally heavy character throughout the classical and medieval periods. Its Meiji reuse — as the cognitive-discriminative element of 意識 (consciousness) and 認識 (cognition) — is therefore not a fresh coinage but a redirection of an already consciousness-bearing term into the Western epistemological vocabulary now shared across Japanese, Chinese, and Korean.

gloss: The large sheep — 羊 over 大: value first seen as fitness and fineness in what is reared and offered, later abstracted into the beautiful as such.

graphic_evolution.form_description: A figure read either as 羊 (sheep) over 大 (a large/standing person) or as a person wearing a feathered headdress
graphic_evolution.notes: The dominant traditional reading (Shuowen) is 羊 + 大, "a large sheep" — beauty grounded in the prized, well-formed animal: the good-to-offer and good-to-eat as the root of the valued and the fine. The alternative ornamented-figure reading already points toward adornment.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 羊-derived top over 大 — 9 strokes; classified under the 羊 radical
graphic_evolution.notes: In the classical language 美 fuses the fine, the excellent, the good, and the beautiful (Confucian 尽善尽美, "perfect in goodness and beauty"). The Meiji disciplinary compounds 美術 and 美学 narrow this broad value-term to the specifically aesthetic.

doctrinal_notes: Classical 美 is not a narrowly aesthetic word: it spans the excellent, the admirable, the morally fine, and the sensuously beautiful, the aesthetic and ethical registers held together (as in 尽善尽美). The Western category of "the aesthetic" as a domain distinct from the good and the useful had no native single term; Meiji coinage 美術 (fine art) and 美学 (aesthetics) carved that distinction by binding 美 to a function (術) or a discipline (学).
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character carrying its broad value-sense — fine, excellent, beautiful — through the whole classical and poetic tradition. It acquired its modern narrowing in the Meiji period: 美術 was fixed in the 1870s to render "fine art / bildende Kunst," and 美学 was stabilized as the name of the discipline of aesthetics through Nakae Chōmin's 維氏美学 (1883–84) and the Tetsugaku Jii (1881). Both compounds, with 美 in its newly disciplinary role, were re-exported into Chinese (měishù, měixué) and Korean (misul, mihak).

gloss: Transformation, becoming-other — the oracle-bone image of one figure upright beside one inverted, a person turned into something else; in Meiji vocabulary the standard suffix for -ization and the agent of 化学's 'transformation-study.'

components.meaning: person radical — a standing human figure
an inverted person (also read as 'ladle' in later reanalysis) — the figure turned upside down, the visual sign of one state passing into another

graphic_evolution.form_description: Two human figures side by side, one upright and one inverted
graphic_evolution.notes: The original sense is the passage of one state into its opposite — life into death, the living person into the corpse, and by extension any thing becoming another thing. Transformation is figured not as gradual growth but as turning, reversal, the flip of a figure.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 亻 (person) on the left beside 匕 on the right — 4 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: In modern Sino-Japanese 化 is one of the most productive bound morphemes: as a verbal suffix it forms -ize/-ify (近代化 modernization, 工業化 industrialization), and as the second element of 化学 it names chemistry as the study of how substances become other substances. The character also carries the older sense of magical transformation in 化け物 (bakemono, a thing that has shape-shifted).

doctrinal_notes: 化 belongs to the classical Chinese cosmological vocabulary of transformation (造化, the spontaneous transforming of nature; 教化, moral transformation through teaching) before it is enlisted by Meiji translators. This double inheritance — natural metamorphosis and the productive -ization suffix — is what made 化 the natural choice to render the operative core of chemistry: a discipline defined precisely by the lawful transformation of matter.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present from the earliest stratum of Japanese literacy and carried in the Confucian-cosmological vocabulary (造化, 教化) and the Buddhist vocabulary of impermanent becoming. Its decisive modern reuse is bakumatsu and Meiji: Kawamoto Kōmin's adoption of 化学 (c. 1860) gives 化 a precise technical role as the marker of substance-transformation, and the 1870s–80s systematization of -化 as the all-purpose -ization suffix makes it one of the engines of modern East Asian compounding, transferring with that function into Chinese and Korean.

gloss: Thing, matter, the myriad concrete particulars — from the multicolored sacrificial ox to 'all things'; in 物理 it supplies the 'matter' whose principle (理) physics reads.

components.meaning: ox radical — the sacrificial animal; the semantic ground of the original 'variegated ox' sense
a banner or streamers (phonetic element supplying the sound; possibly also evoking the many colors of the streamers/ox)

graphic_evolution.form_description: 牛 (ox) beside 勿 (streamers/banner) — phonetic-semantic compound
graphic_evolution.notes: The early gloss connects 物 to the mottled, multicolored sacrificial ox; from 'variegated thing' the sense generalizes to kinds of things, then to things in general, then to matter and the totality of phenomena (万物, the ten thousand things).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 牛 (ox, 4 strokes) on the left beside 勿 (4 strokes) on the right — 8 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern compounds split along the concrete/abstract axis: 物 as tangible object (物質 matter, 動物 animal, 建物 building) and 物 as the philosophical category of the material (物理 physics, 唯物論 materialism, 物自体 the Kantian thing-in-itself). The kun reading もの (mono) carries the native Japanese sense of 'thing' with its affective and grammatical extensions (物の哀れ, ものがたり).

doctrinal_notes: 物 carries the classical Chinese sense of the myriad things (万物) within the Dao, and a Neo-Confucian technical role in 格物 (gewu, 'the investigation of things') from the Great Learning — the program of reaching principle (理) by exhausting the study of concrete things. The Meiji compound 物理 stands directly in this lineage: it reads as 'the principle within things,' the Neo-Confucian格物 program redirected onto Western experimental natural philosophy.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present from the earliest stratum of Japanese literacy, supplying both the kun word もの and the on element 物 across Buddhist, Confucian, and vernacular registers. Its modern philosophical-scientific weight is Meiji: the 物 of 格物 (the Neo-Confucian investigation of things) is repurposed as the 物 of 物理学 and 唯物論, so that the character that named the Confucian study of concrete things becomes the character that names Western physics and materialism.

gloss: Lightning, and from it electricity — the pictograph of a lightning bolt stretching from the clouds, recruited in the Meiji era as the prefix of every electrical technology.

components.meaning: rain radical — the storm-cloud, added to specify the meteorological domain
the original lightning element — a downward bolt (a stretched-out form of the 申 'extend' pictograph)

graphic_evolution.period: Oracle bone / bronze (甲骨文・金文)
graphic_evolution.form_description: A jagged downward stroke depicting a lightning flash — closely related to the 申 graph (lightning, 'extend')
graphic_evolution.notes: The earliest form is simply the lightning bolt; 申 and 電 share an origin in the pictograph of forked lightning. 申 specialized toward 'extend / the cyclical sign,' while the lightning sense was carried by the form that took the 雨 (rain) classifier.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 雨 (rain, 8 strokes) over the lightning element 电 (5 strokes) — 13 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: From the mid-19th century 電 is generalized from 'lightning' to 'electricity,' becoming the obligatory first element of the entire imported electrical lexicon: 電気 (electricity), 電信 (telegraph), 電話 (telephone), 電車 (electric tram), 電力 (electric power), 電子 (electron).

doctrinal_notes: Unlike 理 or 物, 電 contributes little classical philosophical freight; its modern significance is almost entirely as a Meiji technical morpheme. The semantic move that makes the whole electrical vocabulary possible is the metaphor folded into the character itself — electricity grasped through lightning, the domesticated form of the sky's most violent power.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character in its original meaning 'lightning,' present in classical Sino-Japanese (電光 lightning-flash, the simile 電光石火). Its consequential transmission is Meiji: as Western electrical science and technology arrive from the 1870s, 電 is selected to render 'electric-' and becomes a closed, highly productive prefix. The compounds coined in Japanese (電話, 電車, 電気) transfer wholesale into Chinese and Korean, where 電 remains the universal electrical morpheme.

gloss: Vital breath, vapor, atmosphere — the rising steam of cooked rice generalized into the cosmological pneuma of qi; in 電気 it lends electricity the sense of an animating 'energy' filling things.

components.meaning: rising vapor radical — three drifting lines depicting breath or steam ascending
the reduced remnant of 米 (rice) in the simplified Japanese form 気 — the steam off cooked grain (the traditional form is 氣)

graphic_evolution.period: Oracle bone / bronze (甲骨文・金文)
graphic_evolution.form_description: Three roughly horizontal drifting strokes depicting vapor, mist, or breath rising and dispersing
graphic_evolution.notes: The base graph 气 pictures vapor in the air. The 米 (rice) element was later added to specify the steam rising off cooking grain — a concrete image for the invisible animating breath. The Japanese postwar simplification 気 replaces 米 with メ; the traditional and Chinese form remains 氣 / 气.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 气 (vapor, 4 strokes) enclosing メ — 6 strokes in the modern Japanese form
graphic_evolution.notes: 气 anchors an enormous semantic field: cosmological qi (気), air (空気), weather (天気), mood and disposition (気分, 元気, 気持ち), and — via Meiji compounding — the physical-science senses 電気 (electricity), 気体 (gaseous state), 蒸気 (steam/vapor as a power source).

doctrinal_notes: 気 (qi) is one of the central terms of classical Chinese cosmology and medicine — the vital pneuma that constitutes and moves all things, the breath shared by body and cosmos, the medium of resonance and influence. When Meiji translators built 電気 they did not coin a neutral term for 'electricity': they identified the new force with qi, framing it as a kind of animating energy pervading matter — a framing that made electricity intuitively graspable but carried a vitalist residue absent from the Western concept.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, fundamental from the earliest stratum of Japanese literacy and saturating the native lexicon through the Sino-Japanese medical, cosmological, and affective vocabulary (元気, 気分, 天気). Its modern scientific reuse is Meiji: 気 is enlisted for the gaseous and electrical sciences (電気, 気体, 蒸気), so the character of classical pneuma comes to name the physics of gases and electric current, and these compounds carry into Chinese and Korean.

gloss: Sourness rising from the fermenting wine-jar — the taste of acid, and from it the chemical class of acids that Lavoisier's nomenclature made the conceptual hinge of the element vocabulary.

components.meaning: the wine-jar — fermentation, and the sourness of fermented liquid; the semantic root locating 酸 in the domain of taste before chemistry
phonetic element carrying the sound, with a faint sense of slow movement

graphic_evolution.form_description: 酉 (wine-jar) beside the phonetic 夋
graphic_evolution.notes: A standard 形声 phono-semantic compound: the 酉 classifier fixes the meaning in the field of fermented, soured liquid; the right side supplies the reading.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 酉 (7) + 夋 (7) — 14 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: The classical sense is the gustatory 'sour' (酸味, 辛酸). In the 19th century the character is recruited to render the chemical category 'acid' (酸), so that 酸素 reads as 'the element that makes acids' — the calque only works because 酸 already meant sourness/acidity.

japanese_transmission: A first-wave character in its taste sense 'sour,' present throughout classical Sino-Japanese (辛酸, 酸鼻). Its consequential transmission is the rangaku-to-Meiji scientific moment: when Lavoisier's chemistry reached Japan through Dutch sources, 酸 was selected to translate 'acid,' and Udagawa Yōan's 舎密開宗 (1837) built 酸素 on it as a calque of oxygène, 'acid-maker.' The chemical reading of 酸 then became fixed and productive (酸性, 硫酸, 酸化).
doctrinal_notes: 酸 is the character on which Lavoisier's whole analytical program turns in Japanese: because oxygène was coined on the (mistaken) thesis that oxygen is the principle of acidity, the calque 酸素 carries that 18th-century error embedded in the graph. The character thus preserves a fossil of superseded chemical theory long after the theory itself was abandoned in the West.

gloss: Raw, undyed silk hanging plain — and from that unadorned simplicity the abstract sense of 'the basic stuff,' the elemental constituent, made into the standard Meiji suffix for chemical elements.

components.meaning: hanging down — the lengths of silk suspended undyed and unworked
silk thread — the material classifier; raw silk before colour or pattern

graphic_evolution.form_description: A depiction of hanging threads above the 糸 silk element — undyed, unworked silk
graphic_evolution.notes: The concrete sense is 'plain white raw silk,' from which the figurative senses radiate: plain, simple, unadorned, and then 'the basic element / underlying substance.'

graphic_evolution.form_description: The upper 'hanging' element over 糸 (silk) — 10 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical extensions: 素朴 (simple), 素直 (plain/honest), 平素 (ordinarily), 素質 (innate basis). The decisive modern extension is the chemical one: 素 becomes the bound suffix for 'element/elementary constituent' — 元素, 酸素, 水素, 窒素, 炭素 — a closed, highly productive Meiji-scientific morpheme.

japanese_transmission: A first-wave character in its classical senses (plain, raw, basic, ordinarily), fully naturalized in Sino-Japanese. Its consequential transmission is the rangaku-Meiji recruitment of its 'underlying constituent' sense to render the chemical 'element': Udagawa Yōan's 舎密開宗 (1837) fixes 元素 ('origin-element') and the calque-suffix pattern 〜素 for the named gases, and the pattern is then fixed permanently through Meiji school chemistry.
doctrinal_notes: 素 is the morpheme that makes the Japanese chemical-element vocabulary systematic rather than ad hoc: every gas named on the calque principle (water-maker, acid-maker, suffocant) ends in 素, so the suffix itself encodes the Lavoisierian thesis that matter resolves into a fixed set of elementary substances. Korean borrows the whole 〜素 series (산소, 수소, 질소); modern Chinese rejects it, coining single characters with the 气 (gas) radical instead, so 素 marks precisely the line where the Japanese and Chinese scientific lexicons diverge.

gloss: A hole stopped up to the point of obstruction — blockage, and from it suffocation; the character chosen to calque azote, the gas 'without life' in which a flame and a breath go out.

components.meaning: cave, hole, aperture — the passage that can be blocked; the semantic classifier
to arrive, to reach the limit — here, a passage filled or reached to its stopping point

graphic_evolution.form_description: 穴 (hole) over 至 (reach/arrive)
graphic_evolution.notes: The composite reads as an aperture brought to its limit — stopped, plugged, obstructed. Classical senses: 窒塞 (block up), 窒息 (suffocate).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 穴 (5) over 至 (6) — 11 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: The classical 'obstruct / suffocate' sense is carried directly into the chemical coinage: 窒素 names nitrogen as 'the suffocating element,' calquing Lavoisier's azote (a-zōē, 'no life') by way of the gas's inability to support respiration or combustion.

japanese_transmission: A relatively low-frequency first-wave character in its classical sense 'obstruct/suffocate' (窒息). Its consequential transmission is almost entirely the single rangaku-Meiji coinage 窒素: Udagawa Yōan's 舎密開宗 (1837) selects 窒 to render azote on the empirical observation that a creature placed in the gas suffocates. Outside 窒素 and 窒息 the character remains rare in modern Japanese.
doctrinal_notes: 窒 is the clearest case of a calque preserving a privative, negative naming-decision: where 酸素 and 水素 name their gases by what they make (acid, water), 窒素 names nitrogen by what it kills, faithfully reproducing the logic of Lavoisier's azote rather than the later English nitrogen ('niter-former'). The character thus records which of the two competing European names — French azote or English nitrogen — actually entered East Asia.

gloss: Thread-fine, minute, drawn down to the smallest scale — the character that, joined to 胞, names the microscopic compartment biology found at the base of all living form.

components.meaning: silk thread — the classifier for the fine, the slender, the thread-thin
originally 囟 (the fontanelle / fine cranial divisions), later written 田; the phono-semantic element suggesting fine subdivision

graphic_evolution.form_description: 糸 (silk) beside 囟 (the divided crown of the skull), later regularized to 田
graphic_evolution.notes: The original right element 囟 depicted the fine sutured divisions of an infant's skull; with the 糸 classifier the composite means thread-fine, minute, finely divided.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 糸 (6) + 田 (5) — 11 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical and modern senses cluster around fineness and minuteness: 細部 (detail), 詳細 (particulars), 微細 (minute). The consequential modern compound is 細胞, 'fine sac,' coined for the biological cell.

japanese_transmission: A first-wave character, fully naturalized in its sense 'fine/minute/detailed.' Its consequential modern transmission is the 19th-century botanical coinage 細胞: Udagawa Yōan's 植学啓原 (1834), the first Western botany in Japanese, needs a word for the microscopic compartment seen under the lens, and pairs 細 (fine) with 胞 (sac). The compound is later adopted across Chinese (xìbāo), Korean, and Vietnamese.
doctrinal_notes: In 細胞 the character 細 does the conceptual work that the Latin diminutive does in cellula: it specifies that what is named is not a chamber as such but a chamber at the limit of visibility, the unit reached only by descending to the finest observable scale. The coinage thus reproduces the scalar move — from the macroscopic to the microscopic — that constituted cell theory itself.

gloss: The enwrapping membrane — the caul, the placenta, the sac that encloses; the flesh-radical word repurposed to name the bounded compartment of life.

components.meaning: the flesh radical (肉) — the classifier marking a bodily, organic structure
to wrap, enclose, contain — a thing folded around what it holds; both phonetic and semantic

graphic_evolution.form_description: 肉/月 (flesh) beside 包 (wrap/enclose)
graphic_evolution.notes: A 形声 compound whose 包 element is doubly motivated — sound and sense both — yielding 'the fleshy thing that wraps': the caul or amniotic membrane, the placenta (胞衣 ena).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 月 (4) + 包 (5) — 9 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: The classical sense is the enwrapping birth-membrane. The decisive modern extension is biological: in 細胞 the 'enclosing membrane' sense is generalized from the gestational sac to the universal membrane-bounded unit of living matter.

japanese_transmission: A first-wave character in its classical obstetric senses (胞衣, the afterbirth). Its consequential transmission is the 19th-century scientific coinage 細胞 in Udagawa Yōan's 植学啓原 (1834): the 'enclosing membrane' sense is exactly what the new microscopy required to name the bounded living unit, and the compound subsequently becomes the universal East Asian word for the biological cell.
doctrinal_notes: 胞 supplies the membrane to 細's fineness: together they render 'cell' not as Hooke's empty masonry chamber (cellula, a little room) but as a living envelope — a flesh-radical word for a bounded organic interior. The choice quietly shifts the metaphor from architecture to enclosure, anticipating the membrane-centred understanding of the cell rather than the merely spatial one carried by the European etymon.

gloss: The numinous power that descends and shows itself — the altar-sign 礻 beside 申, a forking bolt of lightning; the spirit/vital-force sense that, contracted from 神気, supplies the 'animal spirits' coursing the channels in 神経.

components.meaning: altar / spirit-revealing radical (示) — the offering-stand at which the numinous is made manifest
a forking bolt of lightning (phonetic, and originally the very picture of heaven's power extending downward)

graphic_evolution.period: Oracle bone / bronze (甲骨文・金文)
graphic_evolution.form_description: 申 alone — a zigzag stroke depicting lightning, the descending manifestation of celestial power
graphic_evolution.notes: The earliest sense is the visible discharge of heaven's force; 示 (altar) is added later to mark the object of cult, fixing the meaning as 'spirit, deity, the numinous.'

graphic_evolution.form_description: 礻 (altar, 4) on the left beside 申 (5) on the right — 9 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical range runs from gods and ancestral spirits (神社, 神道) through the 'spirit' of a person (精神) to the marvellous or uncanny (神秘). It is the 'spirit/vital force' pole — 神気, the animating pneuma — that rangaku anatomy recruits for 神経.

japanese_transmission: A first-wave character, central to Japanese literacy from the outset through the Shinto kami (the kun reading かみ) and the Buddhist-Confucian vocabulary of spirit (精神, 神霊). Its consequential modern reuse is Sugita Genpaku's coinage 神経 in the Kaitai Shinsho (解体新書, 1774): 神 is taken from 神気 ('vital spirit, animal spirits') and welded to the 経 of 経脈, so the Western nerve enters Japanese as 'the channel along which the vital spirit travels.'
doctrinal_notes: 神 carries into 神経 an entire pre-modern physiology: the nerve is named not as a discrete anatomical cord but as the conduit of 神気, the animating pneuma of the body. The coinage thus fuses Western dissection-anatomy with the qi-and-channel framework of East Asian medicine at the level of the morpheme itself, and the resulting word — adopted unchanged into Chinese shénjīng and Korean 신경 — silently transmits that hybrid conception wherever it is used.

gloss: The head of a standing figure marked by a stroke above — hence first, primary, the origin from which a sequence begins; in 元素 the 'originary' pole, the primal substances into which matter finally resolves.

components.meaning: two strokes marking the top — the head, the highest and first part of the body
the legs of a standing person — the human figure beneath the emphasized head

graphic_evolution.form_description: A person in profile with the head drawn large or marked by an extra stroke
graphic_evolution.notes: The original referent is the head; from 'head' the sense radiates to what is highest, first, and originary — the beginning of a reign (元年), the prime or fundamental (元来).

graphic_evolution.form_description: 二 (the marked top, 2) over 儿 (standing legs, 2) — 4 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical compounds turn on 'origin/first': 元首 (head of state), 元年 (first year of an era), 元気 (primal vital energy). The rangaku-Meiji extension is chemical — 元素, the 'origin-elements,' the primary substances that are not further decomposable.

japanese_transmission: A first-wave character, fully naturalized in its classical senses (era-names 元年, the Yuan 元 dynasty, 元気). Its decisive scientific reuse is Udagawa Yōan's 舎密開宗 (1837–47), where 元素 ('origin-element') renders Lavoisier's elementary substance, fixing 元 as the marker of irreducible chemical primacy and the head of the productive 〜素 element series.
doctrinal_notes: In 元素 the 元 does precise theoretical work: it asserts that the elements are not merely 'simple' but originary — the floor of decomposition, that beyond which analysis cannot pass. This converts the Lavoisierian operational definition of an element (a substance not yet resolved into others) into a stronger ontological claim of primacy, a small but consequential drift the calque introduces and then exports intact to Chinese yuánsù and Korean 원소.

gloss: A short-tailed bird (隹) set on the road (辶) — and a bird can only go forward; advance, progress, the directional thrust that turns 化's neutral 'change' into the onward motion of 進化.

components.meaning: the movement / road radical (辵) — going, advancing along a way
a short-tailed bird — which, in the graph's traditional reading, can step only forward and never back

graphic_evolution.form_description: 隹 (bird) above or beside 辵 (movement) — a compound of forward motion
graphic_evolution.notes: The traditional gloss (Shuowen) reads the bird as the sign of one-directional movement: a bird hops forward, not back, so the graph means specifically advance rather than mere displacement.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 辶 (movement, 3) wrapping 隹 (bird, 8) at lower left — 11 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical compounds carry the forward/upward sense: 前進 (advance), 進歩 (progress), 進学 (advancing in study), 進献 (presenting upward to a superior). The Meiji extension is 進化 — Darwinian evolution read as directional 'advancing change.'

japanese_transmission: A first-wave character, long naturalized in the vocabulary of advancement and presentation (進歩, 進献, 進退). Its consequential modern reuse is 進化, the standard rendering of Darwinian evolution popularized through the Meiji translation literature (notably Ishikawa Chiyomatsu's 動物進化論, 1883), where 進 supplies the forward vector that distinguishes evolution from undirected 変化.
doctrinal_notes: 進 is the morpheme that loads 進化 with the very teleology Darwin's theory was at pains to exclude: 'evolution' as descent with modification carries no intrinsic direction, but 進化 literally says 'advancing change,' aligning the science with the Spencerian-progressivist reading that dominated its East Asian reception. The character thus encodes an interpretive commitment — evolution as progress — that the English term does not, and that commitment travels with the word into Chinese jìnhuà and Korean 진화.

gloss: The singling-out classifier — 亻 (person) beside 固 (solid, fixed, hard); originally the measure-word that picks one discrete unit out of a mass, enlisted in Meiji vocabulary to name the 'individual' as the irreducible social atom in 個人.

components.meaning: person radical — a standing human figure, here marking the human referent of the unit being counted
solid, firm, fixed (enclosure 囗 around 古 old/hard) — phonetic, but its sense of bounded fixity reinforces the notion of a discrete, self-contained unit

graphic_evolution.form_description: 亻 (person) on the left beside 固 on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: A relatively late phono-semantic compound. The character functions in classical Chinese principally as the universal individuating classifier (一個 'one [item]'), the grammatical device that extracts a single bounded unit from an undifferentiated plurality. The variant 个 (a simplified, much older counter graph) carries the same classifier function.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 亻 beside 固 — 10 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Sino-Japanese retains the classifier use (個数 number-of-items, 三個 three units) while the decisive modern development is the Meiji compound 個人 (kojin, individual), in which 個's individuating function — 'the single one picked out from the mass' — is recruited to render the Western autonomous individual. 個性 (kosei, individuality) and 個体 (kotai, an individual organism) extend the same register.

doctrinal_notes: 個's load-bearing modern role rests on a grammatical fact: it is the character whose native job is to single out one discrete unit from a plurality. Meiji translators rendering the Western 'individual' did not reach for a character meaning 'person' alone (人) but for the one that performs individuation as such — yielding 個人, literally 'the singled-out person.' The character thus carries into the compound exactly the conceptual move the Western term requires: the abstraction of the lone unit from the collective in which classical thought had always kept it embedded.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character in its classifier function, present in Japanese literacy from the earliest stratum and ubiquitous in the counting system (個 as the general-purpose counter). Its philosophically load-bearing use is entirely Meiji: the coinage 個人 (kojin) and its derivatives 個性, 個体, 個人主義 belong to the 1870s–1880s translation of Western liberal and scientific vocabulary, and they transferred with that vocabulary into Chinese (gèrén) and Korean (개인) as the standard rendering of 'individual.'

gloss: The crossed lines of pattern, writing, refinement — a pictograph of interlaced strokes or a tattooed-marked breast; the character of the written and the cultivated, paired downstream with 化 to make 'culture' and with 明 to make 'civilization.'

graphic_evolution.form_description: A standing human figure with a patterned or incised mark on the chest
graphic_evolution.notes: The original referent is most plausibly a design or tattoo inscribed on the body — the mark, the figured pattern. From this concrete sense of patterned incision the character generalizes to design, ornament, and then to writing as the patterning of meaning, and to the cultivated, lettered, refined as opposed to the raw or martial (the classic 文/武 pair, civil versus military).

graphic_evolution.form_description: The body simplifies toward crossed strokes; the chest-mark sometimes a lozenge or 心-like figure
graphic_evolution.notes: Bronze inscriptions already use 文 in its honorific-cultural register (文王, King Wen, 'the cultured/accomplished king'), establishing the value-laden sense of civil accomplishment and moral-cultural refinement that the Confucian tradition would make central.

graphic_evolution.form_description: Four strokes — a top point and crossing strokes over a wide base
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Sino-Japanese 文 is enormously productive across the lettered-cultural field: 文字 (character/letter), 文章 (composition), 文学 (literature), 文化 (culture), 文明 (civilization), 文献 (documentary sources). The kun-readings ふみ (a letter, a document) and あや (figured pattern, as in textile or rhetoric) preserve the indigenous reception of both the writing and the pattern senses.

doctrinal_notes: 文 carries a classical value-charge that the Meiji coinages 文化 and 文明 silently inherit: in the Confucian register 文 is not neutral 'culture' in the anthropologist's sense but the cultivated, the lettered, the morally-aesthetically refined — that which raises the human above the brute. When Meiji translators built 文化 (culture) and 文明 (civilization) on 文, they imported into the new sociological and developmental concepts an older evaluative gradient: to be 文 is to be refined, and its absence is barbarism. The 文/武 (civil/martial) and 文/質 (refinement/substance) polarities stand behind the modern terms.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character of the foundational stratum, central to Japanese literacy from its beginnings — the very word 文 (fumi) names the written document in classical Japanese, and the Heian distinction between 漢文 (Chinese writing) and the vernacular runs through the character. Its classical-Confucian register (文 as civil refinement) is fully inherited in medieval and Edo learning. The decisive modern development is the Meiji re-coinage of the classical compounds 文化 and 文明 to render Western culture/Kultur and civilization, from which both passed into Chinese and Korean as the standard terms.

gloss: Brightness as the conjunction of the two luminaries — 日 (sun) beside 月 (moon); light, clarity, the illumined and the manifest, the 'bright' that joins 文 to render 'civilization' as enlightened development.

components.meaning: sun — the daytime luminary, the source of light and the measure of the day
moon — the night luminary; juxtaposed with the sun to figure light as such, that by which things become visible

graphic_evolution.form_description: A window or moon beside the moon — early forms pair 囧 (a lattice window) or 日 with 月
graphic_evolution.notes: The earliest forms figure brightness either as moonlight through a window or as the two great luminaries together. The constant is the idea of light entering or being made — illumination as event, not substance. From visible brightness the character extends to clarity of understanding (明 as 'to comprehend'), to the manifest and evident, and to the bright as the morally and intellectually enlightened.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 日 (sun) on the left, 月 (moon) on the right — 8 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: The sun–moon analysis becomes canonical. Modern Sino-Japanese 明 spans the full range: 明るい (bright), 明確 (clear/definite), 明白 (evident), 説明 (explanation), 明治 (Meiji, 'enlightened rule'), 文明 (civilization). The era-name 明治 itself enlists 明 in exactly the civilizational-enlightenment register that 文明 names.

doctrinal_notes: In 文明 (civilization), 明 supplies the developmental-evaluative light: civilization is the condition in which the human pattern (文) has become bright, manifest, enlightened — the metaphor of illumination doing the work of 'progress.' This is not incidental: Meiji discourse routinely glossed 文明 through the imagery of light dispelling darkness (the slogan 文明開化, 'civilization and enlightenment,' literally the opening-and-transformation into brightness), and the era-name 明治 ('enlightened government') wove the same character into the period's self-understanding. 明 thus carries the optimistic, teleological charge that distinguishes 文明 from the more inward, particularist 文化.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character of the earliest literacy stratum, mapping onto a rich field of native あか-/あき- vocabulary (明るい bright, 明らか evident, 明ける to dawn) in productive complementary distribution with the Sino-Japanese readings めい/みょう. Classical and Buddhist usage carries the clarity-of-insight register (無明 mumyō, avidyā/ignorance, the absence of 明). Its modern civilizational role — 文明, 文明開化, and resonance with the era-name 明治 — is a Meiji development that transferred with 文明 into Chinese (wénmíng) and Korean (문명).

gloss: Teaching as guided transmission — a hand wielding a rod (攵) beside 孝 (filial devotion); the character of doctrine, instruction, and the moral forming of the young, recruited in Meiji vocabulary for institutional 教育 and the category 宗教 (religion).

components.meaning: filial piety — a child 子 beneath an elder; here the phonetic, but its sense of the intergenerational bond colors teaching as the handing-down between elder and young
a hand holding a rod or stick (the 攴/攵 "rap, strike, urge" element) — the gesture of direction, correction, the applied pressure of instruction

graphic_evolution.form_description: A figure of a child, the counting-sticks or 爻 mark of lessons, and a hand with a rod above or beside
graphic_evolution.notes: The earliest forms assemble three elements: the child to be taught, the lesson (figured by 爻, the trigram/tally strokes), and the adult hand wielding a rod. Teaching is figured from the outset as the active, directed — even coercive — leading of the young toward a transmitted content, not as the child's own unfolding.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 孝 (filial piety) on the left beside 攵 (strike/urge) on the right — 11 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: The left element regularizes as 孝, binding 'teach' etymologically to the filial-generational relation. Modern Sino-Japanese 教 is highly productive: 教える (to teach), 教師 (teacher), 教科書 (textbook), 教育 (education), 教化 (moral transformation through teaching), 宗教 (religion, 'ancestral/sect teaching'), 仏教 (Buddhism, 'the Buddha's teaching').

doctrinal_notes: 教 carries a directed, transmissive, top-down sense — the teacher leads, the doctrine is handed down — that stands in tension with the modern institutional concept it was enlisted to render. The Confucian inheritance 教化 (moral transformation through teaching) names exactly what 教 traditionally did: the forming of character by the moral suasion of superiors. When Meiji translators used 教 + 育 for the imported notion of national, systematic schooling, they fused this directive-moral register with 育's nurturing-growth register; the unresolved tension between the two — schooling as state-directed moral formation versus the drawing-out of the learner's own capacities — is precisely what the Imperial Rescript on Education would later adjudicate.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character of the foundational stratum, load-bearing across the Confucian vocabulary of moral instruction (教化) and the Buddhist vocabulary of doctrine (仏教, 教義, the 教 of 'a teaching/sect') from the earliest Japanese literacy. Its modern institutional life — the wasei compound 教育 (education) and the Meiji category 宗教 (religion) — is a Meiji development that became standard across Chinese (jiàoyù) and Korean (교육) educational discourse.

gloss: The bringing-forth and rearing of a child — an inverted child 𠫓 above 月 (flesh/body); birth turned into nurture, the growth-from-below that 教 (directed teaching) is paired with to make 教育.

components.meaning: an inverted 子 (child) — the infant shown head-downward, in the posture of being born
the 肉 (flesh/body) element written as 月 — the bodily, fleshly substance through which the newborn is fed and grows

graphic_evolution.form_description: A woman or mother figure with an inverted child below her, sometimes with drops indicating birth-fluid
graphic_evolution.notes: The original scene is parturition: the child emerging head-first, the inverted 子. The sense moves swiftly from 'give birth to' to 'rear, nourish, bring up' — the continuous act of sustaining the growth that birth begins. Growth here is figured from the side of the nurturer feeding life upward, the complement to 教's directing it from above.

graphic_evolution.form_description: The inverted-child element 𠫓 above the flesh-body element 月 — 8 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Sino-Japanese 育 spans birth-and-rearing through to abstract cultivation: 育つ (to grow up), 育てる (to raise), 育児 (childcare), 体育 (physical education), 教育 (education), 養育 (upbringing). The kun はぐくむ (to nurture, lit. to brood under the wing) preserves the tender, sustaining pole of the character against 教's directive pole.

doctrinal_notes: 育 contributes to 教育 the register 教 lacks: organic growth nurtured from below, the drawing-out and sustaining of the learner's own development. The compound 教育 thus holds two metaphors in suspension — 教 (the rod, doctrine handed down) and 育 (the child grown, life nourished upward) — and the whole modern history of the term in East Asia can be read as a contest over which pole dominates: education as the state's transmission of authorized content, or education as the cultivation of the person's own capacities. The Spencerian, developmentalist reading foregrounds 育; the Imperial-Rescript, moral-loyalist reading foregrounds 教.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character present from the early literacy stratum, mapping onto native そだつ/そだてる (grow/raise) and はぐくむ (nurture) in the indigenous vocabulary of rearing. Classically used across the birth–nourishment–cultivation range. Its load-bearing modern role is the Meiji wasei compound 教育 (education) and the parallel 体育 (physical education), 保育 (nursery care), which entered Chinese (jiàoyù, tǐyù) and Korean (교육) as the standard institutional vocabulary.

gloss: The ancestral hall, and so the line that descends from it — 宀 (roof) over 示 (altar/spirit): the enshrined source of a lineage, generalized to 'sect, school, what one takes as fundamental.' Recruited in Meiji 宗教 to bound 'religion' as a sectarian teaching.

components.meaning: roof, dwelling — the ancestral building that houses the spirits
altar / spirit / the showing-forth of the numinous — the sacrificial table at which ancestors are addressed

graphic_evolution.form_description: 示 (an altar or spirit-tablet) set beneath 宀 (a roof) — a shrine housing the ancestral spirits
graphic_evolution.notes: The graph is concretely the ancestral temple (祖廟): the building in which the lineage's dead are enshrined and addressed. 'Lineage,' 'clan,' and 'that from which a line proceeds' are all read off this single image of the enshrined origin.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 宀 (roof, 3 strokes) over 示 (altar, 5 strokes) — 8 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical usage extends from 'ancestral temple' to 'ancestor, founder, what is taken as primary' (宗主, 宗家) and, in the Buddhist vocabulary, to 'school / sect' (禅宗 the Zen school, 浄土宗 the Pure Land school, 宗派). It is this sectarian sense that Meiji translators fused with 教 to render 'religion.'

doctrinal_notes: In 宗教 (religion), 宗 supplies 'sect / founding teaching / what one takes as fundamental' and 教 supplies 'teaching, doctrine.' The compound therefore frames 'religion' from the inside of the Buddhist sectarian vocabulary — a 宗 is a transmitted school with a founder and a lineage — which subtly pre-loads the imported Western category with the assumption that a religion is an organized doctrinal sect, the model that fit Christianity and the Buddhist schools but sat awkwardly on diffuse practice like Shintō or ancestral rite.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character of the foundational literate stratum, load-bearing across the Buddhist sectarian vocabulary (禅宗, 真言宗, 宗派, 宗門) from the earliest Japanese literacy and central to the Edo-period temple-registration (寺請) administration of 宗門. Its modern life is the Meiji wasei category 宗教, coined in the 1870s to translate 'religion' as a generic domain and standardized by the philosophical lexicons of the 1880s; it passed into Chinese (zōngjiào) and Korean (종교) as the standard term.

gloss: That through which something proceeds — anciently read as a gourd or a lamp-vessel with its stem; classically 'cause, ground, by way of, the reason.' In 自由 it carries the 'proceeding-from' that turns 自 ('self') into self-origination.

graphic_evolution.form_description: A 田-like enclosure with a stroke rising through the top — variously explained as a gourd on its vine or a lamp with its wick/stem
graphic_evolution.notes: Whatever the original object, the graph stabilizes early on the abstract relational meaning 'that from which / by way of which': the channel, stem, or conduit through which something issues. The concrete pictograph is almost entirely effaced by the relational sense.

graphic_evolution.form_description: A boxed field-like form with the central vertical breaking the upper edge — 5 strokes, classed under the 田 radical
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical senses: 'cause, reason' (理由), 'origin, provenance' (由来), 'to proceed from / by way of' (経由), and the adverbial 'as one likes, following one's own course' that surfaces in the binome 自由自在.

doctrinal_notes: In 自由 (freedom / liberty), 由 means 'proceeding from': the compound is literally 'from-self / following-from-oneself,' autonomy read as self-origination of action. The classical Sino-Japanese binome 自由 already existed but carried the colloquial and often pejorative sense 'as one pleases, doing as one likes' (close to 我儘, willful self-indulgence); the Meiji re-coinage had to scrub this licentious overtone to make 自由 bear the dignified political concept of liberty.
japanese_transmission: Arrives with first-wave Chinese script and is fully naturalized by the medieval period, conspicuously in the Buddhist binome 自由自在 ('free and unobstructed,' said of a bodhisattva's sovereign ease) and in the everyday, faintly disreputable 自由 ('doing as one likes'). Its modern political life is a Meiji repurposing: Fukuzawa Yukichi and Nakamura Masanao recruited the existing binome to render 'liberty / freedom,' and the politically loaded 自由 then flowed into Chinese (zìyóu) and Korean (자유).

gloss: The flight of steps by which a terrace is climbed, and so graded rank — 阝 (terraced mound) beside 皆 (all, ranged together): degrees in an ordered ascent.

components.meaning: mound / terraced slope (the 阜 'hill' element) — a built-up bank that must be ascended by stages
all, together, ranged in a row — here phonetic, but its sense of an aligned series colors 'graded steps'

graphic_evolution.form_description: The 阜 mound element beside 皆 — the stepped face of a raised earthwork or hall platform
graphic_evolution.notes: The concrete referent is the stair (階段) cut into or built against a terrace, especially the ceremonial steps of a hall. From the physical stair the meaning generalizes to any 'grade, degree, rung' in an ordered series.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 阝 (mound, 3 strokes) on the left, 皆 (all/together, 9 strokes) on the right — 12 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical senses run from 'stairs' (階段) through 'rank in officialdom' (位階, 階位) to abstract 'degree, stage' (段階). The graded-rank sense is what pairs with 級 to render the modern sociological 'class.'

doctrinal_notes: In 階級 (social class), 階 contributes 'graded step / tier in an ascending order,' the ceremonial-bureaucratic image of ranked station. Coupled with 級 ('rung, grade') the compound reads as 'steps-and-grades' — a vertical ladder of stations — which is why 階級 could carry both the older sense of court/official rank and, after the importation of European social theory, the modern sociological and Marxist sense of a stratum defined by economic position.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character present in the early literate vocabulary of court rank (位階, the 階 of the ritsuryō rank system) and architecture (階段, 階下). Its modern career is the re-coined compound 階級, repurposed in the Meiji period from 'official rank' to the sociological 'class' and then sharpened by early Japanese socialist writing into the Marxist 階級 (as in 階級闘争, class struggle); the term passed into Chinese (jiējí) and Korean (계급).

gloss: A notch in an ordered scale — 糸 (silk thread) beside 及 (to reach): originally the ranked sequence of threads (and anciently the head-count by which military rank was tallied), generalized to 'grade, rung, class.'

components.meaning: silk thread — the strand whose ordered arrangement gives the sense of a graded sequence
to reach, attain, extend to — here phonetic, with a residual sense of reaching a given level

graphic_evolution.form_description: The 糸 silk element beside 及 (reach)
graphic_evolution.notes: The 糸 element ties the graph to ordered, sequenced strands; an early military usage applied 級 to the tally of severed enemy heads by which rank and reward were graded (首級), fixing the sense 'a step in a scale of rank' very early.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 糸 (silk thread, 6 strokes) on the left, 及 (reach, 3 strokes) on the right — 9 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical and modern senses cluster on 'grade, rank, rung': 等級 (grade), 階級 (rank/class), 上級・下級 (upper/lower grade), and the schoolroom 学級 (class, year-group). It is the 'rung in a graded order' sense that joins 階 in the sociological 階級.

doctrinal_notes: In 階級 (social class), 級 supplies the discrete 'rung / grade' that 階's 'stepped ascent' arranges into a ladder. The compound's internal metaphor is therefore a graduated scale of station rather than a relation of antagonism, which is part of the conceptual remainder when 階級 is asked to render the Marxist 'class': the Sino-Japanese image is of ordered rank, while the European concept centers on a structural relation to the means of production and a latent conflict between strata.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character used across the early vocabulary of grading and rank (等級, 首級). Its modern significance is almost entirely in compounds standardized through Meiji usage — 階級 (class), 学級 (school class), 上級・初級 (advanced / elementary grade) — many of which were re-exported to Chinese (jí) and Korean (급) as the standard terms of graded order.

gloss: Guarding by going round — 行 (the crossroads / to move) enclosing 韋 (to encircle, hide-leather): the patrol that rounds a perimeter, defense as the act of warding by circuit. In 衛生 the guarding is turned upon life itself.

components.meaning: crossroads / to go, move along a way — split around the core to give the sense of going about, patrolling
to surround / enclose (also tanned hide); feet circling a guarded center — the act of encirclement and warding

graphic_evolution.form_description: 韋 (feet circling an enclosure) set within 行 (a crossroads / way) — figures moving in circuit around a guarded center
graphic_evolution.notes: The composite image is the sentry's round: 韋 supplies the encircling motion about a protected point, 行 the going-along-a-way. Defense is figured not as a static wall but as the active circuit of the guard.

graphic_evolution.form_description: The two halves of 行 split around a central 韋 — 16 strokes, classed under the 行 radical
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical senses: 'to guard, defend, ward' (防衛, 護衛, 守衛) and, by extension, the body of guards (衛兵, the palace 近衛). The 'guard / safeguard' sense is what Nagayo Sensai turned upon 生 ('life') to render the European administrative domain of public health.

doctrinal_notes: In 衛生 (hygiene / public health), 衛 means 'to guard, safeguard' and 生 'life'; the compound is 'the guarding of life.' Nagayo Sensai recovered it from the Zhuangzi, where 衛生之經 ('the canon of guarding life,' in the 庚桑楚 chapter) names an inward, Daoist art of nourishing one's own vitality. The Meiji re-coinage overwrites that personal-cultivation sense with its near-opposite: an outward, administrative, statistical project of state sanitary governance — the conceptual remainder being precisely the loss of the term's original interior, self-directed register.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character at home in the early military-court vocabulary of guarding (近衛 the imperial guard, 衛士, 防衛). Its decisive modern role is the re-coined compound 衛生: Nagayo Sensai, founding head of the Home Ministry's Sanitary Bureau (衛生局, established 1875), selected the classical Zhuangzi term to translate the Bismarckian-German administrative field of Gesundheitspflege / public health, and the repurposed 衛生 then became standard in Chinese (wèishēng) and Korean (위생).

gloss: To draw out at length, develop, extend — 氵 (water) beside 寅 (to stretch, extend): the long onward flow of speech, calculation, performance, or argument. In 演説 the structured extension of thought before a listening audience.

components.meaning: water — the radical of flowing extension, lending the sense of continuous onward course
to stretch, draw out, extend — here phonetic but contributing the sense of elongation along a path

graphic_evolution.form_description: The water element beside 寅, a figure of stretched-out extension — water that runs on at length
graphic_evolution.notes: The composite picture is of flow drawn out along its channel; the meaning generalizes early from physical extension to the unfolding of any sequence — a calculation worked through, a piece performed, a doctrine expounded.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 氵 (water, 3 strokes) on the left, 寅 (extend, 11 strokes) on the right — 14 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical senses cluster on the unfolding of a process: 演習 (to drill, exercise), 演算 (to compute), 演劇 (drama, the staging of a play), 出演 (to appear in performance). The 'extended development' sense is what Fukuzawa Yukichi turned upon 説 (speech, doctrine) to render the imported Western practice of oratory.

doctrinal_notes: In 演説 (public speech, oration), 演 supplies the 'drawing out at length' that turns 説 ('exposition') into a sustained spoken performance before an assembled audience. The compound's internal image is of doctrine made to flow, like water given a channel — speech as the unfolded, time-extended development of a thought rather than the compressed statement of a sentence. The same temporal-extensional sense underlies 演劇 (drama) and 演技 (acting): in every case 演 names the laying-out of something along a course.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character used across the classical vocabulary of calculation and exercise (演算, 演習). Its decisive modern career is in the Meiji compound 演説: Fukuzawa Yukichi, having observed parliamentary and lecture-hall oratory in the United States in 1860 and 1867, coined 演説 in his Kaigiben (会議弁, 1874) to translate the English 'speech' and to inaugurate the practice itself in Japan, then institutionalized it in the Mita Speech Society (三田演説会, 1874) and the dedicated speech hall 三田演説館 (1875). The same 演 anchors the Meiji vocabulary of dramatic and rhetorical performance — 演劇, 演技, 出演 — and the compounds passed into Chinese (yǎn) and Korean.

gloss: Speech that persuades — 言 (word) beside 兌 (open, release): the speaking-forth that opens an idea to a listener; doctrine, theory, exposition, and the persuasive presentation of a case.

components.meaning: word, speech — the radical placing the character squarely in the field of articulated language
to open, release, exchange — here phonetic but contributing the sense of opening-out, making accessible

graphic_evolution.form_description: The 言 element on the left, 兌 on the right — speech that opens, sets forth
graphic_evolution.notes: The graph carries from the start the doubled sense that surfaces across its later readings: to say in such a way that the matter is laid open (せつ, 'explain, expound, doctrine'); and to talk so as to persuade or move another to action (ぜい, 'to persuade, win over,' the sense behind the title 遊説 'travelling to persuade rulers').

graphic_evolution.form_description: 言 (speech, 7 strokes) on the left, 兌 (open/release, 7 strokes) on the right — 14 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical senses cluster on speech that exposits or persuades: 説明 (explain), 説教 (preach), 学説 (a scholarly theory), 小説 (the novel — literally 'small explanations'), and the verbal 説く ('to expound, to advocate'). The 'exposition' sense is what Fukuzawa joined to 演 to render Western public oratory as the time-extended unfolding of an exposition before an audience.

doctrinal_notes: In 演説 (public speech, oration), 説 supplies the 'exposition / doctrine' that 演 ('drawing out at length') then extends into a performed address. The pairing reads naturally as 'extended exposition,' and the compound's internal image of doctrinal speech is what made it fit for the imported civic genre of secular political and intellectual oratory. The character anchors a wider Meiji vocabulary of exposition (学説 a scholarly theory, 説明 explanation, 小説 the modern novel as Tsubouchi Shōyō stabilizes it) in which Western analytic genres are housed inside the 説 frame.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character pervasive in classical and modern Sino-Japanese (説明, 学説, 説話, 遊説). Its decisive modern compounds are the Meiji formations 演説 (Fukuzawa Yukichi, Kaigiben 1874) for public oratory and 小説 (used by Tsubouchi Shōyō in his 1885–86 Shōsetsu Shinzui) for the modern novel — two of the most consequential reverse-flow framings of imported cultural genres. Both compounds passed into Chinese (yǎnshuō, xiǎoshuō — though 小説 in Chinese had earlier meanings) and Korean.

gloss: Wide, broad — 广 (slanted roof, an open shelter) over 厶 (a small enclosed element): the spaciousness under an open structure; what extends without narrow bound, spreads abroad, reaches many. The shinjitai simplification of the older 廣.

components.meaning: slanted roof / open shelter — the radical of buildings and bounded spaces, here connoting the open extent under a roof
a small enclosed element (in 廣 the original phonetic 黃 has been reduced) — in the shinjitai form a simple inner stroke

graphic_evolution.form_description: Traditional 廣: 广 (roof) over 黃 (yellow, phonetic) — a wide hall whose phonetic anchors the reading
graphic_evolution.notes: The base sense is 'a hall of broad extent,' generalized very early to 'wide, vast, spreading.' The 黃 element is purely phonetic in the older graph; its disappearance in the postwar simplification leaves only the open shelter and a small inner stroke.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 广 (roof, 3 strokes) over 厶 (2 strokes) — 5 strokes; postwar Japanese simplification of 廣 (15 strokes)
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical and modern senses cluster on extent and diffusion: 広い (wide), 広場 (a public square), 広域 (a wide area), and the verbal 広める ('to spread, make widely known'). The 'spreading to many' sense is what was joined to 告 ('to inform, announce') to render the modern category of paid public notice — the advertisement that informs widely.

doctrinal_notes: In 広告 (advertisement), 広 supplies the 'widely, to many' that turns 告 ('to announce, inform') into a notice broadcast to a mass audience. The compound's internal image is of informing-at-breadth, which fits the modern newspaper advertisement and the broader infrastructure of public posting and circulation that emerged with Meiji print culture.
