The classical compound 広告 existed in literary Chinese in the bare sense 'to inform broadly,' but it had to be re-fitted in the Meiji period to the institutional sense of paid commercial publicity within a mass-media economy.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character used across the classical vocabulary of breadth (広大, 広野, 広範). Its decisive modern compound is 広告: from the 1870s onward Meiji daily newspapers — 横浜毎日新聞 (1871), 東京日日新聞 (1872), later Fukuzawa Yukichi's 時事新報 (1882) — adopted 広告 as the standing heading for paid notices, and the term passed from the newspaper masthead into Meiji commercial law and corporate practice. Re-exported to Chinese (廣告 / 广告 guǎnggào) and Korean (광고), it became the universal modern East Asian word for advertisement.

gloss: Thought that takes the form of its object — 相 (mutual aspect, countenance) above 心 (heart): the heart that takes on the shape of what it considers, image-thought and conception.

components.meaning: mutual, aspect, countenance — 木 (tree) beside 目 (eye): seeing and being seen, the form one shows; here the form thought takes on
heart-mind — the seat of awareness and intention, on which the form-aspect is impressed

graphic_evolution.form_description: 相 (mutual aspect / countenance) set above 心 (heart) — the heart taking on the aspect of an object
graphic_evolution.notes: The compositional logic is that of an image fixed in the heart: 相 supplies the form-aspect, 心 the cognitive seat. Thought, in this graphic theory of mind, is image-bearing — the heart receives the countenance of what it considers. This pictorial register is what gives Buddhist usages like 妄想 (delusory thought-image) and 観想 (contemplative visualization) their natural fit.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 相 (mutual aspect, 9 strokes) over 心 (heart, 4 strokes) — 13 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Senses cluster on the inner act of holding-an-image-in-mind: 思想 (thought, ideology), 想像 (imagination), 連想 (association of ideas), 空想 (fancy), 予想 (anticipation), and the verbal 想う (to think of, to picture). The 'image-thought' sense is what was joined to 理 (principle) to render the Western Ideal as 'principled image-thought.'

doctrinal_notes: In 理想 (ideal), 想 supplies the 'image / conception held in mind' that 理 ('principle') then dignifies as a rationally grounded standard. The compound reads as 'principled image' — a model of perfection figured in thought against which actual things are measured. The 想 element keeps the Western Ideal close to the imaginative-projective register (one envisions an ideal) and saves it from collapsing into the bare logical idea, which is instead carried by 観念 (Lockean / Kantian idea). The same 想 anchors the wider Meiji vocabulary of cognitive-imaginative life: 思想 (thought), 想像 (imagination), 連想 (association).
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character at home in classical and Buddhist Sino-Japanese (妄想, 観想, 思想). Its decisive modern career is in the Meiji compounds 理想 (ideal, stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii of 1881 and the literary criticism of Tsubouchi Shōyō's Shōsetsu Shinzui 1885–86), 思想 (thought, ideology), and 想像 (imagination), through which it became the lexical anchor of the Meiji vocabulary of inner life. The compounds passed into Chinese (xiǎng) and Korean (상).

gloss: The eye — pictograph of the organ of sight, originally drawn horizontally, later stood upright; from seeing come 'to look at, to mark,' and so 'aim, target, heading, item.' In 目的 the eye fixes upon its mark.

graphic_evolution.period: Oracle bone / bronze (甲骨文・金文)
graphic_evolution.form_description: A horizontal almond shape with a central pupil — a clearly drawn eye, sometimes with lashes
graphic_evolution.notes: The earliest graphs are an unmistakable pictograph of the eye laid on its side. The horizontal orientation persists into the bronze inscriptions; the later upright stand of the regular script is a calligraphic regularization, not a change of reference.

graphic_evolution.form_description: A vertical rectangle divided by two horizontal strokes — 5 strokes, classed under itself as a radical
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical and modern senses unfold from the eye: literal 'eye' (目, 眼), 'sight, looking' (注目), 'item, heading' (項目, 目次, 種目), 'mark / aim' (目標, 目当て), and the binding 'purpose / objective' (目的). The aim-and-target sense is what is paired with 的 to render Western purpose / Zweck.

doctrinal_notes: In 目的 (purpose, objective), 目 supplies the eye that fixes on a target, and 的 the bull's-eye on which it is fixed; the compound is the act of aiming itself, the eye-on-mark. The pictorial unity of the compound is what makes it carry both colloquial 'purpose' and the philosophically loaded German Zweck — in either case the meaning is 'that on which the eye is set.' The 'item / heading' sense surviving in 目次 (table of contents) and 項目 (an item) belongs to the same family: each heading is a separate point of attention, a place the eye is meant to rest.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character of the most basic stratum of literacy, present from the earliest Japanese use of Chinese script and pervasive across classical and modern vocabulary (項目, 目次, 注目, 目下). Its decisive modern compound is 目的, which Meiji philosophical and pedagogical writing standardized as the rendering of Western 'purpose / aim / Zweck' (Nishi Amane's lexica; the Tetsugaku Jii of 1881; Fukuzawa Yukichi's writings on the purpose of learning), and which then passed into Chinese (mùdì) and Korean (목적) as the universal modern word for purpose.

gloss: A clear mark — 白 (white, bright) beside 勺 (ladle, here phonetic): the white spot on a target, the bull's-eye; thence 'mark, target, distinct, accurate,' and the all-purpose adjectival suffix '-tic / -al.'

components.meaning: white, bright — the visible whiteness of the painted bull's-eye against the field of the target
ladle / small measure — here phonetic, with a residual sense of a small, concentrated point

graphic_evolution.form_description: 白 (white) beside 勺 (ladle, phonetic) — the white spot in the archery butt
graphic_evolution.notes: The original referent is the painted bull's-eye, the small white mark on the target at which the arrow is aimed. The senses 'clear, distinct, accurate, exactly so' (的中, 'hit the mark exactly') unfold from this concrete image.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 白 (white, 5 strokes) on the left, 勺 (ladle, 3 strokes) on the right — 8 strokes
graphic_evolution.notes: Classical senses cluster on the bull's-eye and accuracy: 的 (まと, target), 的中 (to hit the mark), 目的 (purpose, the marked aim). In Meiji and modern Japanese 的 also functions as an immensely productive adjectival suffix forming 〜的 ('-tic, -al, characterized by'), used to coin equivalents for European adjectives (科学的 scientific, 文化的 cultural, 主観的 subjective); this suffix-use later spread to Chinese (de / dì).

doctrinal_notes: In 目的 (purpose, objective), 的 supplies the bull's-eye on which 目 ('the eye') is fixed; the compound is the very picture of aiming. The same character does double duty in modern Sino-Japanese as the universal adjectival suffix: nearly every imported abstract noun is adjectivalized as 〜的, so 的 is also the principal grammatical instrument by which Western adjectives are housed in Japanese — 科学的 (scientific), 倫理的 (ethical), 客観的 (objective). This grammaticalization is itself a quiet reverse-flow event: a target-mark character pressed into service as a morpheme of conceptual qualification.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character used across the classical archery vocabulary (的, 的中). Its decisive modern life is twofold: as the second element of 目的 (purpose), standardized in Meiji philosophical and pedagogical writing; and as the highly productive adjectival suffix 〜的, by which Meiji translators rendered the suffix-machinery of European adjectives (-isch, -ique, -ical) and which became one of the most distinctive lexical resources of modern Sino-Japanese. The 〜的 suffix-use was re-exported to Chinese, where it appears (alongside the much older grammatical 的 de) as 〜的 in technical and academic writing.

gloss: The skilled way along the road — 朮 (a millet grain, phonetic) inside 行 (a crossroads/road): a learned technique, an acquired method, the cultivated craft as against the raw faculty.

components.meaning: the crossroads / road radical — a way that is travelled, supplying the sense of a path or course followed
a kind of millet (phonetic element); in the received analysis it lends the sound and combines with 行 to figure the trodden way

graphic_evolution.form_description: 朮 enclosed within 行 — the millet-element placed inside the crossroads/road radical
graphic_evolution.notes: Early glosses read 術 as a small road or alley within a settlement; from this concrete sense the character generalizes to a course of action, a method, a learned procedure, and from there to art, technique, craft, and stratagem. The character carries from its origins the sense of a way that has been traced and travelled rather than a raw or natural endowment.

graphic_evolution.form_description: Split form: 彳 on the left, 朮 in the middle, 亍 on the right — 11 strokes; the 行 radical 'opens' around the central element
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Sino-Japanese 術 is the workhorse suffix for the named arts and learned techniques: 美術 (fine arts), 芸術 (the arts in general), 武術 (martial arts), 技術 (technology / technique), 学術 (scholarship / academic learning), 算術 (arithmetic), 医術 (medicine as a healing craft), 魔術 (magic), 戦術 (tactics), 手術 (surgical operation). The kun reading すべ — 'a way / a means' — preserves the original road-as-method sense in vernacular Japanese (なすすべがない, 'there is no way to act').

doctrinal_notes: 術 is the character of the acquired procedure — the craft, method, or stratagem that one has been trained into, as distinguished from the natural faculty or the unstudied gift. In the Meiji disciplinary compounds 美術 (fine arts) and 芸術 (the arts), 術 supplies the 'art-as-trained-practice' that 美 or 芸 needs to become a domain rather than a value: the cultivated technique, the rule-governed craft, the discipline that the practitioner has been formed by. The same suffix-logic structures 技術 (technology), 学術 (scholarship), and 医術 (medicine), so that the Meiji vocabulary of the trained disciplines as a class is largely a vocabulary of compounds in 〜術.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character of the foundational stratum, present in Japanese literacy from the earliest period and carried in the classical vocabulary of the arts and methods (剣術, swordsmanship; 算術, arithmetic; 医術, healing). Its decisive modern role is the Meiji systematization of 〜術 as the standard suffix for the named arts, crafts, and trained techniques (美術 fine arts, 芸術 arts, 技術 technology, 学術 scholarship), a function that transferred with the Meiji disciplinary vocabulary into Chinese (shù) and Korean (sul) as the shared East Asian morpheme for the cultivated discipline.

gloss: Cultivation as art — the simplified form conflating 藝 (the planting of saplings, hand-tending of growth) with the older 芸 (a fragrant rue); in the modern character the agriculturalist's careful tending becomes the model of the artist's skilled cultivation.

components.meaning: grass radical — the vegetal sphere, the realm of cultivated growth that supplies the agricultural metaphor at the root of the character
in the postwar simplified form a phonetic-graphic substitute for the older 埶 (a kneeling figure tending a sapling) of traditional 藝; in 芸 it carries only the sound and the simplification

graphic_evolution.period: Oracle bone / bronze (甲骨文・金文) — traditional 藝
graphic_evolution.form_description: A kneeling human figure with hands extended, planting or tending a sapling (埶) beneath a grass element (艹), later with 云 added
graphic_evolution.notes: The traditional form 藝 figures art as horticulture: the careful, hand-tending cultivation of growth from a seedling. From this concrete agricultural sense (planting, tending, raising) the character extends to learned cultivation in general — the disciplined fostering of capacity, talent, and skill — and from there to the arts (六藝, the six arts of the Confucian curriculum). The cultivated-growth metaphor is the root from which all the later 'art' senses unfold.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 艹 (grass) over 云 — 7 strokes; the postwar Tōyō kanji reform of 1946 collapsed traditional 藝 into the much simpler 芸
graphic_evolution.notes: Postwar Japanese script reform conflated two originally distinct characters: 藝 (yì, art) and 芸 (yún, a fragrant rue used to ward insects from books — preserved in 芸香 ungō, the book-protecting rue, and the proper name 芸閣 'rue-pavilion' for a library). In modern Japanese 芸 carries the full weight of the older 藝 across the entire vocabulary of the arts: 芸術 (the arts), 芸能 (the performing arts and entertainment), 文芸 (literature and the arts), 工芸 (crafts), 武芸 (martial arts), 学芸 (arts and letters). The simplification erased the etymological richness of 藝's planting-figure but preserved the term's full semantic range. In mainland Chinese the parallel simplification yielded 艺.

doctrinal_notes: 芸 (traditional 藝) is the character of cultivated capacity: the original image is the gardener kneeling to plant a sapling, and the extended sense is any learned skill or art understood as growth fostered by careful tending. Confucian usage organized the cultivated arts under 六藝 (the six arts — ritual, music, archery, charioteering, calligraphy, mathematics), and the term has always carried the sense of a discipline that forms a person rather than an extra-personal technique. In the Meiji compound 芸術 (geijutsu, art) this cultivated-capacity sense is bound to 術 (trained procedure), yielding 'the trained arts' — the practiced cultivation of skilled production. The older 六藝 background is what distinguishes 芸 from the more technical 術 alone: 芸 names not just the procedure but the cultivated capacity in which the procedure is rooted.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character (in its traditional form 藝) present in Japanese literacy from the earliest stratum and carried across the classical vocabulary of the cultivated arts — 武藝 (martial arts), 文藝 (the literary arts), the Confucian 六藝. Its decisive modern role is the Meiji recoinage of 芸術 (geijutsu) to render the Western aesthetic concept of 'art' as a unified domain distinct from craft, technology, and entertainment, a usage stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and later academic-philosophical writing. The postwar Tōyō kanji reform (1946) collapsed traditional 藝 into the much simpler 芸, which is now the universal Japanese form across the whole arts-and-cultivation vocabulary; the same vocabulary entered Chinese (yìshù 艺术) and Korean (yesul 예술) as the shared modern East Asian word for art.

gloss: Passing through, succession in time — 止 (a foot) beneath a covered grove of grain stalks: the foot walking the rows of harvest, the steps that have been taken; the character of accumulated passage that, paired with 史, names history as that-through-which-one-has-gone.

components.meaning: the foot radical — a footprint, the trace of having walked; supplies the sense of passage, traversal, and the steps that have been taken
a grove of grain (秝, two 禾 'grain stalks' side by side) under a cliff/shelter (厂) — the field through which the foot passes; supplies the sequential, ordered character of the passage

graphic_evolution.form_description: 止 (foot) beneath 厤 (grain stalks under a shelter) — the foot walking through the rows of grain
graphic_evolution.notes: The original image is the foot moving through the ordered rows of a grain field — passage as the sequential traversal of an arrangement. From this concrete sense of stepwise walking through, the character generalizes to passing-through-time, succession, the experienced sequence, and the catalogue of what has occurred. The same root supplies the cognate 暦 (the calendar — time arranged in sequence), in which the same 厤 element is paired with 日 (day) to give the calendrical sense, while 歴 with 止 keeps the experiential 'walked-through' register.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 厂 (cliff) over 林 (forest, simplified from 秝 'twin grain stalks') over 止 (foot) — 14 strokes; the postwar Japanese simplification of traditional 歷 into 歴 (replacing 秝 with 林)
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Sino-Japanese 歴 carries the full sequential-passage range: 歴史 (history, the recorded succession of events), 歴代 (successive generations), 経歴 (curriculum vitae, the personal sequence of positions held), 学歴 (educational record), 職歴 (employment record), 来歴 (provenance, the sequence by which something has arrived where it is). The kun reading へる ('to pass through, to elapse') preserves the original walking-through sense, as in 年を経る (to pass through years).

doctrinal_notes: 歴's etymological hinge — the foot walking through an ordered sequence — distinguishes the character from the simply temporal: 歴 names the experienced traversal, the sequence-as-walked-through, not merely the flow of time. In the Meiji compound 歴史 (rekishi, history), 歴 supplies precisely this sense of accumulated passage that 史 (the scribe's record) is the writing-down of. The pair thus carries an implicit phenomenology: history is the sequence-walked-through (歴) as taken up into the chronicler's record (史) — a doctrinal weight that the European 'history' inherits from Greek ἱστορία (inquiry, eyewitness account) but that the Sino-Japanese compound carries through its own etymological resources.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character (in its traditional form 歷) present in Japanese literacy from the earliest stratum, carried across the classical vocabulary of succession (歷代 successive generations, 來歷 provenance). Its decisive modern role is the Meiji-period re-coinage of 歴史 to render history as a modern academic discipline (as against the older indigenous chronicle-genres like 国史 or 通鑑), with the compound stabilizing through Meiji historiography — Naka Michiyo's foundational works of 1888–1890s, the establishment of the Tokyo Imperial University history department in 1887, and the Tetsugaku Jii's lexicographic standardization — and transferring with that academic vocabulary into Chinese (lìshǐ) and Korean (역사). The postwar Japanese simplification of 歷 to 歴 (replacing 秝 with 林 in the upper element) is the current Japanese form.

gloss: The chronicler's hand holding the brush — a hand (又) grasping a tablet or writing-implement: the scribe-historian whose recording office stands at the origin of the character, and whose practice (history as written record) is the second element of the modern 歴史.

graphic_evolution.form_description: A hand (又) grasping an implement — traditionally read as a writing-brush, a tablet, or a censing-vessel held by the official scribe
graphic_evolution.notes: 史 in earliest usage is the title of an official: the 史官 (court scribe-historian) who recorded the king's actions, kept the calendar, and served as the ritual-bureaucratic memory of the state. The character thus names a person and an office before it names a genre or a discipline. The semantic shift from 'the scribe' to 'what the scribe writes' to 'history as a body of records' to 'history as the past itself' unfolds across the classical period, with each layer remaining legible in compounds.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 中 (a vertical with a square) over 又 (the hand) — 5 strokes; classified under the 口 radical in the traditional Kangxi system
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Sino-Japanese 史 names history across the full semantic spread: 歴史 (history as accumulated record), 史学 (the discipline of historical scholarship), 史料 (historical sources), 史実 (historical fact), 古代史 (ancient history), 日本史 (Japanese history), 世界史 (world history). The character also survives in titles of figures (太史公 the Grand Historian, Sima Qian's self-designation) and works (the 二十四史, the twenty-four standard dynastic histories of China). The rare kun reading ふひと (fuhito, 'scribe') preserves the original Yamato-court office of the imported continental scribe.

doctrinal_notes: 史 is the character of the chronicler before it is the character of the chronicle: at root it names the official whose work is the keeping of the record, and the entire East Asian tradition of historical writing — from the Spring and Autumn Annals through Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (史記) through the twenty-four standard dynastic histories — proceeds under the sign of this character. In the Meiji compound 歴史 (rekishi, history), 史 supplies the sense of 'that which has been written down by the chronicler,' the catalogued and preserved record, while 歴 supplies the lived sequential passage. The compound thus binds together the experienced succession (歴) and its scribal preservation (史) into the modern academic concept of history as the disciplined study of the recorded past.
japanese_transmission: A first-wave character of the foundational stratum, present in Japanese literacy from the earliest period — the Yamato court's institution of imported continental scribes (the 史 fuhito) is one of the earliest institutional vectors by which writing entered Japan, and the title itself carries through the Nara and Heian official systems. The character is centrally carried across the classical historiographical vocabulary (国史 national history, 正史 standard history, 史記 the Records of the Grand Historian) and through medieval and Edo historical writing. Its decisive modern role is the Meiji recoinage of 歴史 as the term for history as an academic discipline (a usage stabilized through the Tokyo Imperial University history department founded in 1887 and through Naka Michiyo's foundational historiographical work), with the compound transferring across East Asia into Chinese (lìshǐ) and Korean (역사) as the shared modern term.

gloss: Sorrow on the heart — the lower 心 placed under 非 (negation, what is contrary), naming the affective register in which the heart confronts what ought not to be; the standard Sino-Japanese character for the major register of sorrow, grief, and compassion across both Buddhist and modern aesthetic vocabularies.

components.meaning: negation, contrary, that-which-is-not-so (8 strokes) — phonetic element providing the bēi sound; also semantic in supplying the register of contradiction or violation that the heart below it suffers
heart, mind (4 strokes) — semantic element: the affective seat that registers the contrariety of 非 as sorrow

graphic_evolution.form_description: 非 above 心 — the figure of negation placed over the heart, the heart bearing the weight of what is contrary
graphic_evolution.notes: The classical sense of 悲 across Zhou and Han Chinese covers sorrow, grief, lamentation, and — in Buddhist translation — compassion. The character's semantic logic is precise: the heart (心) under the sign of negation (非) is the heart confronted with loss, contradiction, or what ought not to be. The compound 悲哀 (bēi'āi, sorrow and lament) pairs 悲 with 哀 (the older Zhou word for grief) and gives the standard classical register; the Buddhist appropriation in 慈悲 (cíbēi, loving-kindness and compassion) pairs 悲 with 慈 (loving-kindness) and gives the Mahāyāna register of compassion as suffering-with.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 12 strokes — 非 (8 strokes) above 心 (4 strokes); modern form preserves the classical structure
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 悲 covers the full sorrow-and-compassion register: 悲しみ (kanashimi, sorrow), 悲哀 (hiai, sorrow and lament), 悲嘆 (hitan, grief), 悲惨 (hisan, tragic / miserable), 慈悲 (jihi, compassion in the Buddhist sense), 悲劇 (higeki, tragedy as dramatic genre — the Meiji aesthetic coinage).

doctrinal_notes: 悲 carries two distinct doctrinal registers in modern Japanese. Its older and more philosophically loaded register is the Mahāyāna Buddhist sense of compassion, in the compound 慈悲 (jihi, Sanskrit maitrī-karuṇā) — the loving-kindness and compassion of the bodhisattva who suffers-with the suffering of all beings, the standard rendering of the Sanskrit karuṇā across the East Asian Buddhist tradition. Its modern aesthetic register is the Meiji compound 悲劇 (higeki, tragedy), in which 悲 contributes the affective category of sorrow that names the dramatic genre. The two registers are doctrinally distinct: Buddhist 悲 is an active practice of identification with suffering, while aesthetic 悲 is a category of represented affect. The same character carries both, and the polysemy is generally legible in context.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese literacy from the earliest stratum of Buddhist scriptural transmission. The standard Buddhist compound 慈悲 (jihi) arrives with the Nara-period transmission and remains the operating East Asian Buddhist term for compassion across all schools. The aesthetic-literary register of 悲 — sorrow as a category of literary and dramatic representation — is available across classical Japanese poetry (the kanashi register of waka and the Genji Monogatari's aware aesthetic), but its bounded modern sense as the affective category of a specific dramatic genre is a Meiji activation through 悲劇 (higeki, tragedy), stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and the broader Meiji translation of Western aesthetic-dramatic vocabulary.

gloss: Drama, intensity, violent activity — originally the figure of tiger and boar in violent struggle with a knife beside, naming intense or violent action; in modern Japanese the standard character for drama as a represented performance, and the head element of the genre-compounds 悲劇 (tragedy) and 喜劇 (comedy).

components.meaning: the violent struggle of beasts (13 strokes) — composite of 虍 (tiger) over 豕 (boar), naming intense or violent action; phonetic-semantic element providing both the jù sound and the semantic register of vehement activity
knife radical (2 strokes — the right-side variant of 刀) — semantic element: the blade beside the violent struggle, marking the cutting-edge register of intense or decisive action

graphic_evolution.form_description: 豦 (tiger over boar in struggle) beside 刂 (knife) — the figure of violent or intense activity, the struggle of beasts beside the cutting blade
graphic_evolution.notes: The classical sense of 劇 in Zhou and Han Chinese covers intensity, violence, vehement activity, and severe difficulty. The compound 劇務 (jùwù) names heavy or pressing duties; 劇烈 (jùliè) names violent or extreme intensity. The semantic transition from intense activity to dramatic performance is medieval: by the Tang and Song the character extends to name the represented dramatic spectacle (戯劇, the playful intensity of staged drama), and from this register the modern East Asian theatrical vocabulary develops.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 15 strokes — 豦 (13 strokes) on the left beside 刂 (2 strokes) on the right
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 劇 covers two distinct semantic registers. As 'drama / staged performance' it heads the modern theatrical vocabulary: 演劇 (engeki, theatre / drama as cultural form), 劇場 (gekijō, theatre as venue), 劇団 (gekidan, theatrical company), 劇作家 (gekisakka, playwright), and the genre-compounds 悲劇 (higeki, tragedy) and 喜劇 (kigeki, comedy). As 'intense / extreme' it preserves the classical register: 劇薬 (gekiyaku, potent drug), 劇的 (gekiteki, dramatic in the intensity-register), 劇務 (gekimu, heavy duties).

doctrinal_notes: In 悲劇 (higeki, tragedy) and 喜劇 (kigeki, comedy), 劇 carries the bounded modern sense of 'drama as represented genre' — the Western theatrical category of the staged play with its bounded dramatic action, its named genres (tragedy, comedy, tragicomedy), and its institutional theatrical apparatus. The classical East Asian theatrical tradition had its own genre-vocabulary (the no 能 with its waki-shite-tsure roles, the kabuki 歌舞伎 with its jōruri and dance-drama categories, the Chinese xiqu 戯曲 tradition with its operatic forms), but the Western tragedy / comedy distinction is not native to these traditions and required the Meiji coinage of the two compounds to render the Western genre-pair. 劇 supplies the head element 'drama as represented action,' and the affective qualifiers 悲 and 喜 supply the genre-specifying registers. The structural symmetry of the two compounds — 悲劇 / 喜劇, dramas of sorrow / dramas of joy — is precisely calibrated to render the Western genre-distinction in compact Sino-Japanese form.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in classical Japanese literate culture in its classical-Chinese register of intense or vehement activity, available across Heian and medieval Japanese learned vocabulary. Its modern theatrical register — 劇 as drama-as-staged-performance — is a late development through the Tokugawa-period reception of Chinese vernacular drama (the influence of Ming and Qing xiqu on early Japanese theatrical writing) and decisively a Meiji activation through the translation of Western dramatic vocabulary: 演劇 (engeki) as the modern operating term for theatre as a Western-style cultural form, 悲劇 and 喜劇 as the genre-categories, 劇場 as the theatre venue, and the broader Meiji theatrical apparatus (the Shinpa and Shingeki theatrical movements of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the establishment of Western-style theatres including the Imperial Theatre 帝国劇場 in 1911). The Meiji theatrical vocabulary transferred into Chinese (jù 剧) and Korean (geuk 극) as the shared modern East Asian theatre-vocabulary.

gloss: Joy, gladness — originally the figure of a ceremonial drum (壴) over a mouth (口), naming the joyful sound of celebration; the standard Sino-Japanese character for happiness and gladness, and the genre-marking element of 喜劇 (comedy).

components.meaning: drum on a stand (9 strokes) — semantic element: the ceremonial drum that gives voice to celebration; pictographic ancestor preserving the festive-musical register of the character
mouth (3 strokes) — semantic element: the open mouth of celebration, the voice raised in joy below the drum that accompanies it

graphic_evolution.form_description: A drum on a stand (壴) above an open mouth (口) — the figure of the celebratory drum and the joyful voice raised together
graphic_evolution.notes: The character's original sense is the celebration of joy through music and voice: the drum strikes, the mouth opens in song, the gathering rejoices. Across classical Chinese 喜 covers joy, gladness, delight, and — in compound — congratulation and felicity. The compound 歓喜 (huānxǐ, great joy) intensifies the register; 喜悦 (xǐyuè, joyful delight) pairs 喜 with 悦 (delight) for the aesthetic-affective sense; 喜事 (xǐshì) names auspicious matters and especially weddings.

graphic_evolution.form_description: 12 strokes — 壴 (drum-on-stand, 9 strokes) above 口 (mouth, 3 strokes)
graphic_evolution.notes: Modern Japanese 喜 covers the full joy register: 喜び (yorokobi, joy as nominal), 歓喜 (kanki, great joy), 喜悦 (kietsu, joyful delight), 喜怒哀楽 (kidoairaku, joy-anger-sorrow-pleasure, the four emotions), 喜寿 (kiju, the 77th-birthday celebration), 喜劇 (kigeki, comedy as dramatic genre — the Meiji aesthetic coinage).

doctrinal_notes: In 喜劇 (kigeki, comedy), 喜 contributes the affective category of joy that names the dramatic genre, paralleling 悲 in 悲劇 (tragedy). The pair 喜 / 悲 supplies a precise Sino-Japanese rendering of the Western joy-and-sorrow distinction that structures the European genre-pair of comedy and tragedy. The classical Confucian register of 喜怒哀楽 (joy-anger-sorrow-pleasure) had long supplied the canonical taxonomy of the four affects in East Asian moral psychology — the Doctrine of the Mean (中庸) uses 喜怒哀楽 as the four emotions whose pre-arising state constitutes the centered equilibrium (中) — and the Meiji deployment of 喜 and 悲 in the genre-vocabulary draws on this classical affective taxonomy while bounding the affects to the specific aesthetic-dramatic register required by the Western genre-distinction.
japanese_transmission: First-wave character, present in Japanese literacy from the earliest stratum of classical Chinese learning. The native Japanese verb よろこ.ぶ (yorokobu, to rejoice) is mapped onto the character in the earliest stratum, and the joy register is available across all classical and medieval Japanese usage. The character's role in the modern theatrical vocabulary — as the genre-marker of 喜劇 (kigeki, comedy) — is a Meiji activation through the translation of Western dramatic-aesthetic vocabulary, stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and the broader Meiji project of rendering the Western theatrical genre-categories in Sino-Japanese form. The Meiji compound 喜劇 transferred into Chinese (xǐjù 喜剧) and Korean (heegeuk 희극) as the shared modern East Asian word for comedy.
